lessons.plain: A content delivery network, or CDN, is a set of servers spread around the world that keep copies of your files close to the people who ask for them. Amazon CloudFront is AWS's CDN. Instead of every user on another continent travelling back to your one server, a nearby copy answers. Designing with it means deciding what to keep in those copies, how long to keep them, where the original files live, and how to stop people from skipping the nearby copies and hitting your server directly. Each choice trades speed against freshness, protection, and cost.
lessons.guessPrompt: A website has users in Sydney, but its only server is in Virginia. Before any teaching, what would you expect to happen to page load time if the images were also kept in a location near Sydney, and what would worry you if those images changed?
lessons.teach:
An origin is the server or storage bucket that holds the original copy of your content. An edge location is a site near users where a copy can be kept. A cache is that stored copy. A cache hit happens when the edge already has a copy and answers without asking the origin. A cache miss happens when it has to fetch from the origin. The TTL, or time to live, is how long a stored copy may be reused before it expires. The cache key is the set of parts of a request, such as the address and sometimes query strings or headers, that decide whether two requests can share one stored copy.

This works because most users ask for the same files. Serving repeats from a nearby copy cuts latency and protects the origin from load.

Worked example: a file logo.png has a TTL of 24 hours. Step 1: a user in Sydney requests it. The Sydney edge has no copy, so it is a miss. The edge fetches the file from Virginia, keeps it for 24 hours, and returns it. Step 2: another Sydney user asks an hour later. The edge has a copy, so it is a hit and answers locally. Step 3: after 24 hours the copy expires, and the next request goes back to the origin.

Common mistake: a long TTL on a file whose contents change under the same name. Users keep seeing the old version until expiry. The fix is to give each release new file names, and to use invalidation only as a fallback. A second mistake is leaving the origin open to the public, so people bypass the distribution and its protections. Restrict the origin so it accepts requests only from the distribution.

Consequence: during a traffic surge, a high hit ratio shields the origin. If cookies or query strings split the cache key, the hit ratio collapses and nearly every request reaches the origin.

questions.prompt: Lumen Tours serves product thumbnails from an origin in Frankfurt through a CloudFront distribution. The file thumb-204.jpg has a TTL of 6 hours. Step 1: a user in Lisbon requests it. The Lisbon edge has no copy, so this is a miss. The edge fetches the file from Frankfurt, keeps it for 6 hours, and returns it. Step 2: a second Lisbon user asks 2 hours later. The edge still has a copy, so this is a hit and the edge answers locally. Step 3 is left for you: a user asks for the same file 7 hours after step 1. What happens?
choices: The edge answers from its old copy, since it already holds one.
The edge refuses the request until someone manually restores the file.
The edge fetches a fresh copy from Frankfurt, because the TTL has run out.
Every user goes to Frankfurt, because a miss is permanent once a file was cached.
questions.why: The TTL of 6 hours has expired by 7 hours, so the stored copy can no longer be reused and the edge must fetch a new one from the origin.

questions.prompt: A news site's CloudFront distribution includes a query parameter named src in its cache key. The URLs /story/88?src=email and /story/88?src=social return identical content, yet the hit ratio is low. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The TTL is set to zero, so no copy is ever kept at the edge.
The edge ignores query strings, so it fetches every page from the origin.
Each src value gets its own stored copy, so the two URLs cannot share one copy and each first request is a miss.
The origin is too slow to answer, so the edge gives up early.
questions.why: Because src is part of the cache key, two different values produce two different keys, so each variant must be fetched from the origin once before it can be served from cache.

questions.prompt: A team's origin is an object storage bucket. Users can fetch files directly from the bucket's own address, skipping the CloudFront distribution and its protections. Which change closes this gap?
choices: Shorten every TTL to one minute so copies expire quickly.
Rename the bucket with each release so its address changes.
Restrict the bucket so it accepts requests only from the distribution.
Add more edge locations near the bucket's region.
questions.why: Limiting the origin to accept requests only from the distribution forces every visitor through the distribution, which is the only way the protections apply.

questions.prompt: A ticketing site sends 10,000 requests per minute through a distribution with a 90% hit ratio, so the origin sees 1,000 requests per minute. A surge makes total traffic 10 times larger, to 100,000 requests per minute, and the hit ratio stays at 90%. Then a new cookie is added to the cache key and the hit ratio falls to 10%, while total traffic stays at 100,000 per minute. How many requests per minute now reach the origin?
choices: 10,000 requests per minute
1,000 requests per minute
100,000 requests per minute
90,000 requests per minute
questions.why: With a 10% hit ratio, 90% of the 100,000 requests miss the cache and reach the origin, which is 90,000 per minute.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a CloudFront distribution with a long cache lifetime can keep serving old content after a deploy, what you would change in the design to prevent it, and what that change costs.
lessons.modelAnswer: Caching works by reusing a stored copy until its TTL runs out. If a file keeps the same name and has a long TTL, edge locations keep serving the old copy after the origin has been updated, so users see stale content until expiry. The usual fix is to version the file names, so each release produces new names that cannot match old cached copies, and to keep TTLs long on those versioned assets. Invalidation can clear copies on demand, but it is slower and often charged, so it is a fallback rather than the main plan. The cost of versioning is that the deploy process must rewrite references to the new names, and HTML pages themselves need short TTLs so users find the new names quickly.
rubricPoints: Explains that a stored copy at the edge is reused until its TTL expires, so updates can be hidden
Describes versioned file names as the main way to make a change visible
Notes that invalidation is a slower or costlier fallback
States the tradeoff: deploy tooling and short TTLs on pages are needed

suggested.rationale: Choosing caching and origin protection for a distribution is a design judgment best checked by explaining the tradeoff back, and no listed mission covers CDN design.

lessons.plain: When your users are spread across the world, the internet route between them and your servers can be slow or fragile. AWS Global Accelerator gives your application two fixed IP addresses that work everywhere. A user's traffic enters AWS at the nearest point of presence, which is an AWS site close to the user, and then rides AWS's own private network to your servers in whichever Region is healthy and closest. Think of it as a fixed front door in every city, with a fast private corridor behind it, so you can move or fail over the servers behind the door without asking users to change anything.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your users are in Sydney and Paris, and your application runs in two AWS Regions. If a Paris user's connection goes through the public internet and the Paris Region fails, what would make it slow or hard to move that user to the backup Region, and what would you change to fix it?
lessons.teach:
Global Accelerator is a global traffic-management service. It gives you two static anycast IP addresses. Anycast means the same address is announced from many places at once, so the internet delivers a user's packets to the nearest AWS edge location, which is a point of presence close to that user. A listener is the port and protocol (TCP or UDP) you accept traffic on. An endpoint is a resource that receives traffic, such as an Application Load Balancer, a Network Load Balancer, or an EC2 instance. An endpoint group collects the endpoints in one Region. Each endpoint group has a traffic dial, a percentage from 0 to 100 that sets how much traffic that Region may receive. Health checks probe each endpoint, and unhealthy endpoints are taken out of rotation.

Why it works: the client keeps the same IP address, so no DNS cache has to expire before failover happens. Health checks and routing decisions are made inside AWS, and the path from the edge to the Region uses the AWS network instead of the public internet.

Worked example: a booking API runs in Frankfurt and Virginia. The listener is TCP 443, and each Region is an endpoint group with its dial at 100. Step 1: a user in Berlin connects to the static IP, which lands at the Frankfurt edge. Step 2: the accelerator sees the Frankfurt group is healthy and closest, and sends traffic over the AWS network to the Frankfurt load balancer. Step 3: the Frankfurt load balancer begins failing its health checks. Step 4: the Frankfurt endpoint is marked unhealthy and the Virginia group takes the traffic. The user keeps the same IP address throughout.

Common mistake: treating a traffic dial as a health check. Setting a dial to 0 stops traffic on purpose, but it does not detect a failure. Another mistake is expecting Global Accelerator to cache web content; it does not, and content caching is the job of CloudFront.

Consequence in a running system: if every endpoint in every group is unhealthy, the accelerator has nowhere to send traffic, so health checks must test what working actually means for your application.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company runs a seat-booking service in Tokyo and Sydney. Its accelerator has a UDP listener on port 4433, each Region is an endpoint group with its traffic dial at 100, and the endpoints are Network Load Balancers. Trace one request. Step 1: a user in Osaka sends UDP packets to one of the accelerator's static anycast IP addresses, and they arrive at the nearest edge location, which is in Tokyo. Step 2: the accelerator sees the Tokyo group as healthy and sends the traffic over the AWS network to the Tokyo Network Load Balancer. Step 3: the team sets the Tokyo group's traffic dial to 0 for planned maintenance. Step 4 is missing from this trace. Which statement correctly fills it in?
choices: The accelerator deletes the Tokyo Network Load Balancer, so Osaka traffic is dropped until someone recreates it.
The Tokyo endpoints are marked unhealthy by the dial change, and the Osaka user is moved to a new Sydney IP address.
The Osaka user keeps the Tokyo address and Tokyo keeps receiving traffic, because a dial only changes health checks.
New Osaka traffic goes to Sydney, and Tokyo keeps its health status, since the dial stopped traffic on purpose.
questions.why: A dial of 0 stops traffic to that Region deliberately without detecting any fault, so the Tokyo endpoints keep their health status and new traffic moves to the Sydney group while the user's static IP stays the same.

questions.prompt: What does anycast mean for the static IP addresses that Global Accelerator gives you?
choices: The address is cached by the local DNS resolver for a fixed time before it can change.
The same address is announced from many places, so the internet routes packets to the nearest edge location.
Each user is given a different address based on their country, which is refreshed by DNS.
The address is attached to one load balancer, and traffic bypasses the edge when that balancer is busy.
questions.why: Anycast means one address is announced from many places at once, so internet routing delivers each user's packets to the nearest AWS edge location.

questions.prompt: A team's accelerator has two endpoint groups, and every endpoint in both groups is failing its health checks. What happens to a new request, and what does this imply for the health checks?
choices: It is sent to a new Region the accelerator creates on demand, so health checks only matter for cost.
It ignores the health checks and goes to the group with the highest dial value.
It has no healthy destination, so the health checks must test whether the application truly works.
It is served from a cached copy of the last good response, so health checks do not matter.
questions.why: Unhealthy endpoints are taken out of rotation, so with none healthy the accelerator has nowhere to send traffic, which means health checks must reflect real application success.

questions.prompt: A team puts Global Accelerator in front of a product image site and expects it to store copies of images near users so the origin receives fewer requests. What is the flaw in this plan?
choices: Global Accelerator does not cache web content; that job belongs to a content delivery service such as CloudFront.
Global Accelerator caches content only for TCP listeners, so UDP images are never stored.
Global Accelerator keeps images only for the length of the health check interval, which is too short to help.
Global Accelerator needs one endpoint group per image, and the team has not created those groups.
questions.why: Global Accelerator routes traffic and does not cache content, so reducing origin requests through caching requires a service built for that purpose.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose Global Accelerator over Route 53 DNS-based failover for a TCP application, and name one limit of Global Accelerator that you would have to design around.
lessons.modelAnswer: Global Accelerator fits a TCP or UDP application when clients may cache DNS answers, or when customers need fixed IP addresses they can allowlist. Its two static anycast IPs mean failover does not wait for a DNS TTL, the time clients are allowed to cache an answer, to expire, and health checks can move traffic between Regions within seconds. Route 53 DNS-based failover is the better choice when the workload is HTTP content that benefits from caching, or when you need name-based routing rules that the client resolves itself. A limit to design around is that Global Accelerator does not cache content and does not inspect HTTP paths, so any path-based routing has to live in the load balancer behind it. Also, the traffic dials and weights are manual controls, so a wrong value sends traffic somewhere unintended, and changes need review and monitoring.
rubricPoints: Explains that static anycast IPs avoid waiting on DNS TTL during failover
Compares the case for Global Accelerator with the case for Route 53 DNS failover
Names a real limit, such as no content caching or no HTTP path inspection
Notes that traffic dials and weights are manual controls that need careful change

suggested.rationale: Choosing between Global Accelerator, CloudFront, and Route 53 under stated latency and failover constraints is best practised as an exam-style scenario.

lessons.plain: An edge service is infrastructure that sits at the outer boundary of your system, close to the people using it, and decides what traffic gets in before requests reach your core servers. Integrating edge services with load balancers and API gateways means chaining them so each piece does one job: the edge handles nearby encryption, caching and filtering, the load balancer spreads traffic across healthy servers, and the API gateway checks and routes individual API calls. The design question is where each job belongs, and how to stop callers from skipping the edge and reaching the servers directly.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your API runs behind a load balancer in one Region, and users on another continent report slow first requests. Before any teaching, what would you place in front of the load balancer to shorten their trip, and what could a user still do that you would not want them to do?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. An edge service runs at points of presence spread around the world, so a user's first hop lands nearby. Amazon CloudFront is a content delivery network (CDN): it caches responses and terminates TLS, meaning it ends the encrypted connection, at those points. An origin is the backend CloudFront fetches from on a cache miss, such as a load balancer or an API gateway. Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) distributes requests across targets. Amazon API Gateway accepts API calls, applies authorization and rate limits, and forwards them to a backend. A web application firewall (WAF) inspects requests against rules.

Why it works. Each layer answers a different question. The edge asks how far the user is and whether it can answer without bothering the origin. The load balancer asks which healthy server should take this request. The API gateway asks whether this caller may make this call and how often. Chaining them keeps each component simple and lets the edge absorb traffic the origin never sees.

Worked example. A client requests an API path. First, DNS sends the client to the nearest edge location. Second, the edge terminates TLS with a certificate and checks WAF rules. Third, with no cached copy, it forwards the request to the origin load balancer. Fourth, the load balancer picks a healthy target, which returns the response. Fifth, the edge stores the response if its cache rules allow it.

Common mistake. Leaving the load balancer or API gateway publicly reachable, so clients skip the edge and its WAF. The fix is to accept traffic only from the edge, for example by restricting the origin's security group to the edge provider's published address ranges, which AWS publishes as a managed prefix list, and by checking a secret header the edge adds.

Consequence. Timeouts must line up. If the edge gives up after 30 seconds but the load balancer keeps idle connections open for 60, a slow call can fail at the edge with a 504 while the backend is still working. Matching or ordering these timers is part of the design.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company serves seat maps through an edge service in front of an API gateway, which forwards to an internal load balancer. A client requests the seat map for event 884. Step 1: DNS sends the client to the nearest edge location. Step 2: the edge terminates TLS and checks WAF rules, and because the seat map response is marked no-store, the edge does not look for a cached copy and forwards the request to the API gateway. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the API gateway forwards the approved call to the load balancer. Step 5: the load balancer picks a healthy target, which returns the seat map. Which statement best fills the missing step 3?
choices: The edge stores the seat map in its cache anyway, so the next client gets it without contacting the origin.
The API gateway checks that the caller may make this call and that they are within their rate limit before it forwards the request.
DNS is asked again to send the request straight to the load balancer, so the edge and the gateway are skipped.
The load balancer checks the caller's authorization and rate limit before the call reaches the API gateway.
questions.why: The API gateway is the layer that asks whether this caller may make this call and how often, so it performs that check before forwarding, and the other options either put the check in the wrong layer or skip a layer the design depends on.

questions.prompt: In a chain of an edge service, a load balancer and an API gateway, which layer answers the question whether this caller may make this call and how often?
choices: The API gateway, because it applies authorization and rate limits before forwarding.
The edge service, because it runs at points of presence close to the user.
The load balancer, because it chooses which healthy server takes the request.
The web application firewall alone, because it inspects requests against rules.
questions.why: The teaching text assigns authorization and rate limiting to the API gateway, while the edge handles distance and caching, and the load balancer handles choosing a healthy target.

questions.prompt: A team puts a load balancer behind an edge service with a WAF, but the load balancer's security group allows inbound traffic from anywhere on the internet. An attacker discovers the load balancer's address and sends requests that skip the edge and its WAF. Which change best addresses this common mistake?
choices: Move the load balancer to a different Region so the attacker's address is no longer valid.
Restrict the origin's security group to the edge provider's published address ranges and check a secret header the edge adds.
Increase the load balancer's idle timeout so that attacker connections are closed more slowly.
Turn off caching at the edge so that every request reaches the load balancer and is inspected there.
questions.why: Restricting the origin to the edge provider's published ranges and checking a header the edge adds makes the origin accept traffic only from the edge, which is the fix the teaching text describes.

questions.prompt: An edge service gives up on the origin after 20 seconds and returns a 504 error. The load balancer behind it keeps idle connections open for 45 seconds. A legitimate report request usually takes 25 seconds at the backend, so clients see 504 errors even though the backend finishes the work. What is the best design change?
choices: Lower the load balancer's idle timeout to 20 seconds so that both timers match the edge.
Store the report response in the edge cache so that the backend only has to finish it once.
Add more WAF rules so that slow requests are blocked earlier and never reach the backend.
Raise the edge's origin timeout above the slowest legitimate call, so the edge waits for the backend's answer.
questions.why: The edge gives up before the backend finishes, so the edge's timeout must exceed the realistic worst-case backend time; lowering the load balancer's timer, adding WAF rules, or caching a slow dynamic report does not fix the mismatch.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would place CloudFront, a load balancer and API Gateway in front of a regional API, and name one limit or tradeoff of putting an edge service in front of it.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would put CloudFront first, since it terminates TLS close to users and can cache safe responses and run WAF rules. Behind it sits the origin, either an Application Load Balancer for a web or service path or API Gateway for the API path, depending on whether I need API-level authorization and throttling. The origin should only accept traffic from CloudFront, so I would restrict its security group to CloudFront's published address ranges and check a secret header the edge adds. The main tradeoff is caching: cached responses can be stale, so anything user-specific or frequently changing needs careful cache keys or no caching at all. There is also an added hop, so the timeouts at each layer need to be set so the edge does not give up before the origin finishes.
rubricPoints: Names the edge layer's job: closer TLS termination, caching and WAF filtering
Explains that the load balancer or API gateway should only accept traffic from the edge
Identifies caching staleness or cache-key design as a real tradeoff
Notes that timeouts must line up across edge and origin to avoid spurious 504s

suggested.rationale: A scenario where the learner must choose the chain and spot the bypass and timeout failures adds more than reading alone, and no listed mission or planned engine covers this topic directly.

lessons.plain: When people around the world use an app, their requests travel to your servers and the answers travel back. This objective is about choosing how that traffic enters your network and how your systems send traffic out to the internet. Inbound traffic comes in from users or other systems; outbound traffic is what your systems send to places outside your network, such as a payment provider or a software update server. Some services hold copies of content close to users, some carry traffic onto a fast private path across the provider's network, and some sit between your servers and the internet to control and bill what leaves. The skill is matching each service to the kind of traffic, the speed you need, and the cost.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app serves the same product images to shoppers in Tokyo and Sao Paulo, and the images rarely change. Would you rather serve them from one server in one Region, or keep copies near each shopper? Say why in a sentence.
lessons.teach: Inbound traffic is traffic that comes from users or other systems into your application. Outbound traffic is traffic your systems send to destinations outside your network. A distribution solution is the service that decides where inbound traffic enters and how it travels. Three ideas do most of the work. A point of presence (PoP) is a site run by the cloud provider close to end users, where connections can be terminated and copies of content kept. Caching means keeping a copy of a response at a PoP so later requests are answered there without going back to the origin, which is the server holding the original. Anycast means one IP address is announced from many places, so each user's traffic reaches the nearest one. Amazon CloudFront is a content delivery network that caches HTTP and HTTPS responses at its PoPs and fetches from your origin only on a cache miss. AWS Global Accelerator gives you two static anycast IP addresses, carries TCP and UDP traffic from the nearest edge onto the provider's backbone, and routes to healthy endpoints; it does not cache. Amazon Route 53 answers DNS queries, so it chooses which address a user is sent to, but it does not carry the traffic itself. Worked example: a shopper in Tokyo requests a product image through a CloudFront domain. DNS resolves that domain to a Tokyo PoP. The first request is a cache miss, so the PoP fetches the image from the origin in Virginia and stores the copy. The next several thousand requests for that image are answered in Tokyo. Common mistake: putting Global Accelerator in front of cacheable content, so every request travels to the origin and you pay for the full trip. Consequence: when many cached copies expire together or a deploy changes every URL at once, the origin receives the full load in one moment. For outbound traffic, private subnets usually reach the internet through a NAT gateway in each zone, which bills per gigabyte processed, so organisations often send egress through one shared, monitored path. Choose by traffic type, cacheability, and cost.

questions.prompt: A studio in Lagos distributes large game installers from an origin server in Ohio through a CloudFront domain. Trace the flow. Step 1: a player in Lagos requests installer.example-games.net. Step 2: DNS resolves that domain to the Johannesburg PoP, the nearest one to Lagos. Step 3: the first request is a cache miss, so the Johannesburg PoP fetches the installer from the Ohio origin. Step 4: [missing step]. Step 5: a second player in Lagos requests the same installer and is answered from Johannesburg without contacting Ohio. What belongs in step 4?
choices: Route 53 re-resolves the domain to the Ohio origin so the next request skips the PoP.
The Johannesburg PoP forwards every later request to Ohio to confirm the copy is current.
The Johannesburg PoP keeps a copy of the installer response so later requests for it are answered locally.
The Ohio origin sends the installer straight to the player in Lagos, bypassing the PoP.
questions.why: Caching is the step where the PoP keeps a copy of the response, which is why the second request can be answered in Johannesburg without reaching the origin.

questions.prompt: A trading firm runs a TCP-based order API in two Regions and needs clients to reach the healthy Region quickly and keep long-lived connections stable during failover. Which distribution solution fits best, and why?
choices: Amazon CloudFront, because it caches the API responses at PoPs close to traders.
Amazon Route 53 alone, because DNS answers choose the Region and carry the connections themselves.
AWS Global Accelerator, because it gives static anycast addresses, carries TCP from the nearest edge onto the provider backbone, and routes to healthy endpoints.
A NAT gateway in each zone, because it handles outbound traffic and can also accept inbound TCP connections.
questions.why: Global Accelerator suits non-cacheable TCP and UDP traffic that needs healthy-endpoint routing, which is what the scenario describes.

questions.prompt: A retailer puts AWS Global Accelerator in front of a product catalogue made of cacheable JSON pages that change once a day. What is the main problem with this design?
choices: Nothing is wrong, because Route 53 and Global Accelerator both cache responses at PoPs.
Every request still reaches the origin, because Global Accelerator does not cache.
Global Accelerator will cache the catalogue at its edges, so the origin is contacted too rarely and prices may go stale.
Global Accelerator only accepts UDP, so the HTTP catalogue cannot pass through it at all.
questions.why: Global Accelerator carries traffic without caching, so cacheable content pays the full trip to the origin; a caching CDN such as CloudFront fits this case better.

questions.prompt: A media company streams live video and wants viewers to be sent to a nearby edge. A colleague says Route 53 will carry the video packets from the edge to the origin. Which statement is correct?
choices: Route 53 only answers DNS queries to choose which address a viewer is sent to; it does not carry the stream itself.
Route 53 caches each video segment at PoPs after the first viewer requests it.
Route 53 announces one IP address from many places, making it a complete anycast transport for video.
Route 53 carries the video packets from the nearest PoP to the origin, so it is the right transport for streaming.
questions.why: Route 53 is a DNS service that decides which address a user is sent to, but it does not carry the traffic, so the statement about carrying packets is wrong.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between CloudFront, Global Accelerator and Route 53 for a new public API and a product image catalogue, and name one limit or tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: The first thing I check is whether the traffic is cacheable HTTP or something else. If it is, CloudFront is the natural choice: it serves copies from edge locations, which cuts latency and origin load, but the tradeoff is staleness, because copies live until their time-to-live expires, and a bad cache rule can serve the wrong content to many users at once. If the traffic is TCP or UDP, or the client needs fixed IP addresses to allow-list, Global Accelerator fits better: it gives two static anycast addresses and fails over between healthy endpoints, but it adds no caching, so the origin still does all the work, and it carries its own hourly and data charges. Route 53 is a separate decision: it chooses a destination, not the path. For outbound traffic, I would centralise NAT or egress so the per-gigabyte cost and the logging live in one place, accepting that the shared path then becomes a dependency for every account.
rubricPoints: Separates inbound traffic from outbound traffic and names a suitable service family for each.
Chooses CloudFront for cacheable HTTP or HTTPS content and states the staleness tradeoff.
Chooses Global Accelerator for TCP or UDP traffic, static IP needs or fast failover, and notes that it does not cache.
Explains that Route 53 steers DNS answers rather than carrying traffic, and notes per-gigabyte cost for outbound egress.

suggested.rationale: Choosing among distribution services for a given traffic pattern is best practised as an exam-style scenario, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it directly.

lessons.plain: The Domain Name System, or DNS, is the phone book of the internet. People type names like shop.example.com, and DNS answers with the numeric address a computer needs to connect. Each answer carries a time limit saying how long it may be remembered before asking again. Records are the individual entries; zones are the parts of the name tree that one set of servers answers for; delegation hands a piece of that tree to someone else; DNSSEC adds signatures so answers can be checked as genuine. Knowing these four ideas lets you predict what users will actually see after you change something.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you change the address that a website name points to, why might some users still reach the old server an hour later, and what would you check first?
lessons.teach:
A DNS record is one stored answer for a name, tagged with a type. The common types are A (name to an IPv4 address), AAAA (name to an IPv6 address), CNAME (the name is an alias for another name), NS (which servers answer for a zone), MX (mail servers) and TXT (free text, often used to prove domain ownership). A zone is a portion of the name tree that one set of authoritative servers answers for. Delegation is the act of a parent zone naming the servers that run a child zone, recorded as NS records in the parent. TTL, time to live, is the number of seconds a resolver may keep an answer in its cache before asking again. DNSSEC, the DNS Security Extensions, attaches digital signatures to records so a validating resolver can confirm the answer came from the zone owner and was not altered. The signatures form a chain from the root down through each delegation, with each parent vouching for its child's signing key.

Why it works: a resolver starts at the root, follows delegations down the tree, and caches what it learns for the TTL. Caching makes DNS fast and cheap, and it is also why changes are never instant.

Worked example: a record maps www.shop.example to 203.0.113.10 with a TTL of 300 seconds. A client resolves it at 09:00 and caches it until 09:05. At 09:01 the owner changes the record to 198.51.100.7. Clients that cached the old answer keep using 203.0.113.10 until 09:05. A client that asks at 09:06 receives the new address. The worst-case delay for a change equals the old TTL.

Common mistake: lowering the TTL on the same day you need a change. Every resolver still holds the old answer for the old TTL, so the lower value helps only after that window has passed. Lower it well in advance.

Consequence in a running system: a failover that changes an address keeps sending some users to a dead server for as long as the old TTL, and a broken DNSSEC signature can make validating resolvers refuse the answer, so users see errors even though the servers are healthy. A change reaches users only after the old answer's time limit has expired everywhere.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Foods uses a TTL of 1800 seconds on api.brightwater.example. A resolver fetched the record 600 seconds before the owner changes the address. Worked steps: Step 1: the full cache lifetime of the old answer is 1800 seconds. Step 2: the resolver fetched the answer 600 seconds before the change. Step 3 is left out here: work out how much of that cache lifetime remains at the moment of the change. Step 4: the resolver keeps the old address until that remaining time runs out. Which choice correctly fills in step 3?
choices: 600 seconds, the age of the cached answer that has already elapsed
1200 seconds, the TTL minus the 600 seconds already used
1800 seconds, because the full TTL restarts when the owner makes the change
2400 seconds, the cache age added to the full TTL
questions.why: The resolver's cache timer started when it fetched the answer, so 600 of the 1800 seconds are already used, leaving 1200 seconds after the change during which it may still serve the old address.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm sets the TTL on one of its records to 900. What does that value tell a resolver?
choices: The zone is signed again every 900 seconds.
A resolver may cache this answer for up to 900 seconds before asking again.
The owner must answer any query within 900 seconds or the resolver gives up.
The record is deleted from the zone after 900 seconds.
questions.why: TTL is the number of seconds a resolver may keep an answer in its cache before asking again, so 900 means up to 900 seconds of cached use.

questions.prompt: Ferncliff Labs creates a new child zone lab.ferncliff.example and hosts it on new name servers, but the parent zone still lists the old NS records for it. What is the likely result?
choices: Only MX lookups fail, while A records still resolve everywhere.
The parent zone's TXT records become invalid until the child zone is deleted.
Resolvers following the parent's delegation are sent to the old servers and may not get answers for the new zone.
The new zone is used automatically because the child zone's own records override the parent.
questions.why: Delegation is recorded as NS records in the parent, and resolvers follow those records, so stale parent records send them to servers that no longer answer for the child zone.

questions.prompt: A zone is DNSSEC-signed. After an edit, a record's data no longer matches its signature, and a validating resolver receives the answer. What outcome should be expected?
choices: It skips the record and falls back to the next name server automatically.
It returns the altered answer, since the record content is still reachable.
It caches the answer for 0 seconds and ignores the TTL.
It rejects the answer, so clients see errors even though the servers are healthy.
questions.why: DNSSEC signatures let a validating resolver detect altered records, and a failed check causes the resolver to refuse the answer, which users experience as errors even when the servers themselves are running.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a DNS change reaches users, covering records, TTL, and one limit or tradeoff of choosing a short versus a long TTL.
lessons.modelAnswer: A DNS change is a new record published on the authoritative servers for a zone, but users only see it when their resolvers fetch a fresh copy. Each answer carries a TTL, and resolvers cache it for that many seconds, so the old answer keeps being served until its timer runs out. That means the maximum delay for a change is roughly the old TTL. A short TTL makes changes land quickly and suits failover, but it sends more queries to the authoritative servers and makes resolvers look up names more often, which costs money and adds load. A long TTL reduces query volume and is cheaper, but it locks users onto stale answers for longer. So the choice is a tradeoff between how fast you can move traffic and how much lookup load and staleness you accept. In practice I would lower the TTL well before a planned change, not on the day of it.
rubricPoints: A record change reaches clients only when cached answers expire, so the delay is bounded by the old TTL.
Short TTLs speed up change and failover but increase query load on authoritative servers.
Long TTLs reduce lookups and cost but keep stale answers in use for longer.
Lower the TTL in advance of a planned change, not at the moment of change.

suggested.rationale: The core skill for this objective is reasoning about TTL and caching tradeoffs in your own words, which explaining it to a teammate tests directly.

lessons.plain: A name like shop.example.com has to be turned into the address of a computer before anything can connect. Amazon Route 53 is AWS's DNS service, which does that lookup and also decides which answer to give. This lesson covers four of its features. Alias records let a name point at an AWS resource, such as a load balancer, by name rather than by a fixed number. Traffic policies choose among several answers using rules, such as which copy is healthy or closest. Resolvers answer lookups made from inside your private network. Health checks keep testing whether each target is alive, so answers can avoid a dead one. Together they let a name stay steady while the systems behind it move or fail.
lessons.guessPrompt: If the server behind a website's name fails, how could a DNS service send visitors to a working server instead, and what might slow that change down for some visitors?
lessons.teach:
A DNS record is an entry in a zone, the database for one domain, saying what a name points to. Route 53 hosts those zones and answers lookups for them. An A record points a name at an IPv4 address. A CNAME points one name at another name, but DNS does not allow a CNAME at the bare domain, called the zone apex.

An alias record is a Route 53 record that points a name at an AWS resource by name, such as a load balancer or CloudFront distribution. Route 53 resolves the target itself and returns its current addresses. You do not set a TTL (time to live, how long clients may cache an answer) on an alias; the target's TTL applies. Alias records also work at the apex.

A traffic policy is a saved set of routing rules that decides which answer to return. Rules can be weighted (split by percentage), latency-based, geolocation-based, or failover (primary unless it is unhealthy). A health check is a probe Route 53 runs against an endpoint over HTTP, HTTPS or TCP. Several consecutive failures mark the target unhealthy, and failover rules then skip it.

A resolver is the DNS server that answers lookups for a client. Route 53 Resolver serves lookups made from inside your VPCs (isolated virtual networks), including names in private hosted zones that only your network can see.

Worked example: www.example.com is an alias to a primary load balancer, with a failover record pointing to a secondary. Step 1: a visitor's resolver asks for www. Step 2: Route 53 sees the primary's health check passing and returns the primary. Step 3: the primary stops responding and several checks fail, so the check turns unhealthy. Step 4: new lookups now get the secondary. Step 5: resolvers holding the old answer keep sending traffic to the dead primary until their cached copy expires.

Common mistake: assuming a health check alone moves traffic. The check only reports status; a routing rule must act on it.

A long TTL means slow failover for clients that cached the old answer, so the TTL is part of the availability design.

questions.prompt: A team runs a ticket shop. The name api.tickets.example.net is a weighted record set: 70 for the current version and 30 for a new version, each behind its own load balancer. Weighted means Route 53 splits new answers by the given percentages. The team wants to stop sending traffic to the new version. Step 1: they change the new version's weight from 30 to 0 and save. Step 2: Route 53 now returns only the current version's load balancer addresses to new lookups. Step 3: a mobile app that looked up the name ten minutes earlier still holds the new version's answer, so it keeps calling that version until its cached copy expires. Step 4: _. Which completion correctly finishes the trace?
choices: Route 53 sets a zero-second TTL on the record after a weight change, so the app drops the old answer immediately.
Route 53 deletes the new version's load balancer, so the app's cached answer fails right away and it looks the name up again.
The app keeps splitting its calls 70/30 indefinitely, because weights apply to cached answers as well as to new lookups.
When the cached answer expires, the app's next lookup returns only the current version, so the app moves over at that point.
questions.why: A weight change affects only new answers, and a client's cached copy keeps the old answer until its time to live runs out.

questions.prompt: A developer wants the bare domain brightcart.example, with no www, to point at an application load balancer. They propose a CNAME record at the zone apex. What is the problem, and what record fits better?
choices: Nothing is wrong; a CNAME works at the apex as long as its TTL is set to 60 seconds.
A failover record must be used at the apex, because failover records are the only type that can name a load balancer.
The apex can only hold an A record with a fixed IPv4 address, so they should copy the load balancer's current address into it.
DNS does not allow a CNAME at the zone apex, so an alias record that points at the load balancer by name fits instead.
questions.why: The teaching text states that a CNAME is not allowed at the zone apex, while an alias record can name an AWS resource there.

questions.prompt: A company has a private hosted zone named payments.internal.example.com, associated only with one VPC. An instance inside that VPC looks up db.payments.internal.example.com and gets an answer. A staff laptop on a separate corporate network, which has no link to that VPC, looks up the same name. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The laptop gets the answer, because the zone name ends in example.com, and that suffix makes the zone public.
The laptop is sent to a public copy of the zone that Route 53 creates automatically for every private zone.
The laptop gets the answer only after the zone's TTL has expired, because private zones are cached until then.
The laptop gets no answer from that private zone, because only the associated VPC can see it and the laptop sits outside that VPC.
questions.why: A private hosted zone answers only for the networks it is associated with, so a lookup from outside that VPC gets no answer from it.

questions.prompt: A team creates a health check that probes https://status.parcel.example/health every 30 seconds and marks the endpoint unhealthy after three consecutive failures. They add a secondary record, but their primary record is a simple record with no failover rule that references the check. The primary goes down for ten minutes. What happens to lookups?
choices: Lookups fail with an error for ten minutes, because Route 53 removes any record whose health check is failing.
Lookups go to the secondary once the primary record's TTL expires, because the check edits the record when it fails.
Route 53 sends lookups to the secondary after three failed probes, because health checks switch traffic automatically.
Lookups keep returning the primary, because the check only reports status and no routing rule acts on it.
questions.why: A health check only reports whether an endpoint is up, and only a routing rule such as failover uses that report to change answers.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a failover setup can still send some users to a dead server after the health check has marked it unhealthy, and name one tradeoff in choosing the TTL for that record.
lessons.modelAnswer: The health check only detects and reports that the primary is down. A failover routing rule has to act on that report, and it only changes the answer Route 53 gives to new lookups. Resolvers and client devices cache the old answer for as long as its TTL says, so some users keep asking for the dead address until the cache expires. The tradeoff is in the TTL value. A short TTL means faster failover, because stale answers expire quickly, but more lookups reach the DNS service and each resolver has to ask more often. A long TTL cuts lookup load and cost, but a failure can keep affecting users for much longer. For an alias, the target's TTL governs this, so the target's setting matters too.
rubricPoints: A health check only reports status; a routing rule must act on it.
Resolvers and clients cache answers, so changes reach users only after the cached TTL expires.
A shorter TTL speeds failover but increases lookup volume; a longer TTL reduces load but slows recovery.
An alias record takes its TTL from the target resource, not from a value set on the record.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between alias, traffic policy, resolver and health-check behaviour is best practised by reasoning through a scenario rather than reading a list of features.

lessons.plain: A domain name like shop.example.com needs a directory that says where it lives. A DNS zone is one section of that directory for a single domain, and a hosted zone is the managed copy of that section kept by a provider. A public hosted zone is the listing anyone on the internet can look up. A private hosted zone is a listing that only the private networks you attach to it can see, so an internal name can point to an internal address and stay invisible from outside. Deciding which kind to use, and what happens when both exist for the same name, determines whether your services can find each other and whether outsiders learn how your internal systems are laid out.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your public website shop.example.com must be reachable from the internet, while payroll.example.com should resolve only for servers inside your private network. Would you store both names in the same kind of zone, and what could go wrong if you did?
lessons.teach:
A hosted zone is a container of DNS records for one domain, such as example.com, managed by a provider that answers queries for it. A record is a single entry, such as a name mapped to an address. Authoritative means the zone's servers are the final source of answers for that domain. There are two kinds. A public hosted zone is answered to any resolver on the internet, so its records are visible to everyone. A private hosted zone is answered only to queries that originate from virtual networks (VPCs, which are isolated private networks you define in the cloud) that you explicitly associate with it.

Why it works: when a machine asks for a name, its resolver checks whether a private zone matches that name for the network the machine sits in. If one matches, that answer wins and the public zone is not consulted for that name. This lets one name, such as api.example.com, return a public address to the internet and an internal address to your VPC. This pattern is called split-horizon DNS.

Worked example: you create a public zone for example.com with api.example.com pointing to a public load balancer address. You also create a private zone for example.com, associated with VPC A, with api.example.com pointing to 10.0.4.12. Step 1: a laptop on the internet asks for api.example.com, reaches the public zone, and gets the public address. Step 2: a server in VPC A asks the same question, the private zone matches, and it gets 10.0.4.12. Step 3: a server in VPC B, which is not associated with the private zone, gets the public answer.

Common mistake: creating a private zone for example.com but copying in only some of the records. Inside VPC A the private zone now shadows the public zone for the whole domain, so any name missing from the private zone returns no answer, even if it exists publicly. In a running system, internal services that worked yesterday start failing the moment someone adds the private zone, while outside users notice nothing. The two zones are separate objects, so every record needed in each must be placed there on purpose.

questions.prompt: A logistics company, Harbor Freight Co, runs a public hosted zone (a container of DNS records for one domain, managed by a provider that answers queries for it) for harborfreight-demo.net. The public zone has tracking.harborfreight-demo.net pointing to 203.0.113.70. The company also creates a private hosted zone (records answered only to queries from virtual networks, called VPCs, that are explicitly associated with it) for the same domain, associated with VPC warehouse-east. The private zone contains one record: depot.harborfreight-demo.net pointing to 172.31.9.14. Step 1: a customer's phone asks for tracking.harborfreight-demo.net and gets 203.0.113.70 from the public zone. Step 2: a server in warehouse-east asks for depot.harborfreight-demo.net, the private zone matches, and it gets 172.31.9.14. Step 3 (missing from this text): a server in warehouse-east asks for tracking.harborfreight-demo.net. A resolver (the software on a machine that looks up names) checks the private zone first for this network. Which result does the server get?
choices: It gets 203.0.113.70, because a private zone only overrides names it actually contains.
It gets 203.0.113.70 only after the private zone is deleted, because the two zones cannot be active together.
It is refused for security reasons, because private zones block every internet name from internal networks.
It gets no answer for that name, because the matching private zone wins and the public zone is not consulted for it.
questions.why: Once a private zone matches a name for an associated network, that answer wins and the public zone is not consulted, so the name tracking.harborfreight-demo.net returns no answer inside warehouse-east.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly defines a private hosted zone?
choices: A zone that is hidden from search engines but still answers any resolver on the internet.
A zone that answers only queries from the public internet but is kept inside your company network.
A copy of the public zone that is synchronised automatically to every VPC in the same account.
A zone whose records are answered only to queries from VPCs that you explicitly associate with it.
questions.why: A private hosted zone answers only queries that originate from VPCs explicitly associated with it, which is the defining rule the teaching text gives.

questions.prompt: A company, Quill Analytics, has a public zone for quillanalytics.io with every customer-facing name. It needs ingest.quillanalytics.io to resolve to an internal address in two VPCs, pipeline-a and pipeline-b, while everyone else keeps the public address. Which setup meets this with the fewest risks?
choices: Move ingest into a new public zone for a second domain and tell the pipeline VPCs to use that domain instead.
Edit the public zone so the name returns an internal address, which then serves all internet users correctly.
Associate pipeline-a and pipeline-b with a new private zone for quillanalytics.io, copy every name those VPCs need into it, and leave the public zone unchanged.
Create a private zone for ingest.quillanalytics.io alone and associate only pipeline-a with it, leaving pipeline-b on the public address.
questions.why: A private zone for the domain, associated with both VPCs and holding every name they need, gives split-horizon answers while the public zone keeps serving the internet; copying only one name would shadow other names for those VPCs.

questions.prompt: An engineer associates a private zone for ops.kestrel-health.org with VPC metrics-c, and a server in VPC metrics-d still gets the public address for api.kestrel-health.org. The private zone does contain api.kestrel-health.org with an internal address. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Public zones always take priority over private zones, so the private record is ignored everywhere.
The server cached the public answer, and private zones never change answers for a resolver that has cached them.
The record in the private zone must be named with a trailing dot before it can be used by any VPC.
VPC metrics-d is not associated with the private zone, so its queries are answered by the public zone.
questions.why: A private zone answers only queries from networks explicitly associated with it, so a VPC that is not associated falls through to the public zone.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how a public hosted zone and a private hosted zone differ for the same domain, and name one limit or tradeoff of running both.
lessons.modelAnswer: A public hosted zone holds the records for a domain that anyone on the internet can resolve, so it is where you publish names for external users. A private hosted zone holds records that answer only queries from the VPCs associated with it, so internal services can use internal addresses without exposing them. When both exist for the same domain, a VPC associated with the private zone gets its answers from the private zone, not the public one, which is split-horizon behavior. The main tradeoff is shadowing: the private zone hides the public zone for every name in that domain. Any name I forgot to copy into the private zone will fail for internal clients even though it works publicly. So before creating one, I would list every public name the internal clients still need, and I would confirm which VPCs are associated, since associating across accounts is a deliberate step rather than something that happens automatically.
rubricPoints: A public hosted zone answers any internet resolver, while a private hosted zone answers only the VPCs associated with it.
The same name can return different answers depending on where the query comes from (split-horizon).
A private zone for a domain shadows the public zone, so records missing from it break internal resolution.
Associating a private zone with a VPC, including across accounts, is a deliberate step that must be planned.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers DNS zones or resolution behavior, so reading the teaching text and explaining it back is the best fit for this objective.

lessons.plain: Every computer that wants to reach a service first asks a phone-book service: what address does this name point to? In a hybrid setup, some names live in your company's own data center and others live inside the cloud network, and each side's phone book only knows its own names by default. Route 53 Resolver endpoints are the doorways that let those two phone books ask each other. One doorway lets outside askers look up cloud-only names, and another lets cloud machines look up company names. Getting these doorways and their forwarding rules right is what makes a split network behave like one network.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your data center has a server named billing.corp.example.com, and a cloud network has a private name orders.cloud.example.com that only exists inside that cloud network. Without any extra setup, can a server in the data center look up orders.cloud.example.com, and why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. DNS (Domain Name System) turns a name such as db.internal.example.com into an IP address. A resolver is the server that does the asking on a machine's behalf. Route 53 Resolver is the managed resolver AWS provides inside each VPC (a virtual private network inside the cloud). It answers names from private hosted zones, which are DNS zones visible only to the VPCs you attach them to, and it can forward other queries to servers elsewhere. A resolver endpoint is a set of network interfaces placed in your subnets, each with a private IP address, that lets DNS traffic cross the boundary between the VPC and another network. An inbound endpoint accepts DNS queries arriving from outside the VPC, such as from your data center. An outbound endpoint sends queries from inside the VPC to DNS servers outside it. A forwarding rule says which domain suffix should be sent to which target IP addresses.

Why it works: each side cannot see the other's zones by default, so each side needs a known address to send questions to, reached over the VPN or Direct Connect link.

Worked example: an on-premises server asks for orders.cloud.example.com, a private zone in the cloud. Step 1: the data center DNS server has a conditional forwarder for cloud.example.com that points at the IP addresses of the inbound endpoint. Step 2: the query travels over the link to the endpoint's interface in a private subnet. Step 3: the resolver checks the private hosted zone, finds the record, and returns the answer. Step 4: the reply retraces the same path.

Common mistake: opening DNS in the endpoint's security group but forgetting the routes for the on-premises address range, or allowing only UDP port 53 when large answers need TCP port 53 as well.

Consequence: when this path breaks, lookups usually time out instead of failing fast, so applications that resolve names at startup hang, and one broken forwarder looks like a full application outage. Treat the resolver path as a dependency of every service that uses it.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs its warehouse system in a data center whose DNS server is 10.20.0.53 and which hosts the zone wh.lab.test. Its cloud VPC (a virtual private network inside AWS) has a Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint, a set of network interfaces that sends DNS queries out of the VPC, and a forwarding rule that sends wh.lab.test queries to that endpoint. A cloud instance asks for scanner7.wh.lab.test and gets no answer. Step 1: the instance sends the query to the VPC resolver. Step 2: the resolver matches the forwarding rule for wh.lab.test and sends the query out through the outbound endpoint's interface. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the data center DNS server answers, and the reply returns along the same path. Which choice correctly completes step 3?
choices: The query crosses the link to 10.20.0.53, which needs a route in the endpoint's subnet for the data center address range.
The endpoint converts the query to HTTPS and sends it to the data center's web server on port 443.
The rule is copied into a private hosted zone so the resolver answers locally without leaving the VPC.
The data center DNS server answers the instance directly on its private address, so the endpoint is bypassed and no forwarding step is needed at all.
questions.why: The query must physically reach the data center DNS server, and that requires a route from the endpoint's subnet to the data center address range over the VPN or Direct Connect link (a dedicated private line to AWS).

questions.prompt: What does an inbound resolver endpoint do?
choices: It sends queries from inside the VPC out to outside DNS servers, the reverse of what a data center needs.
It stores copies of private hosted zone records so that other networks can read them directly.
It replaces the VPC's DHCP settings (the service that hands out network settings to machines) with on-premises DNS addresses.
It accepts DNS queries arriving from outside the VPC, such as from a data center.
questions.why: An inbound endpoint is the entry point that lets queries from outside the VPC reach the VPC's resolver, while an outbound endpoint handles the opposite direction.

questions.prompt: A cloud application looks up names at startup through an inbound endpoint. After someone edits a security group (a set of firewall rules attached to a network interface), startup hangs for minutes instead of failing at once. Which cause fits this symptom best?
choices: Port 53 is blocked for one transport, such as TCP for large answers, so replies never arrive and the client waits.
The VPC's DHCP options changed, so the application's name lookups are sent to a public resolver instead.
The application's cached configuration expired and must be downloaded again from a server.
The private hosted zone holds too many records, so the resolver silently drops every query it receives.
questions.why: A blocked DNS transport means the query or its reply is dropped with no error, so the client waits until it times out, which matches the hanging symptom.

questions.prompt: A company wants EC2 instances in its VPC to resolve names in its data center zone corp.example.lan, whose authoritative DNS servers are in the data center. Which pair of components should it set up?
choices: An outbound endpoint plus a forwarding rule for corp.example.lan.
A NAT gateway and a DHCP option set that lists the data center's DNS servers.
A public hosted zone with the data center's records copied into it.
An inbound endpoint plus a VPC peering connection to the data center.
questions.why: Instances inside the VPC need an outbound endpoint to send their queries out, and a forwarding rule tells the resolver which suffix goes to the data center's DNS servers.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a server in your data center resolves a name that exists only in a private cloud zone, and name one limit or tradeoff of the design you would need to watch.
lessons.modelAnswer: The data center DNS server does not know the cloud zone, so I set a conditional forwarder for that domain pointing at the IP addresses of an inbound resolver endpoint in the VPC. The query crosses the VPN or Direct Connect link to that endpoint, and the resolver answers from the private hosted zone. The tradeoff is that the cloud side now depends on the link and on the endpoint being reachable. If the link drops, lookups for cloud names time out, so I would run endpoints in two Availability Zones, keep the security group and route tables correct, and monitor query failures. There is also a cost per endpoint and per query that should be weighed against the design.
rubricPoints: Explains the inbound endpoint and the conditional forwarder that points to it
Describes the query path over the private link and the answer's return path
Names a limit such as dependence on the network link or endpoint availability
Mentions a mitigation such as multiple Availability Zones or monitoring

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a hybrid DNS failure scenario builds the path-tracing judgment this objective needs more than reading alone.

lessons.plain: Route 53 is Amazon's DNS service, the system that turns a human name like shop.example.com into the numeric address a computer connects to. Global traffic management means deciding, for each name, which of several copies of an application a visitor should be sent to, based on where they are, how fast each copy answers, or whether a copy is healthy. Domain registration is the separate job of reserving the name itself with a registrar and recording which name servers answer for it. Together these let one name point to many places and keep working when one place fails.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your shop runs in two Regions, and both are reached through the same web name. If the first Region goes down, what would you want the name to do, and which single setting would most affect how quickly visitors notice the change?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A DNS record is one stored answer for a name, such as an address record that gives an IPv4 address. A hosted zone is the container in Route 53 that holds the records for one domain. A routing policy is the rule Route 53 applies when a name has several possible answers. A health check is a probe that Route 53 runs against an endpoint to decide whether it is up. TTL, time to live, is the number of seconds a resolver may reuse an answer before asking again. A registrar is the company where you buy the domain name, and it keeps the list of name servers that are authoritative for that domain.

Why it works. Route 53 answers queries for your names itself. Depending on the policy, it returns one answer, a weighted share, the answer for the lowest-latency Region, the answer for a geographic location, or the first healthy endpoint in a failover pair. A record tied to a failed health check is left out of the answer.

Worked example. You publish two latency-based records for app.example.com, one pointing to Frankfurt and one to Virginia, each with TTL 60 and a health check. A visitor in Paris asks a resolver for the name. Route 53 sees the resolver's location, finds Frankfurt is faster and healthy, and returns the Frankfurt address. The resolver caches it for 60 seconds. Frankfurt's health check then fails three probes in a row, so Route 53 stops offering that record. When the cached answer expires, the next query returns Virginia.

Common mistake. Setting a one-hour TTL on a record meant for failover. Clients keep using the dead address for up to an hour, so the failover looks broken even though Route 53 changed its answer correctly.

Consequence. Recovery speed is the health-check detection time plus the TTL that clients honour. A short TTL speeds recovery but sends more queries; a long TTL reduces load but delays failover. Registration is separate: the registrar's name server list must match the hosted zone's name servers, or resolvers will ask the wrong place and the domain will not resolve, whatever the zone contains.

questions.prompt: Harbor Ledger runs its payments API at pay.harborledger.example with two failover records. The primary record points to a server in Sydney, the secondary to a server in Singapore. Both records have a health check that probes the Sydney endpoint every 30 seconds, and the primary record has TTL 300. Step 1: Route 53 marks the Sydney health check as failed after three probes in a row, which is 90 seconds of probing, so Route 53 stops offering the Sydney address. Step 2: A client resolver that cached the Sydney answer just before the failure keeps using it until its 300-second TTL runs out. Step 3 (missing): To find the longest time a client can keep sending traffic to the dead Sydney address, you combine the two delays. Which completion is correct?
choices: Add the 90-second detection time to the 300-second TTL, giving 390 seconds
Use only the TTL of 300 seconds, because the health check does not affect answers that are already cached
Multiply the TTL by three, giving 900 seconds, because the probes repeat against each cached answer
Subtract the 90-second detection time from the 300-second TTL, giving 210 seconds, because the probes overlap the cache
questions.why: Recovery speed is the health-check detection time plus the TTL that clients honour, so the worst case is 90 plus 300, which is 390 seconds.

questions.prompt: A team manages two unrelated domains, lanternco.example and fieldnotes.example, in Route 53. Which statement correctly describes where the records for each domain are held?
choices: A hosted zone is a single record that stores one IPv4 address for a name
The hosted zone is the list of name servers that the registrar keeps for the domain
Each domain's records sit in its own hosted zone, which is the container that holds the records for one domain
All records for every domain go into one shared hosted zone so that routing policies can read them together
questions.why: A hosted zone is the container for the records of one domain, so each unrelated domain gets its own zone, and the other options describe a single record, a shared container, or the registrar's list.

questions.prompt: Northwind Parcels sets up a failover record for track.northwind.example with TTL 3600 and a health check. The primary endpoint fails, and Route 53 changes its answer to the secondary endpoint within a minute. A customer's browser had cached the old address a few minutes before the failure. What is the most likely result for that customer?
choices: The browser switches to the secondary within a minute, because Route 53 pushes the new answer to every cache
The browser may keep using the dead primary address for up to an hour, because it honours the cached answer until the TTL expires
The browser has no way to reach either endpoint until its DNS cache is manually cleared
The browser fails immediately, because a cached answer is discarded as soon as a health check fails
questions.why: Clients reuse a cached answer for the full TTL, so a one-hour TTL can keep a dead address in use for up to an hour even though Route 53 changed its answer quickly, and the other options assume a push or instant invalidation that DNS caching does not provide.

questions.prompt: A startup registers the domain brightkiln.example with a registrar and creates a hosted zone for it in Route 53. The hosted zone has complete, correct records, but the registrar still lists an older set of name servers from a previous provider. A user types brightkiln.example into a browser. What happens?
choices: The name resolves through the old provider, but the records in the new hosted zone are ignored entirely
Route 53 answers from the hosted zone, because the zone's records take priority over the registrar's list
The name resolves only after the TTL on the hosted zone expires, which corrects the registrar's list automatically
The name fails to resolve, because resolvers ask the name servers the registrar lists, which are not the zone's name servers
questions.why: Resolvers are sent by the registrar to its listed name servers, so if that list does not match the hosted zone's name servers, the domain will not resolve no matter what records the zone contains, and the zone's TTL cannot fix the list.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate suggests setting our failover record's TTL to 24 hours so DNS caching never causes trouble. Explain to them what that choice trades away, and name one limit of health-check-based failover they should understand before relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: A 24-hour TTL means resolvers keep the old answer for up to a day after Route 53 has changed it. If the primary Region fails, users who cached the primary address keep being sent there until their cache expires, so the outage can last hours even though the failover itself took seconds. The benefit is fewer DNS queries and lower load on the resolvers, but that is paid for with slow recovery. A better compromise is a short TTL on failover records, sized to how long you can tolerate stale answers, with a note that more queries will reach Route 53. The limit of health checks is that they only see what they probe. If the health check hits a port or path that still responds while the application behind it is returning errors, Route 53 keeps the record in service and users still fail.
rubricPoints: A long TTL delays failover because resolvers keep stale answers until the cache expires.
A short TTL speeds recovery but increases query volume, so the choice is a tradeoff.
Health checks only detect what they probe, so a shallow check can pass while the application is broken.
Failover speed depends on both health-check detection time and the TTL clients honour.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a routing policy and a TTL for a stated scenario is exam-style reasoning that adds more than a fact list, and no listed mission covers DNS.

lessons.plain: DNS is the directory that turns a name like shop.example.com into a network address. DNS logging means recording the lookup questions being asked and the answers returned, so you can see who asks for what and where lookups fail. Monitoring means counting those answers over time and alerting when the counts shift. This matters because many outages look like network problems but start with a name that no longer resolves, or resolves to the wrong place. Think of a receptionist's call log: who called, what they asked for, and whether they got a reply.
lessons.guessPrompt: An application times out connecting to a database by name, yet the database's IP address still answers a direct ping. What would you check first, and why?
lessons.teach: DNS (the Domain Name System) turns names into addresses. A resolver is the server that answers a client's lookup, and a query is one lookup question, such as asking for the address behind a name. Each answer carries a response code: NOERROR means the name exists, NXDOMAIN means it does not, and SERVFAIL means the server could not complete the lookup. DNS query logging writes a record of each query and its response code, including the name, the record type, and the source address. A Resolver endpoint is the managed forwarder that carries lookups between your cloud networks and on-premises networks. Monitoring turns counts of those responses into metrics you can graph and alarm on. Why it works: to an application, a failed name looks exactly like a failed network. Logs show the failing name and response code, so you can separate a bad name from a broken path in minutes instead of guessing. Worked example: an on-premises service asks a Resolver endpoint for db.corp.example. Step 1: the query arrives from 10.20.4.15 and is forwarded to the on-premises DNS server. Step 2: the log shows SERVFAIL for every query in that zone while public names still succeed. Step 3: a metric counting SERVFAIL per minute crosses its alarm threshold. Step 4: the forwarding rule points at an old DNS address, so the fix is to correct the rule, not the application. Common mistake: assuming that logging on a public hosted zone also captures lookups made from inside your VPCs. Those lookups go through the VPC resolver, which needs its own query logging configuration attached to each VPC. Consequence: without these logs, a resolver fault shows up only as application timeouts, and the on-call engineer chases the network for hours while the record of the failing zone was never written.

questions.prompt: Tallow Credit Union runs an application in a cloud VPC (a virtual private network, meaning an isolated network you define in the cloud). A Resolver endpoint, the managed forwarder that carries lookups between cloud and on-premises networks, is set up to pass lookups for reports.tallow.example to the on-premises DNS server. Step 1: a query for reports.tallow.example arrives at the Resolver endpoint from 10.61.2.40. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: the query log shows NXDOMAIN for reports.tallow.example, and a metric counting NXDOMAIN per minute crosses its alarm threshold. Which sentence correctly fills in step 2?
choices: The application clears its local DNS cache and retries the query over a different transport, which returns the address.
The on-premises DNS server answers that the name does not exist, and the Resolver endpoint passes that answer back to the client.
The Resolver endpoint answers from its own cache with NOERROR, so the forwarding rule is never used for this name.
The query is dropped before it reaches the forwarder, and the forwarder returns SERVFAIL to the client.
questions.why: NXDOMAIN means the name does not exist, so the answer must have come back from the on-premises server with that meaning, which points at the name rather than a broken path.

questions.prompt: A team at Pemberly Freight runs a nightly job that looks up partner names. Their dashboard counts every lookup answer by response code. Which response code means the server could not finish the lookup at all, rather than saying the name is missing?
choices: SERVFAIL, meaning the server could not complete the lookup
A missing query log entry, meaning the name was never asked
NXDOMAIN, meaning the name does not exist
NOERROR, meaning the name exists
questions.why: SERVFAIL is the response code for a lookup the server could not complete, while NOERROR and NXDOMAIN both mean the server gave a real answer.

questions.prompt: Quill Ledger turned on DNS query logging for its public zone quillledger.example. Its workloads inside a VPC look up names like payments.internal.quill for their own services, but no entries for those names appear in the log. What is the most likely reason?
choices: Lookups from inside the VPC go through the VPC resolver, which needs its own query logging setup.
The workloads are using an old DNS cache, so no queries reach any resolver.
Query logs never include names that end in .internal.
The log retention period is too short to keep the entries.
questions.why: Logging on a public zone does not capture lookups that go through the VPC resolver, so the VPC resolver needs its own query logging configuration attached to the VPC.

questions.prompt: Harrow and Vale, a law firm, retired an old file-sharing host last week. Its alarm on NXDOMAIN per minute now fires for a name nobody uses any more. An engineer wants to decide whether the on-premises DNS server is broken. What is the best reading of the log?
choices: The forwarding path is down, since NXDOMAIN always means a broken path.
The name no longer exists, so NXDOMAIN is a correct answer; tune the alarm for this name.
