Reachability Analyzer is the single-route check. Given a source and a destination, it reads the configured route tables, security groups and network ACLs along the path and tells us whether the path is open, or names the first thing blocking it. The limit to keep in mind is that it analyzes configuration, not live traffic. A reachable result means the settings allow the path. It does not prove the application is listening, that a host firewall is not dropping packets, or that the server is healthy. We should confirm with a real connection test after the analysis passes.
rubricPoints: Network Manager gives a topology and health view of the whole transit network
Reachability Analyzer checks configuration along a source-to-destination path without sending live traffic
It reports either reachable or the first component that blocks the path
A reachable result only means configuration allows the path; live checks are still needed

suggested.rationale: A planned path tracer would let the learner walk a route hop by hop through routes and rules, which is the core skill this objective tests.

lessons.plain: When a system serves traffic, it helps to keep records of who talked to whom, what they asked for, and what happened. This objective covers three kinds of record. Network flow logs are summaries of each conversation seen at the network level, like a phone bill that lists calls without recording what was said. Traffic mirroring is a copy of the actual packets sent to a tool for close inspection. Access logs are one line per request written by a load balancer or the content delivery edge, showing what was asked and how it was answered. Knowing which record answers which question is the core skill.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web request to your application times out for some users but not others. Which single record would you check first to learn whether the request reached the load balancer and what status it returned, and why would a network flow record alone not be enough?
lessons.teach:
A flow log is a record of network conversations, not their contents. In AWS it is called VPC Flow Logs, and it can be switched on for a network interface, a subnet, or a whole virtual network (a VPC, a private isolated network inside your cloud account). Each record names a source address and port, a destination address and port, the protocol, how many packets and bytes moved, and whether security rules accepted or rejected the traffic. It never shows the payload. Traffic mirroring is different: it copies the actual packets from a chosen network interface to a monitoring target, such as an appliance that inspects content. The copy is passive, so the original traffic is not changed. Load balancer access logs and CloudFront logs are written by the service at the application layer, one entry per HTTP request, with the client address, path, status code, and timing. They are delivered to object storage in batches, so they arrive minutes or more later.

Worked example: a client cannot reach an application on port 443. Step one, check the flow log for that client address and port. If the record shows REJECT, a security rule is blocking the traffic before it reaches the application. Step two, if the record shows ACCEPT but the user sees errors, check the load balancer access log for that time window to see the status code the balancer returned. Step three, use mirroring only if you need to know what the bytes actually contained.

Common mistake: treating a missing flow record as proof that no traffic happened. Some traffic is not captured, such as certain DNS queries to the built-in resolver and metadata calls, and records are aggregated over short capture windows.

Consequence: flow logs and access logs cost money to store and query at high volume, and mirroring adds load on the source and the target, so enable each source deliberately and scope it to the interfaces or time that matter.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs a mobile app whose traffic reaches a load balancer on port 443. A driver reports that the app spins and then times out, but the driver's device address appears in the flow logs. Support follows this method. Step one: look up the driver's address and port 443 in the flow log for the 10:00 to 10:05 window. The record shows ACCEPT in both directions with bytes flowing, so no security rule blocked the connection. Step two: [missing]. Step three: use traffic mirroring only if the team needs to see the actual bytes of the request. Which step belongs in the blank?
choices: Check the load balancer access log for the same time window to read the status code the balancer returned to the app.
Conclude that the timeout happened on the driver's phone because the flow log shows no REJECT records.
Turn on traffic mirroring on the driver's network interface for a full day before reading any other log.
Delete the flow log and re-enable it on the whole virtual network so that the record is complete.
questions.why: An ACCEPT record shows the network allowed the conversation, so the next place to look is the application-layer access log, which records the status code the balancer returned for each request in that window.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between a VPC flow log and traffic mirroring?
choices: A flow log records conversation metadata such as addresses, ports, byte counts and accept or reject results, and never includes the payload, while mirroring copies the actual packets without changing the original traffic.
Both record the payload, but flow logs do it in batches that arrive minutes late.
Mirroring is a security rule that blocks traffic, while a flow log is a record of traffic that was already blocked.
A flow log copies the packets to a monitoring target, while mirroring records only addresses and ports.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a flow log as a metadata record that never shows contents, and mirroring as a passive copy of the real packets, so option B states both correctly.

questions.prompt: A security engineer reviews flow logs for a compute instance and finds no record of a call to the instance metadata service during a one-hour window. The engineer concludes the instance never made that call. What is the most accurate assessment?
choices: The conclusion is correct, because flow logs capture every packet the instance sends.
The conclusion is unsafe because flow logs only record traffic from load balancers, not from instances.
The conclusion is correct only if traffic mirroring was also enabled on the instance's interface.
The conclusion is unsafe, because some traffic, including metadata calls and certain DNS queries to the built-in resolver, is not captured and records are aggregated over short windows.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that a missing flow record is not proof of no traffic, since metadata calls and some DNS queries are not captured, so option A is the mistake the engineer made.

questions.prompt: An on-call engineer needs the exact status code a load balancer returned to a customer two minutes ago, to decide whether to roll back a release. Which source is most likely to answer this in time, and why?
choices: Neither source will answer in time, because load balancer access logs are delivered to object storage in batches and can arrive minutes or more later.
The CloudFront access log, because it is written in real time to the same bucket as the load balancer log.
Traffic mirroring, because it copies each packet to a monitoring target the moment it is sent.
The VPC flow log, because it records the status code of every HTTP request.
questions.why: Load balancer access logs are batched and can arrive minutes later, and flow logs and mirroring do not carry HTTP status codes, so none of the options gives a reliable answer within two minutes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between a flow log, a load balancer access log, and a traffic mirror when investigating a slow API, and name one limit of the record you would pick first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the record that matches the layer of the problem. If the API is slow for some clients, the load balancer access log tells me each request's path, status code, and timing, so I can see whether the slowness is in the application or before it reaches the balancer. If requests never arrive, the flow log shows whether connections from those client addresses are accepted or rejected at the network level, which points at security rules or routing. I would only mirror traffic if I needed packet contents, for example to check a malformed header, because mirroring copies every packet from the chosen interface and can add load. The limit I would name first is delay: access logs arrive in batches, so they are poor for real-time alerting and I would pair them with live metrics. Flow logs also omit payloads and some service traffic, so an absent record is not proof of absence.
rubricPoints: Matches each record to the layer it observes: access logs for requests, flow logs for connections, mirroring for packet contents
Names the delivery delay of access logs, so they are not used for real-time alerts
Notes that flow logs omit payloads and some service traffic, so a missing record is not proof of no traffic
Mentions that mirroring adds load and should be scoped to the interfaces or time needed

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario asking which log source answers which question adds the most here, and no listed mission or planned engine covers choosing network log sources directly.

lessons.plain: Before you can say a network is slow or broken, you need two things: a record of what it normally does, and a plan for what you will write down and watch. The record is a baseline, a set of normal measurements such as how much data crosses a link during a quiet hour and how long requests take during a busy one. The plan is your logging and monitoring requirements: which events must be kept, for how long, who needs to read them, and which numbers should trigger action. Think of a doctor who records your resting heart rate before deciding whether today's reading is worrying. This lesson is about deciding what to record and measuring what normal looks like before anything goes wrong.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web service's users report it feels slower on Tuesdays. You can see that latency rose, but nobody recorded what latency looked like on a normal Tuesday. What would you have needed in place beforehand to judge whether Tuesday was actually unusual?
lessons.teach:
A metric is a number measured over time, such as bytes sent per minute, packets dropped, or the time a request takes (latency). A log is a record of individual events, such as a connection being accepted or rejected. A flow log is a log of network conversations: for each flow of traffic it records source, destination, port, byte count, and whether the traffic was allowed. Monitoring means watching metrics and logs continuously against thresholds. A baseline is a set of measurements taken while the system behaves normally, over a window long enough to show daily and weekly rhythms. A logging and monitoring requirement is a stated answer to four questions: what must be captured, how long it is kept, who reads it, and what triggers action.

Why it works: a single value such as 40 milliseconds means little on its own. Compared with a baseline of 35 to 45 milliseconds at this hour, it is ordinary; compared with 120, it is an anomaly. Without a baseline you cannot separate normal variation from a fault, so you either alarm constantly or never alarm at all.

Worked example: a team serves a regional API. Step 1: they write the requirement, keeping per-minute latency at the load balancer and flow records at the network boundary for 30 days. Step 2: they collect two weeks of data. Step 3: they find weekday mornings sit at 40 to 50 milliseconds, while the 99th percentile latency peaks at 180 milliseconds on Monday mornings. Step 4: they set the alarm at 250 milliseconds sustained for five minutes, above the normal peak, so a real regression stands out.

Common mistake: reducing everything to one average. An average hides a small group of very slow requests, so the baseline should include percentiles and peak values, not just the mean.

Consequence: when an incident happens without a baseline, responders spend the first hour arguing about whether the numbers are abnormal, and an alarm set without one either fires all night or stays silent during a real outage.

questions.prompt: A payments team at a different company tracks latency for its checkout API. Step 1: they write a requirement covering per-minute p99 latency at the load balancer and flow records at the VPC boundary, kept for 60 days and read by the on-call rota. Step 2: they collect three weeks of data. Step 3: they find weekday lunchtime p99 sits near 90 ms, while Saturday evening p99 peaks near 300 ms. Step 4 is missing: they must set the alarm threshold so that normal peaks do not fire it but a real regression does. Which choice fills Step 4?
choices: Set it at 350 ms, sustained over five minutes, above the Saturday peak.
Drop the alarm and review the dashboard each morning instead.
Set it at 90 ms, the weekday lunchtime value, so any rise is flagged.
Set it at 300 ms on any single one-minute sample, matching the observed peak.
questions.why: The threshold should sit above the normal peak in the baseline and be sustained over a window, so ordinary peaks stay quiet while a real regression stands out.

questions.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes a metric from a log?
choices: A metric is a record of each individual event, and a log is a number measured over time.
A log is a record of individual events, and a metric is a number measured over time.
A metric records only whether traffic was allowed, while a log records byte counts.
A metric and a log are the same thing, recorded at different intervals.
questions.why: A metric is a number tracked over time, such as latency or dropped packets, while a log is a record of individual events such as a connection being accepted.

questions.prompt: A team's baseline for an internal service shows a mean latency of 45 milliseconds over two weeks, and they consider the baseline complete. What is the main gap?
choices: The mean is measured at the wrong network boundary.
The mean should be replaced with a count of dropped packets.
The baseline lacks percentiles and peak values, so a small group of very slow requests is hidden.
The window is too short to show anything about the service.
questions.why: An average can hide a small group of very slow requests, so a useful baseline also needs percentiles and peak values.

questions.prompt: A team sets a latency alarm at 100 milliseconds without measuring a baseline first. Their system normally runs 20 to 30 milliseconds overnight and 80 to 95 milliseconds at busy hours. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The alarm proves the system is healthy whenever it stays silent.
The alarm will never fire, so the team can stop watching latency.
The alarm is safe because a higher threshold is always more conservative.
The alarm sits close to normal busy-hour values, so it may fire on ordinary variation and make real faults hard to separate from busy hours.
questions.why: Without a baseline the threshold is not anchored to normal behaviour, so it can sit too close to ordinary peaks and produce noisy or misleading alarms.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should just turn on every log we can and sort it out later. In your own words, explain what you would require to be captured before enabling anything, and name one tradeoff of capturing too much.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from the questions we need to answer, not from what the tools offer. For each network component, I would write down what must be recorded, how long we keep it, who reads it, and which metric crossing which threshold triggers action. Then I would capture a baseline over a representative period, at least two weeks so daily and weekly peaks appear, recording averages along with high percentiles and peak values, because averages hide slow tails. The tradeoff of capturing everything is cost and noise: detailed flow logs and per-request records are expensive to store and query, and a flood of unrelated events makes the real signal harder to find during an incident. So I would keep detailed records for the paths we troubleshoot most, use summary metrics elsewhere, and review the list every quarter.
rubricPoints: Requirements state what to capture, how long to keep it, who reads it, and what triggers action.
A baseline is measured over a representative period that shows normal daily and weekly patterns.
Baselines use percentiles and peak values as well as averages, since averages hide slow outliers.
Capturing everything has cost and noise tradeoffs, so detail should match what must be diagnosed.

suggested.rationale: Deciding what to log and what counts as normal is a judgement skill best shown by explaining it to a teammate.

lessons.plain: Network visibility means being able to tell, at any moment, whether the network is working and where it is slowing down or breaking. Choosing the right metrics is like choosing the gauges on a car dashboard: a fuel gauge alone will not warn you that the engine is overheating. For a cloud network, useful signals include how much traffic is moving, how many packets or connections are being dropped or refused, how long replies take, whether links and tunnels are up, and whether the servers behind a load balancer pass their health checks. The skill is picking a small set of signals that each answer one specific question, rather than collecting everything and hoping someone notices a problem.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose users say a website feels slow, but the CPU graph on your application servers looks normal. Which network-side signal would you check first, and why might CPU alone mislead you?
lessons.teach: A metric is a numeric measurement recorded over time, such as the number of bytes moved per minute or the number of connections refused per minute. Each metric is attached to a dimension, which names the specific thing being measured, such as one particular load balancer or one VPN tunnel. An alarm is a rule that watches a metric and changes state when it crosses a threshold for a set number of periods. A baseline is a record of what normal looks like for your system, captured while things are healthy, so you can tell a real problem from ordinary daily variation. Good network metrics fall into a few families: capacity (throughput and connection counts), loss (dropped packets, refused or reset connections), latency (response time), health (how many targets pass their checks, whether tunnels are up), and errors (server error rates and timeouts). Why this works: each family answers a different question, so together they point toward a cause. Worked example: a load balancer fronts four servers. At 09:14 the healthy host count falls from four to two. Within a minute the 99th percentile response time climbs from 120 ms to 2.3 seconds. The rejected connection count rises, showing the balancer is turning traffic away because the remaining servers are full. An alarm on healthy host count below three for three minutes fires, and the team starts from the right place. Common mistake: alarming only on average latency. An average can stay calm while one request in ten waits several seconds, which is exactly the experience a slow-site complaint describes, so use percentiles. Consequence: without a baseline, nobody can say whether 300 ms is alarming or normal, and the alarm either fires constantly or never fires. Pick a few metrics that each answer one question, and keep their thresholds tied to the baseline.

questions.prompt: A retailer connects its warehouse network to its cloud network through two VPN tunnels, A (primary) and B (backup). The team traces an incident in four steps. Step 1: at 06:40 the tunnel-state health metric for tunnel A changes from up to down, while tunnel B stays up. Step 2: traffic moves to tunnel B, and B's bytes-per-minute capacity metric roughly doubles. Step 3 (missing): the team checks tunnel B's dropped-packet metric, which was near zero in the baseline, and sees it rising sharply. Step 4: the 95th percentile latency on the inventory API climbs from 45 ms to 310 ms, and the team concludes the backup tunnel is hitting its limit and turning traffic away. What is the missing Step 3 for, and what should it establish?
choices: It shows whether tunnel B is losing packets under the new load, which confirms the limit that explains the latency rise in Step 4.
It resets the baseline to the current traffic level, so the new doubled volume counts as normal from then on.
It replaces the 95th percentile latency with the average, so the spike is smoothed before the conclusion is drawn.
It proves tunnel A has recovered, so the team can move traffic back to it without reading any other metric.
questions.why: A rising dropped-packet count on tunnel B is the loss family of metrics, and it shows the backup is turning traffic away, which connects the capacity change in Step 2 to the latency rise in Step 4.

questions.prompt: A payments team runs a pool of six worker servers behind a load balancer and wants one metric that answers the question: are enough workers passing their checks to take traffic right now? Which metric family fits best?
choices: Health, because the count of targets passing their checks answers that question directly
Latency, because response time shows whether workers are passing checks
Capacity, because total bytes moved shows how many workers are passing checks
Loss, because refused connections are the clearest sign of unhealthy workers
questions.why: The health family counts how many targets pass their checks, which is exactly the question asked, while the other families answer different questions such as speed, dropped traffic, or volume.

questions.prompt: A file-sync service has an alarm on the average response time of 180 ms, which stays under its threshold all day. Users keep reporting that uploads hang for several seconds at busy times. What is the most likely reason the alarm stays silent?
choices: The threshold is set in milliseconds when it should be in seconds, so it can never fire.
An average can stay calm while a minority of requests wait several seconds, so percentiles such as the 99th should be used instead.
The alarm needs a dimension for each user, otherwise it cannot see the uploads.
The alarm watches the health family, which does not measure response time at all.
questions.why: Averages blend fast and slow requests together, so a small share of very slow requests can leave the mean looking normal while users experience the delay; percentiles expose that tail.

questions.prompt: A team has just created a VPN tunnel to a new branch office and sets an alarm that fires whenever tunnel latency exceeds 200 ms, with no prior measurements of that tunnel. Within a week the alarm either fires every few minutes or never fires at all. Which change best addresses the cause?
choices: Record a baseline of the tunnel's latency during healthy periods, then set the alarm relative to that normal range.
Switch the alarm from latency to the tunnel-state health metric, since latency cannot be trusted.
Add more dimensions to the alarm so it covers every packet in the tunnel.
Raise the threshold to 2,000 ms so that the alarm fires less often.
questions.why: Without a baseline there is no known normal, so a fixed threshold cannot be tied to what healthy operation looks like; capturing healthy-period measurements first lets the threshold separate real problems from ordinary variation.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate which three to five network metrics you would put on one dashboard for a service behind a load balancer and a VPN link, and name one limit of relying on those metrics.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would put healthy target count, the 99th percentile response time, rejected or reset connection counts, the VPN tunnel up or down state, and throughput on one dashboard. Healthy target count tells us capacity is lost, percentile latency shows what the slowest users feel, rejected connections show traffic being refused, tunnel state shows whether the hybrid link is up, and throughput gives the baseline for normal load. The limit is that metrics are aggregates. They tell you that something is wrong and roughly where, but not why a particular packet was dropped or which route it took. For that, you need logs such as flow logs, and you need a baseline so a threshold means something. Too many alarms also cause fatigue, so each alarm should map to an action someone would take.
rubricPoints: Names metrics from distinct families such as capacity, loss, latency and health, each answering a different question
Explains why percentile latency is preferred over average latency for user-facing slowness
States that a baseline of normal behaviour is needed to set meaningful thresholds
Names a limit: metrics show symptoms in aggregate and do not explain individual packet paths, so logs are also needed

suggested.rationale: Choosing metrics and turning them into thresholds with baselines is what a metric alarm builder would let the learner practise hands-on.

lessons.plain: Routing is how a piece of data finds its way from one network to another, much like following road signs at each junction. A routing table is the list of signs a router reads: for each destination range, it records which neighbour to hand the traffic to. Static routing means a person types those entries in by hand. It is simple and predictable, but it does not notice when a road closes. Dynamic routing means routers talk to each other and update their tables automatically when links change. BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol, is the dynamic protocol that exchanges routes between separate networks, such as your office and a cloud provider. Choosing between them is a tradeoff between control and effort.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your office has two links to the cloud, a primary and a backup. Someone types in a fixed route that sends cloud-bound traffic over the primary link, and the primary link then fails. What do you think happens to that traffic, and what would have to change for it to move onto the backup?
lessons.teach:
A route is an entry that says: traffic for this destination range should go to this next hop. A destination range is a block of addresses, written like 10.2.0.0/16. The next hop is the neighbouring router the traffic is passed to. The set of these entries is the routing table. When a packet arrives, the router picks the most specific matching range, which is called longest-prefix match, and forwards it to that route's next hop.

Static routing means an engineer writes each route by hand. Dynamic routing means a routing protocol learns and withdraws routes automatically. BGP is that protocol between separate networks. Each network is an autonomous system with its own AS number. Routers that peer with each other advertise the ranges they can reach. Where two paths reach the same range, BGP uses path attributes, such as local preference, to choose one.

Worked example. The office advertises 10.1.0.0/16. The cloud network 10.2.0.0/16 is reachable over link A and link B. Step 1: both links run BGP sessions. Step 2: the cloud advertises 10.2.0.0/16 on both. Step 3: the office sets a higher local preference on link A, so A is chosen. Step 4: link A fails, its BGP session drops, and the route is withdrawn. Step 5: only the link B path remains, and traffic moves within seconds without anyone editing a table.

Common mistake: adding a static route for the same range as the BGP-learned routes. A static route can override the dynamic path, so traffic keeps heading into the dead link even though BGP has already withdrawn its route.

In a running system, a static route with no failover causes a blackhole: packets are sent and silently lost until a human notices and fixes the table. Dynamic routing trades setup effort for automatic recovery.

questions.prompt: A retail firm has a store network at 10.60.0.0/14 reachable through router P, and a more specific range 10.60.8.0/21 reachable through router Q. A packet addressed to 10.60.9.7 arrives. Step 1: both ranges contain 10.60.9.7. Step 2: the /21 is the more specific match, because its prefix is longer. Step 3: [missing step]. Which choice completes the trace?
choices: The router splits the packet and sends half through P and half through Q.
The router forwards the packet to Q, the next hop of the /21 route.
The router drops the packet, because two routes match and the table is ambiguous.
The router forwards to P, since the /14 covers more addresses overall.
questions.why: The router uses longest-prefix match, so after choosing the most specific route it forwards the packet to that route's next hop, which is Q.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the difference between a static route and a dynamic route?
choices: A dynamic route is typed in by an engineer once and then never changes unless the hardware is replaced.
A static route forwards packets faster in every case, so dynamic routes are only a backup for it.
A static route is written by hand and stays until edited; a dynamic route is learned and withdrawn by a routing protocol.
A static route is used only between separate autonomous systems, while dynamic routes stay inside one site.
questions.why: A static route is a hand-written entry that persists until someone changes it, whereas a dynamic route is learned from a protocol and removed automatically when the path is lost.

questions.prompt: Two BGP paths both reach 172.24.0.0/16 inside one office. Which path attribute is used to prefer one of them?
choices: The size of the packet that is about to be sent.
The AS number of the local router alone, with no other input.
Local preference, set higher on the path you want to prefer.
The order in which the two routes were typed into the table.
questions.why: Local preference is a BGP path attribute that lets an engineer rank competing paths to the same range, and the higher value is chosen.

questions.prompt: An engineer runs BGP over a VPN link that advertises 192.0.2.0/24. The engineer also adds a static route for that same range pointing at the same link. The BGP session then drops, but traffic still goes into the dead link. What is the most likely cause?
choices: BGP needs a restart before it can withdraw any route from the routing table.
The static route is still in the table and can override the BGP-learned route, so traffic keeps heading into the dead link.
The partner router keeps advertising the range, so the path is still treated as valid.
Static routes always have lower priority than BGP routes, so the BGP route is ignored.
questions.why: A leftover static route for the same range can take precedence over the withdrawn BGP path, which is why packets continue to be sent into a link that is no longer up.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose static routing over BGP for a link to a cloud network, and name one limit or tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use static routing for a small, simple link with one path, where the remote ranges rarely change and the team wants minimal configuration and no routing protocol to troubleshoot. The downside is that it has no failover: if the link or the remote device fails, the static route keeps pointing at it and traffic is silently lost until someone changes the configuration by hand. For anything with a backup link, many address ranges, or a need to shift traffic between paths, I would use BGP. It withdraws routes automatically when a session drops and lets us set preferences, but it adds peering setup, requires an AS number and careful advertisement of prefixes, and gives us more to troubleshoot. So the choice depends on whether we value simplicity or automatic recovery.
rubricPoints: Defines static routing as manually configured routes with no automatic failover
Defines BGP as a dynamic protocol that exchanges routes and withdraws them when a path fails
Names a concrete tradeoff such as silent blackholing with static routes or added configuration effort with BGP
Explains when each fits, such as one simple path versus redundant links needing automatic recovery

suggested.rationale: Choosing between static and dynamic routing and justifying it to a teammate is the core skill, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: Physical interconnects are the real cables, fibre, ports and light-based modules that carry network traffic between two devices. Layer 1 is the physical signal itself. Layer 2 is the local link layer, where data units called frames move between devices on the same segment. This objective covers four tools that shape these links. VLANs split one physical link into several separate logical networks. Link aggregation bundles several physical links into one logical pipe. Optics are the transceivers that turn electrical signals into light and set how far and how fast a link can run. Jumbo frames let each frame carry a larger payload than the usual size. Each tool is simple alone, but a mismatch between the two ends of a link can make it look healthy while quietly losing traffic.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two servers are connected by two identical cables bundled together into one logical link. A single large file copy between them runs at roughly the speed of one cable, not two. Why might that be?
lessons.teach:
A frame is one unit of data sent across a single link at layer 2. A VLAN (virtual local area network) is a logical network carried over shared physical gear. Frames for each VLAN are marked with a numeric tag, defined by the IEEE 802.1Q standard, so a switch knows which logical network a frame belongs to. A trunk port carries many tagged VLANs; an access port carries one untagged VLAN. A link aggregation group (LAG) combines several physical links into one logical link, using a negotiation protocol (often LACP) so both ends agree on membership. The MTU (maximum transmission unit) is the largest payload a frame can carry. The standard Ethernet MTU is 1500 bytes; jumbo frames allow larger values, commonly 9000 bytes. Optics are pluggable transceivers. Their type, such as single-mode or multimode fibre, sets maximum reach and speed.

Worked example: a trunk carries VLAN 100 and VLAN 200 between two switches. A server on VLAN 100 sends a frame. The switch adds tag 100. The far switch reads the tag, forwards the frame only to ports that belong to VLAN 100, and strips the tag before delivery. Traffic on VLAN 200 never reaches those ports.

Common mistake: assuming a LAG of four 10 Gbps links gives one transfer 40 Gbps. The LAG hashes each flow onto one member link, so a single flow is still capped at 10 Gbps; the 40 Gbps is an aggregate across many flows.

Consequence: if one end of a link is set to jumbo frames and the other is not, large frames are dropped silently and the transfer stalls while small traffic appears fine. Matching MTU across every hop is required.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's warehouse sets the MTU to 9000 bytes on its storage servers and on the switch they connect to, and on the link between that switch and a second switch. A firewall on the path to a backup server has an interface set to 1500 bytes. A storage server sends an 8000-byte frame to the backup server. Step 1: the storage server sends the frame, and the MTU check passes because 8000 is under 9000. Step 2: the first switch forwards it over the 9000-byte link, and it passes. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the backup server never receives the frame, large transfers stall, and small test pings still succeed. Which choice correctly completes step 3?
choices: The firewall splits the 8000-byte frame into smaller 1500-byte frames and forwards each piece.
The firewall raises its interface MTU to 9000 automatically to match the switch it is connected to.
The firewall's interface cannot accept a frame larger than its 1500-byte MTU, so it discards the frame without notifying the sender.
The firewall strips the VLAN tag from the frame and forwards the unchanged 8000-byte frame onward.
questions.why: A frame larger than a link's MTU cannot be carried over that link at layer 2, and the receiving interface drops it silently, which is why only large transfers stall.

questions.prompt: A switch port is configured as a trunk. Which statement best describes what that port carries?
choices: Only jumbo frames of 9000 bytes, because trunks are reserved for large transfers.
One physical link that has been bundled with other links under LACP into a single logical link.
Several tagged VLANs at once, with each frame marked by its VLAN number so the switch knows which logical network it belongs to.
One untagged VLAN for a single end device, such as a printer.
questions.why: A trunk carries many VLANs over one link, and the 802.1Q tag on each frame tells the switch which VLAN the frame belongs to.

questions.prompt: Four 25 Gbps links are bundled as one link aggregation group between a storage array and a switch. One backup job copies a single large file between two hosts. What is the most that this one copy stream can use?
choices: 12.5 Gbps, because the bundle halves the capacity of every flow.
25 Gbps, because the bundle hashes each flow onto one member link and that flow stays on it.
100 Gbps, because all four member links are available to it.
50 Gbps, because the bundle always splits a flow across two links.
questions.why: A link aggregation group spreads different flows across its member links, but a single flow is pinned to one member, so one stream is capped at that member's speed while the 100 Gbps is only the total across many flows.

questions.prompt: A 10 km link between two campus buildings uses multimode fibre transceivers on both ends. The link never comes up, although a short test run inside one building worked. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The VLAN tags differ between the two buildings' switches, so frames are dropped before they reach the optics.
The link aggregation group lacks LACP, so the two buildings cannot agree on which fibre pair is active.
The multimode optics' maximum reach is shorter than 10 km, so single-mode optics are needed for that distance.
The MTU is set to 1500 bytes on both ends, which prevents the link from negotiating a connection.
questions.why: An optic's type sets its maximum reach, and multimode optics are built for short runs, so a 10 km run needs single-mode optics.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a VLAN and a LAG each do on a physical link, and name one limit that stops a LAG from doubling the speed of a single transfer.
lessons.modelAnswer: A VLAN lets one physical link carry several separate logical networks. Frames are tagged with a VLAN number, so the switch keeps each network's traffic apart, and a trunk port carries many tags at once. A LAG bundles several physical links into one logical link, which adds capacity for many flows together. The main limit is that the LAG hashes each flow onto a single member link, so one transfer is still capped at the speed of one physical cable. Doubling a single flow needs a different design. A related caveat is MTU: jumbo frames only help if every device on the path uses the same larger MTU, otherwise large frames are dropped.
rubricPoints: VLAN separates logical networks over one physical link using tags on frames
LAG bundles physical links for aggregate capacity
A single flow in a LAG is hashed onto one member, so it is capped at one link's speed
Jumbo frames require matching MTU on every hop or large frames are dropped

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly reference facts about standards, optics and settings that are best learned by reading, and no listed mission or planned engine covers physical-layer concepts.

lessons.plain: Encapsulation means wrapping one packet inside another so it can travel across a network that would not otherwise carry it correctly. A tunnel is the path those wrapped packets take between two endpoints. GRE is a simple wrapper that carries many kinds of traffic, including traffic that cannot normally cross the network, but it hides nothing. IPsec is a set of rules that encrypts and authenticates the traffic, so anyone watching the public path sees only scrambled data and the receiver knows the sender is genuine. Teams often use the two together: GRE for flexibility, IPsec for privacy. Knowing which one does what decides how you size, secure and troubleshoot a hybrid link.
lessons.guessPrompt: A link can carry packets up to 1500 bytes. If every packet must gain a few dozen bytes of extra headers before it crosses that link, what do you think happens to packets that were already close to 1500 bytes?
lessons.teach: Encapsulation means placing a complete packet inside the payload of another packet. The outer packet has its own IP header with new source and destination addresses, so it can cross a network that only understands those addresses. The logical path between the two outer endpoints is called a tunnel. GRE, Generic Routing Encapsulation, is a simple wrapper. It adds a small GRE header, typically 4 bytes, and it can carry multicast and routing protocol traffic such as BGP. GRE does not encrypt anything; its job is flexibility, not secrecy. IPsec is a framework for protecting IP traffic with confidentiality, integrity and authentication. IKE, Internet Key Exchange, lets both ends agree on keys and settings, forming a security association (SA) that describes how traffic is protected. ESP, Encapsulating Security Payload, then encrypts and authenticates each packet; in tunnel mode it wraps the whole original packet. Worked example: the path MTU, the largest packet the link carries, is 1500 bytes. An inner packet of 1400 bytes gains 24 bytes from GRE and about 60 from ESP tunnel mode, reaching roughly 1484 bytes, which fits. An inner packet of 1500 bytes becomes about 1584 and exceeds the path. With the Don't Fragment flag set, it is dropped, so small requests work while large transfers stall. The common mistake is assuming GRE is encrypted, or that IPsec alone carries routing multicast. Many designs run GRE inside IPsec so routing protocols work over an encrypted link. In production, an unnoticed MTU shortfall appears as hung large responses and BGP sessions that flap under load. Tunnel overhead shrinks the usable payload, so the size budget must be set before deployment, not after the first outage.

questions.prompt: A design runs a GRE tunnel inside an IPsec tunnel using ESP tunnel mode, so routing traffic can cross an encrypted link. The path MTU on this link is 1420 bytes. Assume GRE adds 24 bytes and ESP tunnel mode adds exactly 60 bytes. Worked check: an inner packet of 1300 bytes becomes 1300 + 24 + 60 = 1384 bytes, which fits. The missing step is finding the largest inner packet that still fits on this path. What is that size?
choices: 1396 bytes
1346 bytes
1360 bytes
1336 bytes
questions.why: The total overhead is 24 + 60 = 84 bytes, and subtracting 84 from the 1420-byte path MTU leaves 1336 bytes, while the other options subtract only one wrapper's overhead or make an arithmetic slip.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does a GRE tunnel do for the packets it carries?
choices: It encrypts the inner packet so that only the far end can read it.
It agrees on encryption keys with the far end and stores them in a security association.
It splits a large inner packet into fragments so each one fits the path MTU.
It wraps the inner packet in a new outer IP header with a small GRE header, so the packet can cross a network that only routes the outer addresses.
questions.why: GRE is an encapsulation wrapper that adds an outer IP header and a small GRE header, and it does not encrypt or split packets.

questions.prompt: A GRE-only tunnel crosses a path with a 1500-byte MTU. A 1480-byte inner packet is sent with the Don't Fragment flag set. Which outcome is correct?
choices: It is encrypted by GRE and then delivered, so size does not matter.
It is dropped, because the wrapped packet is about 1504 bytes and exceeds the path MTU.
It is fragmented by the tunnel and delivered in two pieces.
It is delivered unchanged, because 1480 is smaller than 1500.
questions.why: GRE adds 24 bytes, so 1480 becomes 1504, which exceeds the 1500-byte path and is dropped when Don't Fragment is set.

questions.prompt: Routing protocol traffic such as BGP must run between two sites over a link that must be encrypted. Which design fits this need?
choices: Use IPsec alone, since IPsec carries routing multicast by itself.
Use GRE alone, since GRE encrypts the routing traffic it carries.
Run GRE inside IPsec, so GRE carries the routing traffic and IPsec protects it.
Send BGP directly with no tunnel, since IPsec is only needed for user data.
questions.why: GRE provides the ability to carry routing protocol traffic, IPsec provides confidentiality and integrity, and combining them gives both; IPsec alone is not what carries routing multicast, so the correct design needs GRE inside IPsec.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we run GRE inside IPsec on our hybrid link instead of picking just one. Explain what each protocol contributes, and name one limit or tradeoff the combination creates.
lessons.modelAnswer: GRE and IPsec do different jobs, so the combination covers two needs. GRE gives us a tunnel that can carry things IPsec handles awkwardly on its own, such as multicast and dynamic routing with BGP, because the routers see the tunnel as an ordinary interface. IPsec protects that tunnel so traffic crossing the internet is encrypted and authenticated. Neither alone gives both properties: GRE alone is readable by anyone on the path, and IPsec in its common policy-based form often needs extra work to support routing protocols. The tradeoff is overhead. Each layer adds header bytes, so the usable MTU shrinks and large packets can fragment or drop unless we lower the tunnel MTU and clamp TCP MSS. We accept that cost and test the path size before go-live.
rubricPoints: Explains that GRE provides the tunnel and carries routing or multicast traffic but does not encrypt
Explains that IPsec provides encryption, integrity and authentication for the tunnel
States a concrete limit, such as added header overhead reducing the usable MTU
Mentions a remedy such as lowering the tunnel MTU or clamping TCP MSS, or testing path size

suggested.rationale: This objective is protocol facts and header arithmetic, and none of the listed missions or planned engines teaches tunnel encryption or MTU budgeting directly.

lessons.plain: Hybrid connectivity means linking the computers and networks you run in your own building or data center with the cloud accounts where other computers run. Before anyone picks a link type, a cable, a tunnel, or a routing setup, the design needs a list of answers: how much data must move, how quickly, how often the link must stay up, which addresses each side uses, and who may send what across it. This objective is about writing that list first and checking whether it is complete, so the design that comes later is justified rather than guessed.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company says it needs a private link between its office data center and the cloud by next month. Before you choose any link type, what three facts would you most want to know, and why would each one change your choice?
lessons.teach:
Hybrid connectivity is the set of network paths between an on-premises site (your own data center or office) and one or more cloud networks. In AWS terms, a cloud network is a VPC, a virtual private cloud: an isolated network inside a cloud account, addressed by a CIDR block such as 10.0.0.0/16, which is a range of addresses written as a prefix. Requirements are the measurable facts a design must satisfy. The main ones are bandwidth (how much data per second, at peak), latency (the delay for a packet to travel one way or round trip), availability (the percentage of time the link must work), address space (which IP ranges each side uses), and routing (whether routes are typed in by hand, called static routing, or exchanged automatically, called dynamic routing using BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol). Why this comes first: every link option trades these numbers against each other, so a choice made without them cannot be defended.

Worked example. A site has 800 Mbps peak traffic to the cloud, a round-trip budget of 25 ms, a 99.9% availability target, and an on-premises range of 10.0.0.0/16. Step 1: 800 Mbps peak with headroom points to a link of at least 1 Gbps. Step 2: 99.9% allows about 43 minutes of downtime per month, which a single link without a tested failover path usually cannot promise, so redundancy becomes a requirement. Step 3: the 25 ms budget depends on distance to the cloud region, so you check that before committing. Step 4: if the cloud VPC also uses 10.0.0.0/16, the two ranges overlap, and routing cannot tell them apart. That must be found now. Step 5: failover between redundant paths needs dynamic routing, so BGP is required.

Common mistake: starting from a product ('we need a dedicated link') and then backfilling the numbers. Consequence: if an overlapping range is found after cutover, traffic for the shared addresses goes to the wrong place or nowhere, and the migration stops until addresses are renumbered or translated.

Requirements gathered first are what make the hybrid design defensible.

questions.prompt: A distributor has a warehouse site with 300 Mbps peak traffic to its cloud network, a 20 ms round-trip budget, a 99.95% availability target, and an on-premises range of 192.168.0.0/16. Its planned cloud VPC uses 10.40.0.0/16. Step 1: 300 Mbps peak with headroom points to a link of at least 500 Mbps. Step 2: ____ (this step is missing; it converts the 99.95% target into allowed downtime per month). Step 3: the measured round trip to the chosen region is 35 ms, which is above the 20 ms budget, so the region choice must change. Step 4: the two ranges do not overlap, so addressing is clear. Step 5: because the target needs a failover path, redundancy and dynamic routing (BGP) are required. Which completion fills Step 2?
choices: About 4 hours, since 99.95% is only a small change from 99%
About 2 minutes, because 0.05% of an hour is the full monthly allowance
About 22 minutes, because 99.95% allows half the downtime that 99.9% allows
About 43 minutes, the same as 99.9%, because both round to three nines
questions.why: The 99.9% target allows about 43 minutes of downtime per month, and 99.95% halves the 0.1% failure budget to 0.05%, giving about 22 minutes.

questions.prompt: A clinic's nightly file sync needs about 200 Mbps during its busiest hour. Which requirement does that figure describe?
choices: Bandwidth
Latency
Availability
Address space
questions.why: Bandwidth is the amount of data per second that must move, measured at peak, so a 200 Mbps busiest-hour figure is a bandwidth requirement.

questions.prompt: A university's on-premises range is 10.8.0.0/16 and the planned cloud VPC is 10.8.64.0/18. What is the main problem with this plan?
choices: The latency budget is too tight for any region
The VPC is too small to hold the on-premises site
Static routing cannot carry traffic to a VPC at all
The two ranges overlap, so routing cannot tell shared addresses apart; find this before cutover
questions.why: The VPC range sits inside the on-premises range, so the two overlap, and routing cannot distinguish them, which must be caught before migration.

questions.prompt: A design uses one link and a 99.99% availability target. Which conclusion is correct?
choices: Redundancy is required: 99.99% allows only about 4 minutes of downtime a month, which a single unprotected path usually cannot promise
Dynamic routing is unnecessary, because availability depends only on bandwidth
A bigger link alone meets the target, because bandwidth limits downtime
A single link suffices, since availability describes only the cloud side
questions.why: Scaling the 99.9% figure of about 43 minutes down by a factor of ten gives about 4 minutes, which a single path without tested failover usually cannot guarantee, so redundancy is needed.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should order a dedicated hybrid link to the cloud this week because the application is moving. In your own words, explain which requirements you would gather first, which of them would change the link choice, and one limit or tradeoff that remains even after you have the answers.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not order anything yet. First I'd collect the peak data rate and growth, the round-trip latency the application can tolerate, the availability target, the on-premises and cloud address ranges, and whether the routing must fail over automatically. Peak rate and latency narrow the link size and the region choice. The availability target usually rules out a single path, so we'd need redundancy and dynamic routing with BGP. The address ranges are the quickest to check and the most damaging if missed, since overlapping CIDR blocks break routing. The remaining limit is that these numbers are estimates. Traffic can grow faster than forecast, and a link that meets today's requirements may need a new design in a year, so the design should be reviewed when the numbers change.
rubricPoints: Names the core requirements to gather before choosing a link: bandwidth at peak, latency, availability, address ranges, and routing needs.
Explains that the requirements determine the link type and redundancy, not the other way round.
Flags overlapping address ranges as an early check, since they block routing or force translation.
States a real limit: requirements are estimates and can change, so the design needs review.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the requirements back to a teammate, with a named tradeoff, is the core skill for this objective, and no listed mission or engine covers hybrid requirements gathering.

lessons.plain: Hybrid connectivity links your own data centre or office network to a cloud network so traffic can flow both ways. AWS Direct Connect is a dedicated private line you order into AWS through a provider in a shared facility. AWS Site-to-Site VPN sends encrypted traffic over the public internet between your router and AWS. Designing redundant hybrid connectivity means planning for one path failing: you use two or more paths, decide which one carries traffic normally, and make sure the backup takes over without someone intervening. The real question is not just whether you have two links, but whether they fail independently and whether routing actually switches to the backup.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your office reaches AWS through one leased private line, and that line is its only path to the cloud. What single failure would cut off all hybrid traffic, and what would you add to remove that single point of failure?
lessons.teach:
Terms first. A Direct Connect connection is a dedicated private link from your facility to AWS, ordered through a provider at a colocation facility, which is a building where many networks meet. A Site-to-Site VPN is an IPsec tunnel, an encrypted tunnel carried over the internet, between your router and AWS; each VPN connection gives you two tunnels to two AWS endpoints. BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the routing protocol both sides use to announce which address ranges they can reach. An AS path is the list of network numbers a route has crossed, and BGP normally prefers the shorter one. Prepending means adding your own network number to the AS path again so a route looks longer and is less preferred.

Why it works: redundancy is about independent failure. Two circuits in one facility can still fail together if the building or its equipment fails, and a VPN over the same internet provider shares that provider's fate. So you pair a primary path with a backup on a different path and let BGP choose. The primary advertises routes with a short AS path; the backup advertises the same prefixes with a prepended, longer path, so your routers prefer the primary. When the primary BGP session drops, its routes are withdrawn and only the backup routes remain. Each side chooses its own outbound path, so you set preferences on both your router and the AWS side.

Worked example: your data centre advertises 10.20.0.0/16 over both paths. Over Direct Connect the AS path is 65000. Over the VPN it is 65000 65000 65000. Your router compares the two, picks the shorter one, and sends traffic over Direct Connect. If the circuit fails, BGP notices when its session times out, the Direct Connect route disappears, and traffic moves to the VPN. Failover speed is therefore set by BGP detection time.

Common mistake: adding a static route for the same prefix on the VPN with no preference set. Traffic may split unpredictably, or the backup never carries traffic until the primary fails, so the failover was never tested.

Consequence: a backup that has never carried live traffic is an untested assumption, and you will discover it is broken during an outage.

questions.prompt: A clinic runs a Direct Connect circuit and a Site-to-Site VPN to reach its cloud VPC. Its on-premises range is 172.20.0.0/16. The team has completed these steps: (1) advertise 172.20.0.0/16 over Direct Connect with AS path 64512, where an AS path is the list of network numbers a route has crossed, and BGP (Border Gateway Protocol, the routing protocol both sides use to announce reachable ranges) normally prefers the shorter one; (2) advertise 172.20.0.0/16 over the VPN with prepending, meaning the clinic's own network number is repeated so the route looks longer, giving AS path 64512 64512 64512. The clinic's router now prefers Direct Connect for outbound traffic. The team has not yet done one more step needed so that replies from the cloud also prefer Direct Connect. Which step is missing?
choices: Set a matching preference on the AWS side so that traffic coming back toward the clinic also prefers the Direct Connect path.
Add a static route for 172.20.0.0/16 on the VPN with no preference set, so both paths are always in use.
Shorten the VPN AS path to 64512 so it matches the Direct Connect path and the router balances traffic.
Nothing else is needed, because BGP on the clinic router automatically controls return traffic from the cloud.
questions.why: Each side chooses its own outbound path, so the AWS side needs its own preference set for return traffic to follow the primary.

questions.prompt: In BGP, what is an AS path?
choices: The number of encrypted tunnels a Site-to-Site VPN connection provides to AWS.
The physical cable route a Direct Connect circuit takes through the colocation facility.
The list of network numbers a route has crossed, which BGP normally prefers when it is shorter.
The range of IP addresses a router is permitted to announce to its neighbours.
questions.why: The teaching text defines the AS path as the list of network numbers a route has crossed, with shorter paths normally preferred.

questions.prompt: A company has an on-premises range of 10.80.0.0/18 and wants a Site-to-Site VPN used only when its Direct Connect circuit fails. Which setup meets that goal?
choices: Advertise the prefix over both paths and prepend the VPN advertisement so its AS path is longer than the Direct Connect path.
Advertise the same prefix over the VPN with the same AS path length as the Direct Connect route so both are used.
Advertise the prefix over the VPN with no prepending and no static route, so the VPN is used whenever it is up.
Add a static route for 10.80.0.0/18 on the VPN with no preference set, so the backup is always in place.
questions.why: Prepending makes the VPN path longer so BGP prefers Direct Connect, and the VPN carries traffic only after the primary routes are withdrawn.

questions.prompt: A primary Direct Connect BGP session times out. What happens to traffic, based on how the backup is designed?
choices: Traffic stops until an engineer manually edits the router configuration to point at the VPN.
AWS reroutes the traffic on the company's behalf without any change needed on the company's router.
The VPN tunnels take over instantly with zero delay because they were already established before the failure.
The routes learned over Direct Connect are withdrawn and traffic moves to the remaining VPN routes, with failover speed set by BGP detection time.
questions.why: When the primary BGP session drops, its routes are withdrawn, and the remaining backup routes carry traffic after BGP detects the failure.

lessons.explainPrompt: A colleague says we already have Direct Connect, so we do not need a VPN. Explain to them in your own words what the VPN adds, how you would make it a backup rather than a second active path, and one limit of this design.
lessons.modelAnswer: The VPN adds a second, independent path. Direct Connect is a private circuit, but it still runs through one provider and one facility, so a site-level outage or a carrier problem can take it down. A Site-to-Site VPN runs over the internet, which has different failure points. To make it a backup, I would advertise the same office prefixes over the VPN with a longer AS path, using AS path prepending, so our routers prefer Direct Connect while it is healthy. When the circuit's BGP session drops, the VPN routes become the only ones and traffic moves over. The limit is that failover is only as quick as BGP detection, and the VPN usually has less bandwidth than the circuit, so performance may drop during failover. I would also test the failover on purpose rather than assume it works.
rubricPoints: The VPN is a second path with different failure points, not just extra capacity.
The backup is made less preferred with BGP attributes such as AS path prepending.
Failover speed depends on BGP session detection and route withdrawal.
Names a limit such as lower VPN bandwidth or the need to test failover.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a scenario with a failed primary path adds the most here, and no listed mission or planned engine covers hybrid routing design directly.

lessons.plain: BGP is the protocol two networks use to tell each other which address ranges they can reach. When you have two or more links to the same place, such as a cloud connection and a backup link, BGP attributes are labels on each route that decide which link gets used. You can make one link the preferred path and the other a standby, or let traffic split across both. The labels only influence choices, and each one only affects traffic in the direction it is set on.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have two links to the same cloud network, and you want most traffic to use the first one with the second as a backup. Before any rules are explained, which side of the connection would you change first, and why might changing only one side not be enough?
lessons.teach:
BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol, is the routing protocol that exchanges reachability between autonomous systems, meaning separately run networks that each have their own number, called an ASN. Each route it advertises carries attributes, which are pieces of metadata. The AS path is the list of networks a route has crossed. Local preference is a value used only inside your own network to rank exits. MED, the multi-exit discriminator, is a hint sent to a neighbor about which of your entry links it should prefer. Communities are tags the other side reads and acts on.

Why it works: when several routes reach the same destination, a router compares attributes in a fixed order and keeps one best path. Local preference is checked early, so a higher value on one exit makes your outbound traffic leave that way. The AS path is checked later, and a shorter path wins. Prepending repeats your own ASN in the path on the backup link, making that path look longer, which steers the other network's inbound traffic toward the primary.

Worked example: your data center advertises the same prefix over link A and link B. You set local preference 200 on A and 100 on B, so outbound traffic uses A. On B you prepend your ASN three times, so remote networks prefer A for inbound too. If A fails, its BGP session drops, its routes are withdrawn, and B carries everything. That is active/passive. For load sharing, you give both links equal preference so the router can use both, or you split by prefix, sending one range preferentially over A and another over B.

Common mistake: tuning only one direction. Local preference affects only what you send out, and prepending affects only what others send in. A route that looks correct from one end can silently send return traffic down the backup link, which may have less capacity and can break stateful firewalls that only saw the outbound leg. Verify the best path from both ends.

BGP attributes give you control of traffic shape, but they guide choices rather than guarantee them.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm with ASN 64520 advertises its depot prefix 10.60.0.0/16 over two links, east and west. The goal is that outbound traffic leaves by the east link and that remote networks send inbound traffic to the east link too. The team's plan has three steps. Step 1: advertise 10.60.0.0/16 over both links. Step 2: [MISSING]. Step 3: prepend ASN 64520 two times on the west link so its path looks longer to remote networks. Which choice correctly fills step 2?
choices: Set MED on the west link to 500 so that the outbound path from the depot prefers east
Add a community tag to the east link so that the depot's own routers prefer it
Set local preference to 120 on the west link and 250 on the east link so outbound traffic chooses east
Remove the prepend from the east link so its AS path is shorter than the west link's path
questions.why: Local preference is the attribute checked early and used only inside your own network to rank exits, so giving east the higher value sends outbound traffic east, which is what step 2 needs to achieve.

questions.prompt: Which BGP attribute is used only inside your own network to rank which exit your outbound traffic should take?
choices: Community
Local preference
MED
AS path
questions.why: Local preference is set and compared only within your own network and controls which exit outbound traffic uses; the other three either describe route length, tag routes for a neighbor, or hint to a neighbor about entry links.

questions.prompt: A media company sets a higher local preference on its primary link, but its remote peers keep sending inbound traffic over the secondary link. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The primary link's routes are being ignored because local preference values above 100 are not valid
Local preference only controls the company's outbound exit, so the remote peers' inbound choice depends on attributes they compare, such as AS path length
Community tags on the secondary link have replaced local preference for everything
The secondary link has a higher ASN, which overrides local preference on the remote side
questions.why: Local preference affects only what the company sends out, so inbound steering depends on the attributes the remote network compares, such as AS path length, which the company must influence separately.

questions.prompt: A fintech company has two links to the same provider and two prefixes, 10.80.0.0/17 and 10.80.128.0/17, both advertised on each link. It wants both links carrying real traffic at the same time, with each link handling a different prefix. Which design achieves this?
choices: Prepend both links by the same number of times so that they tie, then leave the choice to the routers
Prefer the first /17 over the first link and the second /17 over the second link, using per-prefix preferences
Add the same MED value to both links so the neighbor splits traffic evenly across every prefix
Set local preference to 0 on the second link so that it stays idle until the first link fails
questions.why: Splitting by prefix, with each prefix preferring a different link, lets both links carry traffic at once, whereas the other options either keep one link idle or leave the split to chance.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would make one of two hybrid links the preferred path with the other as a standby, and name one limit or tradeoff of the method you chose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would keep both links advertising the same routes, then set a higher local preference on the primary link so our outbound traffic leaves through it. On the standby link I would prepend our ASN a couple of times so remote networks prefer the primary for inbound traffic too, and I would confirm the best path from both ends. The limit is that prepending is only a preference, not a guarantee. The other network can override it through its own policy, so some inbound traffic may still arrive on the standby. Local preference also only controls exits from my side. Failover speed depends on the primary session dropping, so slow failure detection means a slower switch.
rubricPoints: Local preference sets the outbound preferred exit inside your own network.
AS path prepending on the backup link influences the remote network's inbound choice.
Attributes must be verified in both directions, not only one.
Preference is not a guarantee, since the other network can override it, and failover depends on session failure detection.

suggested.rationale: Choosing which side to tune and how to verify both directions is best learned by reasoning through a hybrid failover situation, and no listed mission or planned engine covers BGP attributes directly.

lessons.plain: Many companies connect branch offices over ordinary internet links that are managed by a software-defined wide area network (SD-WAN) appliance, which chooses paths and encrypts traffic between sites. Connecting that setup to AWS means the cloud side must learn which branch networks sit behind which appliance. This objective is about letting the SD-WAN's routes and the AWS transit hub share that knowledge automatically, so the hub can reach the branches and the branches can reach cloud workloads, without rebuilding the whole network by hand.
lessons.guessPrompt: A branch office reaches AWS through a vendor SD-WAN box, and only that box knows which addresses sit behind the branch. How would you get those addresses into your AWS network without typing every route by hand, and what could go wrong if two branches used the same address range?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. An overlay network is a virtual network built on top of another network, called the underlay, such as internet links. An SD-WAN appliance builds encrypted overlay tunnels between branch sites and cloud sites. AWS Transit Gateway is a regional hub that connects VPCs, VPNs and Direct Connect, and a route table inside it decides where each packet goes. Transit Gateway Connect is an attachment that lets a third-party appliance peer with the hub. It runs over Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE, a simple tunnel wrapper) for the data path and Border Gateway Protocol (BGP, which exchanges route announcements) for the control path. It sits on top of a normal VPC attachment, called the transport attachment, where the appliance lives.

Why it works: BGP carries branch prefixes from the SD-WAN into the hub dynamically, so the hub learns a new branch without an operator editing static routes. GRE carries the packets, and multiple tunnels let the hub spread load across them.

Worked example: an appliance in a transport VPC learns branch prefix 10.50.0.0/16 from the overlay. First, it announces that prefix to the hub over BGP on a Connect peer. Second, the hub's route table, with propagation enabled, installs 10.50.0.0/16 pointing at the Connect attachment. Third, a workload in a spoke VPC at 10.20.1.10 sends to 10.50.4.7, and its VPC route table forwards the 10.50.0.0/16 range to the hub. Fourth, the hub matches the route, wraps the packet in GRE, and hands it to the appliance. Fifth, the appliance sends it across the overlay to the branch.

Common mistake: two branches using the same 10.50.0.0/16 range, or a missing route table association. Overlapping ranges make routes ambiguous, so reachability to one site fails quietly.

Consequence: if the only appliance fails, every branch behind it becomes unreachable from AWS. Running two appliances or two tunnels per attachment lets BGP fail over to the surviving path.

questions.prompt: A retail company has a branch office with prefix 172.18.0.0/20 reached through an SD-WAN overlay. An appliance in a transport VPC reaches the AWS Transit Gateway hub over a Transit Gateway Connect attachment (a hub attachment that runs GRE for the data path and BGP for route exchange). A workload in a spoke VPC at 10.90.2.15 must reply to a branch host. Trace the return path in five steps. Step 1: the branch host sends a packet to 10.90.2.15 across the overlay, and the appliance receives it. Step 2: the appliance wraps the packet in GRE and passes it to the hub over the Connect peer. Step 3: [MISSING]. Step 4: the hub hands the packet to the spoke VPC attachment, and the spoke delivers it to 10.90.2.15. Fill in step 3.
choices: The spoke VPC's route table forwards 172.18.0.0/20 to an internet gateway so the reply can leave AWS.
The branch router is given a static route to 10.90.0.0/16 that points at the transport VPC subnet, so the hub is bypassed.
The appliance re-announces 172.18.0.0/20 to the spoke VPC over BGP so the spoke learns the branch.
The hub's route table, which has propagation enabled from the spoke VPC attachment, matches 10.90.0.0/16 and selects that spoke attachment as the next hop.
questions.why: The hub's route table decides where each packet goes, and a propagated route from the spoke attachment tells it that 10.90.0.0/16 belongs to that spoke.

questions.prompt: In an SD-WAN setup with Transit Gateway Connect, what is the main job of BGP (Border Gateway Protocol, a protocol that exchanges route announcements)?
choices: To assign IP addresses to each branch office from the transport VPC's subnet.
To wrap packets in an encrypted tunnel so they can cross the public internet.
To carry the packets themselves between the appliance and the hub.
To announce branch prefixes from the SD-WAN to the hub so the hub learns new branches without manual static routes.
questions.why: BGP carries route announcements; the tunnel wrapping is GRE and the address assignment is not part of this design.

questions.prompt: A company has two branch offices, and both are announced into the hub with the same prefix 192.168.10.0/24. A host at one branch cannot reach a server that is reachable from the other, and nothing in the logs flags an error. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The transport attachment has been deleted, so the hub has no path to any branch.
The hub has two equal-looking routes for the same range, so reachability to one site fails quietly.
The GRE tunnel has exceeded its maximum packet size and silently drops all traffic.
The Connect peer is using BGP, which cannot carry more than one route per prefix.
questions.why: Overlapping ranges make routes ambiguous, so one site's reachability fails without an explicit error.

questions.prompt: A transport VPC runs one SD-WAN appliance on a Connect attachment that serves four branch offices. The team wants to remove the single point of failure. Which change most directly helps the hub keep reaching all four branches if the appliance fails?
choices: Add a second appliance with its own Connect peer, so BGP can fail over to the surviving path.
Move the four branch prefixes into a single larger summary range to reduce route count.
Turn off route propagation on the hub so routes stay static and do not change during a failure.
Increase the size of the appliance instance so it has more CPU to handle the traffic.
questions.why: Running a second appliance or tunnel gives BGP a surviving path to fail over to, while a bigger instance or static routes do not remove the single point of failure.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an SD-WAN overlay connects to a Transit Gateway through Connect, and name one limit or tradeoff of the design.
lessons.modelAnswer: The SD-WAN appliance runs in a VPC attached to the Transit Gateway as the transport. A Connect attachment on top of that VPC attachment carries GRE tunnels for the packets and BGP sessions for the routes. The appliance advertises branch prefixes over BGP, the hub installs them in its route table, and traffic from spoke VPCs follows those routes into the tunnels. The tradeoff is that the design depends on the appliance and its BGP sessions: if the appliance or its tunnels fail, branch reachability drops unless there is a second appliance or tunnel. Address planning matters too, because overlapping branch ranges cannot be routed cleanly through one hub. Bandwidth is shared across tunnels, so capacity has to be planned, not assumed.
rubricPoints: Describes the Connect attachment as sitting on a transport VPC attachment that hosts the SD-WAN appliance.
Explains that GRE carries the data path and BGP carries the dynamic route exchange.
Notes that branch routes reach the hub dynamically and must be propagated into the right route table.
States a concrete limit: a single appliance or tunnel is a single point of failure, so redundancy is needed.
Mentions that overlapping address ranges across branches create ambiguous routing.

suggested.rationale: A design scenario that forces the learner to reason about routes, failure, and address overlap adds more than reading the facts alone, and no listed mission or planned engine covers hybrid network design directly.

lessons.plain: When a company runs several separate networks, such as one per team or per project, those networks start out isolated, so traffic cannot pass between them by default. This lesson covers three common ways to let them talk. One is a direct link between two networks, like a private bridge between two houses. Another is a central hub that many networks plug into, like a roundabout where every road meets at one junction. The third lets one network offer a single service to another without exposing the rest of its network, like handing over one door key instead of the house key. Choosing among them depends on how many networks there are, whether their address numbers overlap, and how much each side should be able to see.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have five separate office networks, and all of them need to reach one billing service that lives on one of those networks. Would you connect every office directly to every other office, or route them through one shared point? Give your reason.
lessons.teach:
A VPC (virtual private cloud) is an isolated network you define inside a cloud account, with its own address range written in CIDR notation, such as 10.1.0.0/16. Two VPCs cannot reach each other until you connect them. VPC peering is a direct, private, one-to-one connection between two VPCs, in the same or different accounts and Regions. Each side must add a route in its own route table that points the other side's address range at the peering connection, and the two ranges must not overlap. Peering is not transitive: if A peers with B and B peers with C, A cannot reach C through B.

A Transit Gateway is a regional hub that VPCs, VPNs and Direct Connect links attach to.
