Each attachment is associated with a route table inside the hub, and routes in those tables decide which attachments can reach which. Traffic can flow through the hub from any attachment to any other attachment that the route tables allow. This replaces a full mesh: ten VPCs need ten attachments instead of forty-five peering links. Because the hub routes between attachments, it is transitive, and you control who talks to whom through the route tables.

AWS PrivateLink works differently. A provider publishes one service behind a Network Load Balancer. A consumer creates an interface endpoint, which places network interfaces with private addresses inside the consumer's own subnets. Only that service is reachable, and only in one direction, from consumer to provider. Because the consumer sees only local addresses, overlapping CIDR ranges do not block it.

Worked example: three VPCs, A 10.1.0.0/16, B 10.2.0.0/16 and C 10.3.0.0/16. Step 1: peer A with B and B with C. Step 2: A sends to C, but no peering links A and C, so the packet has no route and fails. Step 3: attach all three to one Transit Gateway, add a route in each attachment's table for the other two ranges, and A reaches C through the hub.

Common mistake: adding a route only on the requesting side of a peering. Replies then go nowhere and the failure looks like one-way timeouts.

Consequence in a running system: a half-built route makes a service appear reachable from one side while the other side's health checks or callbacks silently time out.

Pick the pattern that matches how many networks you have, whether their addresses overlap, and which direction traffic must flow.

questions.prompt: Lumen Freight has VPC North at 192.168.0.0/20 and VPC South at 192.168.64.0/20, both in eu-west-1, and wants them connected with VPC peering. The steps completed so far are: (1) South's owner sends a peering request to North. (2) North's owner accepts the request. (3) North's owner adds a route in North's route table for 192.168.64.0/20 pointing at the peering connection. Which step is still missing so that traffic works in both directions?
choices: Add a route in South's route table for 192.168.0.0/20 pointing at the peering connection
Attach both VPCs to a new Transit Gateway so the route tables do the work
Change South's range to 192.168.0.0/20 so the two ranges match
Send a second peering request from North to South so the first one is not used
questions.why: Peering needs a route on each side that points the other side's range at the connection, so without South's route, replies from North have no path back.

questions.prompt: A company runs seven VPCs across two accounts, all in one Region, and every VPC must be able to reach every other VPC. Which connection pattern keeps the number of links manageable as more VPCs are added?
choices: A Transit Gateway hub with one attachment per VPC
A single subnet shared across both accounts
A full mesh of VPC peering links, one link for each pair of VPCs
One PrivateLink interface endpoint for each pair of VPCs
questions.why: A Transit Gateway hub needs one attachment per VPC, while a full mesh of peering needs a link for every pair, so the hub scales far better and also routes between attachments transitively.

questions.prompt: A consumer VPC uses 10.1.0.0/16 and a provider VPC also uses 10.1.0.0/16. The provider publishes a service behind a Network Load Balancer. Can the consumer reach the service through a PrivateLink interface endpoint, and why?
choices: No, because the provider's service must sit inside the consumer's own address range
Yes, because the endpoint's network interfaces sit in the consumer's subnets with local addresses, so the overlap does not block it
Yes, but only after peering is added between the two VPCs first
No, the ranges must be renumbered before any connection is possible
questions.why: PrivateLink places interfaces with private addresses inside the consumer's own subnets, so the consumer never routes to the provider's address range and overlapping CIDRs do not block it.

questions.prompt: A provider team publishes a service through PrivateLink. Which statement correctly describes which side can start connections to that service?
choices: Either side can start connections, because the endpoint is bidirectional
Only the provider can start connections, through the endpoint it creates
Only the consumer can start connections to the published service, through its interface endpoint
Both sides must each create an endpoint that points at the other
questions.why: PrivateLink is one-directional: the consumer creates an interface endpoint and initiates traffic to the provider's single published service, not the other way around.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate proposes connecting six VPCs with VPC peering so that every pair can talk. Explain to them what that costs, what a Transit Gateway would change, and one limit that still applies.
lessons.modelAnswer: A full mesh of six VPCs needs fifteen peering connections, and each one needs routes on both sides. Peering is not transitive, so every new network means more links, and the routes become hard to audit. A Transit Gateway gives each VPC one attachment to a central hub, and its route tables decide which pairs may talk, so adding a network means one attachment. The cost is a hub charge plus data processing, and the hub is a regional resource with its own quotas. One limit still applies to both designs: overlapping address ranges cannot be routed to each other, so address planning still matters. If only one service needs to be shared, PrivateLink may be the simpler fit.
rubricPoints: Peering is one-to-one and not transitive, so a full mesh grows quickly in links and routes.
A Transit Gateway uses one attachment per network and route tables to control which pairs can talk.
The hub has costs and quotas that must be weighed in the design.
Overlapping CIDR ranges still create routing problems, so address planning is still required.
PrivateLink suits sharing one service in one direction without exposing the whole network.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet hop by hop across peering links and hub route tables is the skill this objective needs, and a path tracer would practise it directly.

lessons.plain: Imagine a building owned by one landlord with several floors. Each tenant company can set up its own office on a floor, but the landlord still controls the doors, the wiring and the front entrance. VPC sharing works like that for cloud networks. One account owns a private network and hands some of its smaller sections to other accounts in the same company. Those accounts can place their own servers in those sections, but they cannot rewire the building. Keeping one set of network rules in one place lets many teams build without each running a separate network that has to be connected and planned on its own.
lessons.guessPrompt: If three teams in one company each need servers on a private cloud network, why might one central team own that network and simply hand out sections of it, instead of every team building its own network?
lessons.teach:
A VPC (virtual private cloud) is an isolated private network inside a cloud account. A subnet is a smaller address range carved out of a VPC, placed in one availability zone (one isolated data center within a region). VPC sharing means the account that owns the VPC shares selected subnets with other accounts in the same organization. In AWS this is done through Resource Access Manager (RAM), a service for sharing resources between accounts. The owner account keeps control of the network layer: the VPC itself, route tables (rules that decide where traffic goes), network ACLs (stateless filters on traffic entering or leaving a subnet), internet and NAT gateways (which let private servers reach outside networks), and connections to other networks. Participant accounts launch their own resources, such as servers, into the shared subnets. They manage their own security groups (per-resource firewall rules), pay for their own resources, and cannot see or change each other's resources.

Why it works: many teams draw from one large, governed address space and one set of routing and egress controls. Separate networks would each need their own connections, peering and address planning, and overlapping address ranges make those connections hard to build.

Worked example: Account A owns VPC 10.0.0.0/16 with a private subnet 10.0.1.0/24 in one availability zone, and shares that subnet with Account B. Step 1: B sees the subnet and launches an application server into it, which receives an address such as 10.0.1.25. Step 2: the route table belongs to A, so B's server uses A's routes to reach outside networks through A's NAT gateway. Step 3: B tries to add a route or change the VPC's settings and is refused, because B does not own the VPC.

Common mistake: assuming sharing gives participants a copy of the VPC or the right to edit its routing. Consequence: if the owner deletes a route or changes a network ACL, every workload in that subnet changes behavior at once, so these changes need central ownership and review.

questions.prompt: Halvorsen Logistics owns a VPC with address range 172.20.0.0/16 and shares the subnet 172.20.4.0/24, which sits in one availability zone, with its warehouse team's account (Account C) through Resource Access Manager. Step 1: Account C launches a barcode-scanner service into the shared subnet, and it receives the address 172.20.4.60. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: Account C's scanners reach the partner network 192.168.50.0/24 through the owner's VPN connection, even though Account C has no permission to edit the route table.
choices: Account C adds the same route to its own copy of the route table, and the owner then copies that change back into the VPC.
Account C creates a second subnet using the same 172.20.4.0/24 range so that the partner route can apply to it.
The owner account adds a route for 192.168.50.0/24 that points to the VPN connection in the owner's route table.
Account C turns on VPC peering with the partner network, which removes the need for any change to the owner's route table.
questions.why: Because the owner keeps control of the route tables, the owner must add the route to its own table, and that single change is what lets the shared subnet's workloads reach the partner network.

questions.prompt: In a multi-account setup using VPC sharing, which set of permissions best describes a participant account?
choices: It may launch resources into the shared subnets and manage its own security groups, but it cannot change the VPC's routing or see other accounts' resources.
It controls the NAT gateway and internet gateway, but not the security groups of its own servers.
It owns the shared subnets and decides which other accounts may launch servers into them.
It receives a full copy of the owner's VPC and may edit its route tables and network ACLs.
questions.why: A participant launches its own resources into shared subnets and manages its own per-resource firewall rules, while the owner keeps the VPC, route tables, network ACLs, and gateways.

questions.prompt: A participant team reports that its servers in a shared subnet lost outside connectivity after the owner account removed a route from the shared route table. Which explanation best fits the teaching text?
choices: The participant's security groups were changed by the owner, which blocked the traffic.
The subnet was deleted and recreated, which gave the servers new addresses without routes.
The servers were moved to a different availability zone, which always removes outside access.
The route table belongs to the owner, so the removal affects every workload in that subnet at once, and the participant could not have prevented it.
questions.why: Route tables are owned by the VPC owner and apply to all resources in the shared subnet, so one removed route changes behavior for every workload in that subnet.

questions.prompt: Three teams in separate accounts each built their networks on the same address range, 10.0.0.0/16. The company now wants them connected to each other and to a shared service. Why does this make the plan hard, and why does VPC sharing help?
choices: Overlapping ranges make connections hard to build, and sharing one large governed address space avoids the overlap by letting teams draw from a single plan.
Overlapping ranges only slow down traffic, so sharing fixes performance but not connectivity.
Identical ranges are a security feature that VPC sharing removes, so the teams must rebuild their networks from scratch.
Identical ranges force each team to use a different cloud region, and sharing only works within one region.
questions.why: The teaching text notes that overlapping address ranges make connections hard to build, and that many teams drawing from one governed address space avoids that problem.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we do not give every team its own full network account. Explain what sharing subnets from one owner account gives us, and name one limit or tradeoff we would have to accept.
lessons.modelAnswer: With VPC sharing, one account owns the network: the VPC, its route tables, network ACLs, and the gateways that reach outside networks. It shares some subnets with the other accounts in the organization, and their teams launch servers into those subnets. We get one governed address space and one set of egress and routing controls, so we do not have to build and peer a separate network for each team, and we avoid the address overlap that makes later connections hard. The tradeoff is central dependence. The owner team controls routing and network rules, so a change in the owner account can affect every participant's workloads in the shared subnet at once. Participants also cannot change the VPC itself, so they need to request network changes from the owner. We would need clear change review and monitoring to manage that.
rubricPoints: Names the owner account and the shared subnets, and says participants launch their own resources into them
Explains that the owner keeps control of routing, network ACLs and gateways
States a concrete benefit such as one governed address space or avoiding many peering links
Names a real limit, such as central dependence, shared blast radius, or participants being unable to change the VPC

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining who owns what and what sharing limits, which is best practiced by saying it back to a teammate.

lessons.plain: Two networks overlap when they use the same block of private addresses, for example if both use 10.0.0.0/16. When you try to connect them, a router cannot tell which network a packet belongs to, so traffic goes to the wrong place or nowhere. This objective is about choosing a way around that problem. You can translate addresses at a boundary so each side sees a different range, you can expose one specific service through a private endpoint so no routes between the networks are needed, or you can use a central hub that routes between networks while each keeps its own address plan. Each choice trades off simplicity, cost, and how much of one network the other side can see.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company's office network and your cloud network both use the address range 10.0.0.0/16. A server in the cloud needs to reach a database at 10.0.5.10 in the office. Why might simply connecting the two networks fail, and what single change would you consider first?
lessons.teach: A CIDR block is a range of IP addresses written like 10.0.0.0/16, where the number after the slash says how many leading bits are fixed. Two networks overlap when they share addresses from their ranges. NAT (network address translation) is a device at a network edge that rewrites the source or destination address of packets as they pass, and keeps a table so replies can be mapped back. PrivateLink lets one network reach a specific service in another network through a private endpoint, which is a network interface with an address inside the consumer's own subnet, so only that service is exposed. Transit Gateway is a regional hub that connects many attached networks; its route tables decide which attachment receives traffic for each destination range. Why it works: a router sends a packet by choosing the most specific matching range. If two attachments both claim the same range, the hub has no sound way to choose, so the design must keep that range from appearing in the same routing context twice. Worked example: the cloud VPC uses 10.0.0.0/16 and the office also uses 10.0.0.0/16. First, pick an unused range such as 172.20.0.0/16 to stand for the office inside the VPC. Second, the application sends to 172.20.5.10. Third, the NAT device at the boundary rewrites the destination to 10.0.5.10, rewrites the source to its own range, and records the mapping. Fourth, the reply returns to the NAT device, which restores the mapping. Common mistake: assuming an attachment with an overlapping range will work in the hub, or assuming a PrivateLink consumer needs a route to the provider's whole range; the consumer only needs the endpoint address in its own subnet. Consequence in a running system: an ambiguous route can silently send traffic to the wrong network, and the symptom often looks like random timeouts rather than a clear error. Overlap must be designed out before the networks are connected.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm has a VPC using 192.168.0.0/16. Its freight partner's network also uses 192.168.0.0/16, so the two ranges overlap. The firm sets up a NAT device, a network edge device that rewrites addresses in packets and keeps a table to map replies back, and assigns the partner the stand-in range 100.64.0.0/16. Step 1: an application in the VPC sends to 100.64.7.20. Step 2: the NAT device rewrites the destination to 192.168.7.20 and records the mapping. Step 3 is missing: the partner's reply arrives at the NAT device from 192.168.7.20. What must happen next?
choices: The application receives the reply from 192.168.7.20 and must be reconfigured to accept traffic from the partner's real address.
The NAT device drops the reply because it did not originate from inside the VPC and so has no permission to be forwarded.
The NAT device matches the reply to its recorded mapping, restores the source to 100.64.7.20, and delivers it to the application.
The NAT device forwards the reply directly to the application because 192.168.7.20 is already inside the VPC's own range.
questions.why: The NAT device keeps a mapping table so it can match each reply to the original request, restore the stand-in address the application used, and then deliver the packet.

questions.prompt: In a PrivateLink design, what does the consumer network actually need in order to reach a provider service?
choices: A private endpoint, which is a network interface with an address inside one of the consumer's own subnets.
A peering connection that copies the provider's route table into the consumer's account.
A route covering the provider's entire address range, so every provider address is reachable.
A public IP address on each consumer instance that calls the provider service.
questions.why: PrivateLink exposes only the specific service through an endpoint address in the consumer's own subnet, so the consumer does not need the provider's whole range.

questions.prompt: A company attaches two VPCs to one Transit Gateway. Both VPCs use 172.31.0.0/16. What is the most accurate description of what goes wrong?
choices: Nothing changes, because the gateway routes by source address first and destination range only when sources match.
The gateway automatically splits the duplicate range between the two attachments by alternating packets, so traffic is shared.
The gateway rejects only the second attachment and keeps the first working with no visible symptom.
Both attachments claim the same destination range, so the hub has no sound way to choose which one receives traffic, and the result can be silent misdelivery or random timeouts.
questions.why: A router picks the most specific matching range, and when two attachments claim an identical range there is no sound choice, so the overlap must be removed in design.

questions.prompt: A team uses NAT to connect an office network 10.44.0.0/16 to a VPC that also uses 10.44.0.0/16. Which design fix best matches the teaching principle that overlap must be handled before networks are connected?
choices: Keep both ranges and add a second Transit Gateway route table so the duplicate range is announced twice.
Remove NAT and have applications connect to the office by its public IP address.
Shrink both networks to /24 blocks so the overlapping addresses become less likely to match.
Assign the office a unused stand-in range in the VPC, such as 172.20.0.0/16, and have the NAT device translate between the stand-in and the real range.
questions.why: Mapping the overlapping network to an unused stand-in range at the boundary removes the ambiguity while leaving each network's real range intact.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would connect a cloud application network to an on-premises network when both use 10.0.0.0/16, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would first confirm which side needs to initiate traffic and how much of each network must be visible. If only one application or service needs to be reached, I would use a private endpoint so the consumer side gets a local address and no full routes are shared. If whole networks must talk, I would put a NAT device at the boundary and translate one side into a non-overlapping range, so routers only ever see unique prefixes. The tradeoff is that NAT hides the real source addresses, so logs and access rules on the far side see translated addresses, and the NAT device becomes a component to size and monitor. Also, translated ranges have to be documented, because a later change to either network can silently reintroduce an overlap.
rubricPoints: States that overlapping ranges make routing ambiguous, so the router cannot choose a correct path.
Explains that NAT rewrites addresses at the boundary so each side sees a unique range.
Explains that a private endpoint exposes one service through a local address without sharing whole routes.
Names a real tradeoff, such as hidden source addresses in logs or the extra component to operate.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between NAT, a private endpoint, and a hub under a stated address constraint is best learned by reasoning through a realistic design situation, which no current mission covers.

lessons.plain: Before a cloud network can reach your office or data center over a private link, a real fibre cable has to run between your equipment and the cloud provider's equipment. That usually happens inside a colocation facility, a building where many companies rent secure space, power and racks, and where cloud providers keep their connection points. Installing the cable takes paperwork, too. A Letter of Authorization is a document that says you are allowed to ask a facility to connect your port to a particular provider port. This objective covers those physical pieces: where the link lives, who must sign off on it, and what the private connection service expects from them.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your office router sits in one building and your cloud provider's connection equipment sits in another building across town. What physical thing has to exist between them before any routing or encryption can run, and who would have to agree to install it?
lessons.teach:
Key terms. A colocation facility (colo) is a data center run by a company that rents out space, power and cooling to many tenants; your equipment sits in a locked rack or cage there. A cross-connect is a single fibre patch cable run inside the facility between two tenants' ports, such as your router and a cloud provider's port. A Letter of Authorization (LOA) is a document issued by the owner of a port or circuit, authorising the facility to order or install a cross-connect to it. It is usually paired with a connecting facility assignment, which names the exact building, room and port. Direct Connect is the provider's service for a private, dedicated link from your location into its cloud network, avoiding the public internet. A dedicated connection is reserved for you on a port you order directly; a hosted connection is a slice of a port sold through a partner.

Why it works. Routing, VLANs and tunnels are logical configuration, and they only run on a physical link that already exists. Software cannot create light between two buildings. So the order is: choose a facility where the provider has a connection point, order the connection, obtain the authorization documents, have the facility install the cross-connect, and only then configure the logical layers on top.

Worked example. Your router is in colo A, rack 12, port 3, and the provider's connection point is in the same facility. Step 1: you order a dedicated connection for that location and receive a connection identifier. Step 2: the provider supplies an LOA naming that identifier and the facility's assignment for the target port. Step 3: facility staff patch rack 12 port 3 to the provider's port. Step 4: the link comes up, and only then can routing be built. If the document names the wrong room, the cable lands nowhere useful.

Common mistake. Treating the console 'create connection' step as if it finished the job. That step reserves capacity; the physical cable still has to be installed and authorised.

Consequence. Until the physical link is up, every route and tunnel built on it stays down. A single connection in a single facility is also a single point of failure.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm keeps its router in colo M, cage 4, port 9. It wants a second, separate path into the provider's cloud network from colo N, rack 18, port 2, where the provider has a connection point. Step 1: the firm orders a dedicated connection for colo N and receives connection ID LX-7741. Step 2: the provider issues a Letter of Authorization naming LX-7741 and the connecting facility assignment for colo N port 2. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the link on the colo N path comes up, and only then does the team configure routing across it.
choices: Ask the facility in colo N to install a cross-connect from the firm's port to the provider's port 2, using the LOA as authorization.
Copy the colo M cage details into the LOA so the two paths share one authorization document.
Configure the BGP session on the colo N router before any cable is installed, so the link is ready when it comes up.
Create a second dedicated connection in the console using the same LX-7741 identifier to reserve more capacity.
questions.why: The cross-connect is the physical patch that actually joins the firm's port to the provider's port, and the facility installs it under the LOA, which must happen before the link can come up.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does a Letter of Authorization (LOA) do in a Direct Connect setup?
choices: It sets the BGP routing policy that the provider applies to your traffic.
It proves that the colocation facility has passed its security audit.
It reserves bandwidth on the provider's port for a fixed monthly fee.
It authorises the facility to order or install a cross-connect to a specific port or circuit.
questions.why: The LOA is issued by the owner of a port or circuit and authorises the facility to order or install a cross-connect to it, and it is usually paired with a connecting facility assignment.

questions.prompt: A team creates a dedicated connection in the provider console. The status shows the connection as ordered. They configure their routing session and it stays down. The provider has issued no LOA and no cross-connect has been installed. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The hosted connection type was chosen instead of a dedicated one, which blocks routing.
The team used the wrong account, so the provider cannot see the connection.
The console step only reserved capacity, and the physical cable has not been installed and authorised.
The routing session needs a larger MTU before the status will change.
questions.why: Creating the connection in the console reserves capacity but does not install the physical cross-connect, so no link exists for routing to run on.

questions.prompt: A company has one dedicated connection into its cloud network, and that connection is in one colocation facility. A fibre cut in that facility takes the link down. Which statement best describes the risk?
choices: The cloud provider will automatically move traffic to a second facility at no extra cost.
Routes and tunnels built on that link stay down until the physical link is restored, so the single connection is a single point of failure.
The risk is limited to the BGP routes, because the physical link stays up when the routing session fails.
Only new tunnels are affected, since existing routes keep working on the cached path.
questions.why: Logical layers such as routing and tunnels only run on an existing physical link, so losing that link takes down everything built on it, and one connection in one facility has no backup path.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, what has to be physically in place before a Direct Connect link can carry traffic, and name one limit of relying on a single connection.
lessons.modelAnswer: Before a Direct Connect link can carry anything, a fibre cable has to run from our router to the cloud provider's port, and that normally happens inside a colocation facility where both sides already have equipment. The cable is installed by the facility, not by the cloud console. We order a dedicated connection in the console, which gives us an identifier. We then need a Letter of Authorization that names that identifier and the exact rack and port, so the facility staff can patch a cross-connect to the right place. Only when the light is up can we build routing on top. The main limit of a single connection is that it is one physical path in one building: a fibre cut, a power failure or a facility outage takes the whole hybrid link down. That is why production designs usually add a second connection in a different location, or a backup path over an encrypted VPN.
rubricPoints: A physical cable between your equipment and the provider's port must exist before any logical configuration can work.
A colocation facility is where the cross-connect is installed, and the facility acts on an authorization document.
A Letter of Authorization names the connection and exact location so the cable is patched to the correct port.
A single connection is one physical path and a single point of failure, so resilience needs a second location or a backup path.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly documents, facility arrangements and console facts, which no listed mission or planned engine currently exercises.

lessons.plain: Hybrid connectivity links your office or data-center network to cloud networks so traffic can flow both ways. Routing is how each network decides which way to send a packet. With static routing, a person types the route by hand, such as 'to reach this address range, send traffic to that gateway.' With dynamic routing, routers exchange what they can reach automatically, usually using a protocol called BGP, and adjust when a link fails. Static routes are simple and predictable but do not notice failures. Dynamic routes adapt, but they need careful setup so they do not advertise the wrong things.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your office has two links to the cloud, and you typed only one route by hand. If the link that route points to goes down, what happens to traffic bound for that cloud network, and who notices first?
lessons.teach:
A route is an entry in a router's table saying that packets for a given address range should be sent to a given next hop, the next device on the path. When several routes match a destination, the router picks the most specific one. This is called longest prefix match, so a route for 10.1.0.0/16 beats a route for 10.0.0.0/8 for addresses inside it. A static route is one you configure by hand, and it stays until someone changes it. It is easy to read and predictable, but the router cannot tell whether the next hop is still alive unless you add separate health checks.

A dynamic routing protocol lets routers tell each other what they can reach. For hybrid links the common choice is BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol. Each network has an autonomous system number (ASN), a unique label for its routing domain. Two routers that agree to exchange routes form a BGP session, and each advertises the address ranges it owns. Every advertised route carries an AS path, the list of ASNs it has crossed. When there is a choice, routers prefer shorter paths, and they reject routes that loop back through their own ASN. Raising local preference, or lengthening a backup path by prepending extra ASNs, steers traffic toward a primary link while the backup stands by.

Worked example: an on-premises router advertises 192.168.10.0/24 to the cloud gateway over two sessions. Session A carries an AS path of length one, and session B carries length three. The gateway installs the route via A. If session A drops, BGP withdraws that route, and the gateway falls back to B once the session failure is detected, with no human editing anything.

Common mistake: advertising a broad range such as 10.0.0.0/8 from both sides, or leaving an old static route in place alongside BGP. Either can make the wrong path win, or send traffic into a dead end.

In a running system, an advertised route whose next hop is unreachable sends traffic into a black hole. The failure looks like random timeouts rather than a clean outage, which is why route tables must be checked whenever connectivity seems to break in only one direction.

questions.prompt: A branch office router in a company with ASN 65010 has two routes that both cover the destination 172.16.40.25. Route 1 is a static route for 172.16.0.0/12 pointing at a VPN tunnel. Route 2 is a BGP route for 172.16.32.0/20 learned from the cloud gateway. Step 1: list every route whose range contains 172.16.40.25. Both do, so both are candidates. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: the router forwards the packet to the next hop of the winning route, which is the cloud gateway session.
choices: Choose the route whose next hop has the lowest IP address, since the router always breaks ties that way
Send a copy of the packet down both routes so that whichever one is alive delivers it
Choose the static route, because a hand-configured route always overrides a route learned from a routing protocol
Choose the most specific matching range, here 172.16.32.0/20, because longest prefix match prefers the narrowest range that contains the destination
questions.why: Longest prefix match means that when several routes contain the destination, the router picks the most specific one, which is the /20 rather than the /12.

questions.prompt: A router holds two routes: 10.2.0.0/16 with next hop X and 10.2.8.0/22 with next hop Y. A packet is addressed to 10.2.9.14. Which route does the router use, and why?
choices: Neither route, because the destination is not an exact match for either range
10.2.8.0/22 via Y, because it is the more specific range that contains 10.2.9.14
Both routes at once, splitting the packet's bytes between X and Y
10.2.0.0/16 via X, because the shorter prefix length is listed first in the table
questions.why: Both ranges contain the address, and longest prefix match selects the narrower /22 over the /16.

questions.prompt: An engineer configures a BGP session to a cloud gateway and also leaves a hand-written static route for 10.9.0.0/16 pointing at a fixed next hop on the same link. The BGP session then fails. What is the most likely result for traffic to 10.9.4.7?
choices: Traffic keeps going to the static next hop, which may be dead, because static routes stay until someone changes them and the router cannot tell the next hop is down without a health check
The router refuses all traffic to 10.9.0.0/16 until a human restarts the session
The router ignores the static route and immediately switches to the BGP path, which is now gone
The router withdraws the static route automatically together with the BGP session
questions.why: A static route is not withdrawn by a routing protocol failure, so the router keeps using it unless a separate health check or a manual change removes it, which can produce a black hole.

questions.prompt: A router with ASN 64520 receives an advertisement for 192.0.2.0/24 with AS path 64511 64530 64520. What should the router do with this route?
choices: Install it and prepend its own ASN to the path before forwarding it on
Install it with the lowest preference so it is used only if no other route exists
Reject it, because the AS path already contains the router's own ASN, which indicates a loop
Install it but mark the path as primary, because it is the longest path and so the most reliable
questions.why: BGP rejects any route whose AS path passes through the receiving router's own ASN, since accepting it would create a routing loop.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose a static route over BGP for a hybrid link, and name one limit of the approach you pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use a static route when the on-premises side has one simple path, the design is small, the far-end device cannot run BGP, or we do not control the peer's routing. It is predictable: anyone can read it and audit it. The limit is that it does not notice failure. If the next hop dies, the route stays in the table and traffic goes into a dead end, unless we add health checks or a second static route with a higher administrative distance as a backup. For redundant links, multiple sites, or routes that change over time, I would use BGP, because sessions detect failure and withdraw routes automatically. The cost is more setup. We must control exactly which prefixes we advertise, avoid leaking a broad range, and watch the AS path, or we can send traffic the wrong way without any error being raised.
rubricPoints: Static routes are set by hand and do not react to a link failure on their own.
BGP exchanges reachability between routers and withdraws routes when a session fails.
Route selection uses longest prefix match first, then path attributes such as AS path length.
Dynamic routing requires control over which prefixes are advertised, to avoid leaks or black holes.
Leaving a static route alongside BGP can let the wrong path win.

suggested.rationale: Telling a static route apart from a BGP-learned route is easiest to check by tracing which path a packet actually takes before and after a link failure.

lessons.plain: Layer 2 and layer 3 are the two lowest working floors of a network. Layer 2 is the local neighbourhood: devices on the same switch find each other by hardware addresses, and a VLAN is a label that splits one switch into separate, isolated groups. Layer 3 is the postal system between neighbourhoods: every device gets an IP address that says which network it belongs to, and routers, guided by a routing table and a default gateway, carry packets from one network to another. Configuring these means deciding which groups exist, what addresses they use, and where traffic should go when it leaves its own group.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two laptops are plugged into the same switch but are placed in different VLANs, and both have IP addresses in 192.168.5.0/24. Before any teaching, do you expect them to reach each other directly, and why?
lessons.teach:
Layer 2 means the data link layer of the network model: delivery between devices that share a local link, addressed by MAC addresses, which are hardware identifiers built into network cards. A switch learns which MAC address sits behind which port and forwards frames only where they are needed. A VLAN (virtual local area network) is a numbered tag, defined by the IEEE 802.1Q standard, that a switch uses to keep traffic from separate groups apart even when they share the same cables. Devices in VLAN 10 do not receive broadcasts from VLAN 20 unless a router connects the two.

Layer 3 means the network layer, where IP addresses live. An IP address is split into a network part and a host part, written with a prefix length such as 10.0.1.0/24, meaning the first 24 bits name the network. Two hosts talk directly only if they share a prefix; otherwise a host hands the packet to its default gateway, the router address configured on the host. The router looks up the destination in its routing table, a list of prefixes and next hops, and when several prefixes match it uses the most specific one, the longest prefix.

Worked example: host A at 10.0.1.25/24 wants to reach 10.0.2.40. Its network is 10.0.1.0/24, and 10.0.2.40 falls outside it, so A addresses the frame at layer 2 to its gateway, 10.0.1.1. The router sees that the destination matches 10.0.2.0/24 on its second interface and forwards the packet out that interface toward the next hop.

Common mistake: placing two ranges that overlap, such as 10.0.0.0/16 and 10.0.1.0/24, on the two ends of one connection. The routing table can no longer say which path a destination belongs to, so traffic goes the wrong way or stops. In a running hybrid network this often breaks a link that worked yesterday, the moment someone adds a new subnet that collides with an existing range.

questions.prompt: A retail chain's branch router holds two routes: 172.20.0.0/16 via next hop 10.9.0.2, and 172.20.64.0/19 via next hop 10.9.0.6. A packet arrives for 172.20.70.15. Step 1: the router finds every prefix in its table that contains 172.20.70.15, and both routes match. Step 2: the router compares the prefix lengths of the matching routes. Step 3 is missing and you must supply it. Which completion is correct?
choices: The router chooses the /19 route as the longest matching prefix and forwards the packet to next hop 10.9.0.6.
The router picks the /16 route because a shorter prefix covers more addresses and so is the safer match.
The router splits the packet between 10.9.0.2 and 10.9.0.6 so both links carry part of the load.
The router sends the packet to 10.9.0.2 because that route was listed first in the table.
questions.why: The router uses the most specific matching prefix, which is the longest one, so the /19 route wins and the packet goes to 10.9.0.6.

questions.prompt: A server is configured with address 172.31.200.9/21 and default gateway 172.31.200.1. Which destination does the server reach directly on the local link, without sending the packet to the gateway?
questions.why: A /21 prefix covers third-octet values 192 through 199 in this case, so 172.31.199.250 shares the network and the others fall outside it.

questions.prompt: Your company runs 172.18.0.0/16 on premises, and a cloud network is newly given 172.18.4.0/24, which lies inside that larger range. What is the most likely consequence for traffic to 172.18.4.x?
choices: Nothing breaks, because the /24 is more specific and always wins on both sides of the link.
The routing table rejects the /24 outright because a /16 can hold too many addresses to route alongside it.
Traffic to 172.18.4.x may be routed the wrong way, because the two ranges overlap and the routing table cannot say cleanly which path owns those addresses.
The link stops only if the two sides write their masks with different prefix lengths, not because of the overlap itself.
questions.why: Overlapping ranges leave the routing table without a single clear path for the shared addresses, so traffic can go the wrong way or stop.

questions.prompt: A switch has ports tagged VLAN 30 and VLAN 40. A server on a VLAN 30 port sends a broadcast frame. Which devices receive that broadcast?
choices: Every port on the switch, because broadcasts flood all ports regardless of their tag.
Only the VLAN 40 server, because broadcasts are delivered to the other VLAN.
Both servers, because they are connected to the same switch.
Only the other ports in VLAN 30, because a VLAN keeps broadcasts within its group unless a router connects it to another VLAN.
questions.why: A VLAN is a tag that confines broadcasts to its own group, so only the other VLAN 30 ports receive the frame.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a VLAN does, what a subnet does, and why a host sends traffic to its default gateway. Name one limit or tradeoff of putting every device into one large subnet.
lessons.modelAnswer: A VLAN is a label on Layer 2 frames that keeps groups of devices separated on shared switches, so a broadcast in one group never reaches another. A subnet is a Layer 3 range of IP addresses defined by a prefix, and two hosts reach each other directly only when their addresses fall in the same subnet. When a host's destination is outside its own subnet, it cannot deliver the packet itself, so it sends the frame to its default gateway, a router that reads the routing table and forwards the packet toward the right network. The tradeoff of one huge subnet is that every device shares one broadcast domain, so broadcast traffic grows with the number of hosts, and a single misbehaving device or address conflict affects everyone in it. Splitting into smaller subnets and VLANs limits that blast radius, but it adds routing decisions that must be planned and kept free of overlaps.
rubricPoints: A VLAN separates Layer 2 broadcast domains on shared switches using a tag.
A subnet defines which IP addresses are local, using a prefix length.
Traffic to an address outside the local subnet goes to the default gateway, which routes it.
One large subnet means shared broadcast traffic and a wider failure impact, a real tradeoff.

suggested.rationale: A virtual network path tracer would let the learner watch a packet's subnet check, gateway hop and routing table lookup, which this objective needs practice with.

lessons.plain: A VPN, or virtual private network, creates an encrypted tunnel across a public network so two private networks can talk as if a cable joined them. Think of a sealed pipe run through a public street: traffic goes in scrambled and comes out the other end readable only to the two ends. In this objective you connect an office or data centre network to a cloud network this way, and you set it up so that if one pipe fails, traffic keeps flowing through a second one. Doing that well means knowing how the pipes are secured, how routes are told about them, and how to make the path faster than a plain internet route when distance hurts.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your office network and a cloud network both use private addresses, and traffic crosses the public internet between them. Before reading on, what would you need to agree on between the two ends so that the traffic is unreadable to anyone watching the internet link?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. An IPsec tunnel is an encrypted channel built between two gateways using the IPsec suite of protocols. IKE (Internet Key Exchange) is the handshake that lets both ends agree on keys and encryption settings before any user data moves. A pre-shared key is a secret string both sides already hold, used to prove identity during that handshake. The customer gateway is the device or software on your side of the link. The cloud side terminates the tunnel at a virtual private gateway or a transit gateway. A site-to-site VPN connection bundles two tunnels, each landing on a different endpoint in the cloud, so one can fail while the other carries traffic.

Why it works: encryption and integrity are applied to each packet inside the tunnel, so the internet in between only carries scrambled envelopes. Routing decides what enters the tunnel. Static routes list prefixes by hand. BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) exchanges prefixes automatically and withdraws them when a tunnel drops.

Worked example: a branch uses 10.20.0.0/16 and the cloud network uses 10.0.0.0/16. Step 1: both tunnel ends agree on IKE version, cipher and pre-shared key. Step 2: tunnel one comes up. Step 3: BGP advertises 10.20.0.0/16 over tunnel one. Step 4: tunnel two comes up and advertises the same prefix. Step 5: the cloud prefers tunnel one by default; if it drops, BGP withdraws that route and traffic shifts to tunnel two.

Common mistake: overlapping address ranges on the two sides. Routing becomes ambiguous, and no tunnel setting can fix that. Pre-shared keys should be long, random and rotated, never stored in plain text in a template.

Accelerated VPN: a site-to-site VPN can be accelerated, meaning the public leg of the tunnel enters the provider's global edge network near the customer and crosses the provider backbone for most of the distance instead of the public internet. It typically requires a transit gateway and changes the path, not the encryption.

Consequence: when one tunnel is down and the other is healthy with its route still held by BGP, the application stays reachable at reduced headroom. That is a degraded link, not a broken VPN, and it should be investigated before the second tunnel fails too.

questions.prompt: Riverside Clinic's office network is 192.168.70.0/24 and its cloud network is 10.60.0.0/18. It runs two site-to-site tunnels. Step 1: both ends agree on IKE version, cipher and pre-shared key, and tunnel A comes up. Step 2: BGP on tunnel A advertises 192.168.70.0/24 to the cloud. Step 3: tunnel B comes up and advertises the same prefix. Step 4 is the one left blank: tunnel A drops, and ______. Which choice completes the sequence?
choices: the cloud keeps sending traffic toward tunnel A until its cached route expires on a fixed timer that the clinic's administrator has to set by hand
the clinic renumbers its office network to a range that overlaps less with 10.60.0.0/18, which restores tunnel A without any routing change
the pre-shared key is copied into the template in plain text so both tunnels rebuild with the same secret and carry traffic at once
BGP withdraws the 192.168.70.0/24 route learned over tunnel A, so traffic moves to the route still advertised over tunnel B
questions.why: BGP withdraws a prefix when the tunnel that advertised it drops, so the cloud shifts traffic to the route still advertised by the healthy tunnel.

questions.prompt: Kestrel Labs runs IPsec software on its data-centre firewall to connect to the cloud. In the terms used by this course, what is that device called?
choices: the customer gateway
the transit gateway
the virtual private gateway
the pre-shared key
questions.why: The customer gateway is the device or software on the customer's side of the link, and the firewall here is on that side.

questions.prompt: Harbor Freight Co. has a branch on 10.44.0.0/16 and a cloud network on 10.44.128.0/17. Both tunnels are up. What is the core problem?
choices: BGP will refuse to advertise either prefix over either tunnel until the cloud side switches to static routes only
The IKE handshake will fail because the cipher is too strong for the branch firewall to negotiate, and both tunnels stay down until it is weakened
The two ranges overlap
Only the first tunnel will carry traffic because the second is kept as a stand-by that cannot advertise its routes
questions.why: Overlapping address ranges make routing ambiguous, and no tunnel setting can fix that, which is the common mistake the teaching text describes.

questions.prompt: Blue Mesa Analytics turns on accelerated VPN for its site-to-site connection. Which change does this involve?
choices: the pre-shared key was swapped for a plain-text value stored in the template so both sides can reconnect faster after any drop
the two tunnels were replaced by static routes, so BGP no longer withdraws routes when a tunnel drops during failover
the route the public leg takes changed, while encryption stayed the same
the encryption cipher was weakened so packets are processed faster across the public internet, which the team must review later
questions.why: Accelerated VPN changes the path: the public leg enters the provider's edge near the customer and crosses the provider backbone, while the encryption applied to each packet is unchanged.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a site-to-site VPN is built with two tunnels, and name one limit of this design that you would raise in a design review.
lessons.modelAnswer: Two tunnels exist so that a single failure, such as one endpoint being unavailable or one internet path dropping, does not take the whole link down. Each tunnel terminates on a different cloud endpoint, and BGP advertises the same routes over both. When one tunnel fails, BGP withdraws its routes and traffic moves to the surviving tunnel automatically. The limit I would raise is that both tunnels still share the customer side: if the customer gateway device or its internet connection fails, both tunnels fail together. Also, the usable bandwidth of a single tunnel is capped, so a second tunnel adds resilience rather than doubling throughput unless traffic is spread across both. I would ask whether the design needs a second customer-side path too.
rubricPoints: Two tunnels give redundancy across separate cloud endpoints, with BGP shifting traffic when one fails
The customer-side gateway or its internet link is still a shared single point of failure
A single tunnel has a throughput ceiling, so two tunnels are mainly for resilience

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers VPN configuration directly, so reasoning through a tunnel-down exam-style situation adds the most.

lessons.plain: Most companies already run networks in their own offices and data centres. That is called an on-premises network. Connecting one to the AWS Cloud means building a safe, reliable path so machines on each side can reach the other as if they shared one larger network. You can do this over the public internet using an encrypted tunnel, or over a private dedicated line rented through a data centre provider. Either way, both sides must agree on which address ranges each one owns and how traffic finds its way across the link.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your office has a server at 192.168.10.5 and an AWS subnet at 10.20.0.0/16. Without any teaching, what would you need to set up before the office server could open a connection to a machine in that subnet, and what could go wrong if the office also used 10.20.0.0/16 for its own machines?
lessons.teach:
An on-premises network is the network an organisation runs itself, in its own offices or data centres. Connecting it to AWS means joining two networks so packets can travel between them. There are two main link types. A site-to-site VPN (virtual private network) builds an encrypted IPsec tunnel across the public internet. It is quick and inexpensive to set up, but its speed depends on internet conditions. AWS Direct Connect is a dedicated private connection. You order a physical cross-connect inside a colocation facility, a data centre where many networks meet, and the traffic bypasses the public internet, giving steadier latency and more bandwidth.

A link alone is not enough. Routing tells each side which destinations are reachable through the link. A prefix is a block of addresses written in CIDR notation, such as 10.20.0.0/16. BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the common way two routers exchange prefixes automatically. Each side has an ASN (autonomous system number) that identifies it to its peer. Static routes are the manual alternative, where you type the prefix and the next hop yourself.

Worked example. The office uses 192.168.0.0/16 and a VPC (virtual private cloud, an isolated network inside AWS) uses 10.20.0.0/16. Step 1: the office router learns that 10.20.0.0/16 is reachable through the tunnel or the Direct Connect link. Step 2: an office laptop sends a packet to 10.20.4.7. Its router matches that address to the 10.20.0.0/16 route and forwards the packet across the link. Step 3: the AWS side has a route for 192.168.0.0/16 pointing back over the same link, so the reply returns.

Common mistake: choosing overlapping ranges, such as both sides using 10.0.0.0/16. A router then cannot tell which side owns 10.0.4.7, so traffic goes to the wrong place or is dropped.

Consequence: if one return route is missing, requests leave but replies never arrive. That looks like a firewall fault but is really a routing gap. Plan address ranges before building the link.

questions.prompt: Harbor Dental keeps its patient records server at 192.168.50.20 in an office that uses 192.168.50.0/24. Its AWS VPC uses 10.40.0.0/16 and is joined to the office by a site-to-site VPN. An application instance at 10.40.7.12 needs to reach the server. Step 1: the instance sends a packet addressed to 192.168.50.20. Step 2: the VPC route table matches 192.168.50.0/24 and hands the packet to the virtual private gateway, which sends it into the VPN tunnel. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: the server's reply reaches 10.40.7.12. Which description fills in Step 3?
choices: The instance's security group is changed to allow traffic from 192.168.50.0/24 before the packet leaves the VPC.
The office router sends the packet back up the tunnel to AWS so the VPC can check its route table a second time.
The office router receives the packet from the tunnel and delivers it to the server, because 192.168.50.20 is on its local subnet.
The VPN tunnel translates 192.168.50.20 into a public address before the office router sees the packet.
questions.why: Once the packet arrives through the tunnel, the office router sees that 192.168.50.20 belongs to a directly attached subnet and delivers it there, which is the step that completes the forward path.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a prefix in the context of linking an on-premises network to AWS?
choices: A login name that a router uses to authenticate its BGP peer before routes are accepted.
The first address in a subnet, which a gateway reserves for itself.
The numeric label a colocation facility gives each physical cross-connect port.
A block of addresses written in CIDR notation, such as 172.16.8.0/22, that describes a range of destinations.
questions.why: A prefix is a block of addresses expressed in CIDR notation, and routers use prefixes to describe which destinations are reachable through a link.

questions.prompt: Ridgeline Logistics runs an office network on 172.20.0.0/16 and plans an AWS VPC for its warehouse analytics. Which VPC range is the safest choice for connecting the two networks with routing?
choices: 172.21.0.0/16, a block that does not overlap with any office address.
172.20.0.0/16, the same block as the office so the two sides match.
172.2.0.0/16, a block that is shorter than the office range but still private.
172.20.64.0/18, a smaller block placed inside the office range.
questions.why: Overlapping ranges leave a router unable to tell which side owns an address, so the VPC block must be entirely separate from the office block.

questions.prompt: Pinecrest Clinic's VPN tunnel is up and the BGP session shows established, yet staff in the office can send requests to an AWS-hosted scheduling API but never receive replies. Which fault best explains this pattern?
choices: The office firewall is blocking all outbound traffic from the staff laptops by default.
The BGP session is using the wrong ASN, which prevents any packet from leaving the office.
The AWS side has no route for the office prefix pointing back over the tunnel, so replies have nowhere to go.
The VPC subnet is too small to hold the scheduling API's instances.
questions.why: Requests reach AWS, but replies fail, which points to a missing return route on the AWS side rather than a firewall or session fault, since the session is already established.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would connect an office network to an AWS VPC, choosing between a site-to-site VPN and Direct Connect, and name one limit or tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by checking that the office and VPC address ranges do not overlap, because overlapping blocks make routing ambiguous. For a quick, low-cost link I would use a site-to-site VPN. It builds an encrypted IPsec tunnel over the public internet, so it is fast to set up and inexpensive, but latency and throughput depend on internet conditions and each tunnel has a bandwidth ceiling. If the workload needs steady latency or high bandwidth, I would order Direct Connect through a colocation provider. That gives a dedicated private path, but it takes longer to provision and costs more. In both cases I would exchange routes, either with BGP or with static routes, and confirm the return route exists on both sides, since a missing return route is the most common silent failure. The tradeoff I would name is cost and lead time against predictability: VPN is cheap and quick to build but less consistent under load.
rubricPoints: Checks that address ranges on both sides do not overlap
Compares a VPN over the internet with a dedicated Direct Connect link on cost, speed and stability
Explains that routes must be exchanged in both directions, dynamically with BGP or statically
Names a concrete limit or tradeoff of the chosen option

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet's path through on-premises and cloud route tables would build the route-reasoning this objective depends on.

lessons.plain: Your company already keeps a directory for its own machines, such as intranet.corp or db1.office, and the cloud side keeps its own names. Name resolution is the step that turns a name into an address. Connecting the two sides means a machine on either side can look up a name on the other side and get an answer, without anyone typing addresses by hand. This lesson covers three pieces: a rule that says which questions go to which server, a zone that holds the answers for one domain, and a relay that carries questions across the network link between the two sides.
lessons.guessPrompt: A laptop in your office resolves intranet.corp fine but cannot resolve a database name that exists only inside a cloud network. Where would you expect that question to go, and what single piece of configuration would you add first?
lessons.teach:
DNS (the Domain Name System) turns names into addresses. A recursive resolver is the server a machine asks first. It either answers from what it already knows or asks other servers on the machine's behalf. A hosted zone is a container of DNS records for one domain, such as corp.example. A private hosted zone answers only for queries that come from networks attached to it, so internal names stay internal. Forwarding means a resolver passes a question to another resolver instead of answering it. Conditional forwarding narrows that: only questions for one specific domain, such as corp.example, are sent to a named target, and everything else follows the normal path.

Why it works: each side keeps authority over its own names. The on-premises DNS server remains the source of truth for corp.example, and the cloud side does not copy it. The cloud resolver is told to send only the on-premises domain back across the link. The on-premises servers are told to send cloud-side domains to a resolver endpoint, which is a set of managed network interfaces placed in your VPC. An inbound endpoint accepts queries from on-premises. An outbound endpoint sends queries out to on-premises DNS servers over the private link.

Worked example: an instance in a VPC asks for app.corp.example. The VPC resolver checks its rules and finds a forwarding rule for corp.example. It sends the question out through an outbound endpoint to the on-premises DNS server at 10.1.0.53 across the private connection. That server answers, and the answer travels back the same way. A question for a public name does not match the rule, so it resolves normally.

Common mistake: forwarding everything, or forwarding the on-premises domain to a server that cannot be reached over the link. Lookups then hang until they time out, and the application looks broken even though the network is fine.

Consequence: if the link drops, on-premises names stop resolving from the cloud side, and retries pile up. Almost every service call starts with a lookup, so one wrong rule can look like a total outage.

The rule is narrow: send only the domains you do not own back to the team that does.

questions.prompt: A team runs an instance in a VPC that has a forwarding rule for ops.lakeside.test. The instance asks for billing.ops.lakeside.test, and the on-premises DNS server for that domain is at 172.20.4.25. Step 1: the VPC resolver checks its rules and finds the rule for ops.lakeside.test. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: the server at 172.20.4.25 answers. Step 4: the answer travels back to the instance. Which step fills the gap?
choices: The resolver answers from a copy of the ops.lakeside.test records it stored locally.
The resolver sends the query out through an outbound endpoint over the private link to 172.20.4.25.
The resolver sends the query to an inbound endpoint so the on-premises server can pull it in.
The resolver forwards the query to public root servers, which then find the on-premises server.
questions.why: A matching forwarding rule sends the question out through an outbound endpoint across the private link to the named on-premises server, which is the only step that gets the question to that server.

questions.prompt: A private hosted zone for example.lab is attached only to VPC-A. Which query receives an answer from that zone?
choices: A query from an instance inside VPC-A.
A query from any VPC in the account, because hosted zones are shared account-wide.
A query from an on-premises server, because every hosted zone answers everywhere.
A query from a laptop on the public internet.
questions.why: A private hosted zone only answers queries that come from networks attached to it, so only instances inside VPC-A get answers.

questions.prompt: A team has a conditional forwarding rule for partners.bluefin.test that sends its queries to 192.168.77.10. Because of a typo, the team instead sets the rule to forward every query, including public names, to 192.168.77.10, which the private link cannot reach. What happens when a user looks up a public website?
choices: The lookup falls back to a copy of the public records stored on the on-premises server.
The lookup returns an error immediately because the link has no route for it.
The lookup returns instantly from the public internet because public names skip forwarding.
The lookup hangs until it times out, even though the public internet itself is reachable.
questions.why: Forwarding everything sends public names to an unreachable server, so the lookup hangs until timeout; the public internet is fine, the DNS path is the problem.

questions.prompt: Northwind owns plant.example.internal on its on-premises DNS servers, and the cloud team owns cloud.example.internal in a private hosted zone. Which setup follows the rule of sending only the domains you do not own back to the team that does?
choices: On-premises servers forward every query, including plant names, to the inbound endpoint.
On-premises servers forward plant.example.internal queries to the outbound endpoint.
On-premises servers forward cloud.example.internal queries to the resolver endpoint in the VPC.
The cloud resolver forwards cloud.example.internal queries to the on-premises servers.
questions.why: On-premises servers should send the cloud-owned domain to the resolver endpoint in the VPC, while the cloud side forwards only the on-premises domain back across the link.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an on-premises server and an instance in a cloud VPC can each resolve the other's private names. Name one limit or tradeoff of forwarding that the teammate should watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each side keeps its own private names and answers for them. The cloud VPC has a resolver with a conditional forwarding rule: any question for the on-premises domain, such as corp.example, is sent out through an outbound resolver endpoint over the private link to the on-premises DNS server. The on-premises DNS server has the reverse arrangement: questions for the cloud private zone are sent to the inbound endpoint's addresses in the VPC. Only the owning domain is forwarded, so everything else resolves normally. The tradeoff is dependency. Every cross-link lookup now relies on the link and on the remote DNS server being reachable, so an outage on either shows up as slow timeouts rather than clean errors. Watch the timeout settings and monitor the forwarding path, not just the servers.
rubricPoints: Each side keeps authority over its own private domain and forwards only that domain
Outbound endpoints carry cloud-originated questions to on-premises DNS, and inbound endpoints accept on-premises questions
A forwarding rule is narrow, so public and other names still resolve normally
A tradeoff is that cross-link lookups depend on the link and remote server, so failures appear as timeouts

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining which side answers which question and why forwarding must stay narrow, which is best practiced by talking it through.

lessons.plain: A load balancer is a traffic director that sits in front of several copies of the same service and hands each incoming request to one of them, so no single copy gets overwhelmed and a broken copy can be skipped. A reverse proxy is a close relative: it is the server clients actually connect to, and it forwards their requests to the real servers behind it. It can also handle chores such as decrypting connections or caching responses on the backends' behalf. Load balancing is about spreading the work, while a reverse proxy is about being the front door. Many products do both at once, and the core ideas stay the same whether the front door is a hardware box, open-source software, or a managed service in a cloud.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have three identical web servers behind one address, and one of them crashes at 2 a.m. Without any further information, how could the traffic director know to stop sending requests to that server, and what would go wrong if it never found out?
lessons.teach:
A load balancer receives client traffic on a listener, which is a port and protocol it watches. It forwards each request to one member of a target group, the set of backend servers running the same service. An algorithm picks the target. Round robin cycles through targets in turn, while least outstanding requests favours the target with the fewest requests still being handled. Each target is checked by a health check, a periodic probe such as an HTTP request to a specific path. A target that fails several probes in a row is taken out of rotation until it passes again.

Load balancers work at different layers. A layer 4 balancer routes on address and port and does not look inside the request, which is fast. A layer 7 balancer reads the application request, so it can route by host name or URL path, and it can end encrypted sessions itself, a function called TLS termination. A reverse proxy is the same idea seen from the client side. The client talks only to the proxy, which opens its own connections to the backends, so the backends see the proxy's address unless the original client address is passed along in a header.

Worked example: a layer 7 balancer listens on port 443. A request for /api/orders matches a rule and goes to the orders target group, which has three targets. Round robin picks target two. Target three has failed its last two HTTP checks on /health, so it is skipped. When a deployment removes a target, connection draining lets requests it is already handling finish before it leaves.

Common mistake: a health check that only confirms the port accepts connections. A process can accept connections while every real request returns errors, so the balancer keeps sending it traffic. A useful check exercises the application in a cheap way.

In a running system, a shallow check leaves the error rate high while every target shows healthy, which makes the failure hard to diagnose. Load balancing spreads work and removes sick servers, but only as well as its health checks can tell sick from well.

questions.prompt: A team runs a reverse proxy on port 8443 in front of three inventory servers, R1, R2 and R3. Here is how one request is handled. Step 1: a request for host orders.example.net arrives on the listener at port 8443. Step 2: a rule matches the path /v2/refunds and sends the request to the refunds target group. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: among the remaining targets, least outstanding requests picks R3, which has 1 request in progress, over R1, which has 4. Which step fills the gap at Step 3?
choices: Close the listener on port 8443 until R2 recovers.
Remove R2 from the candidate set, because it failed several health probes in a row, and keep it out until it passes again.
Switch the algorithm to round robin so R2 gets the request in turn.
Send the request to R2 anyway, since it is still listed in the target group.
questions.why: A target that fails several probes in a row is taken out of rotation until it passes again, so the algorithm only chooses among the targets that remain, which is why R2 must be excluded before least outstanding requests is applied.

questions.prompt: A team runs two balancers. Balancer X routes only on IP address and port and never reads the request. Balancer Y routes on the URL path inside the request. Which statement is accurate?
choices: Both are layer 7, because every balancer must read the request to forward it.
Y is layer 4 because the URL path is part of the transport header.
X is layer 7 because it is the faster option, and Y is layer 4 because it sees the path.
X is layer 4 and Y is layer 7, since Y can route by URL path.
questions.why: A layer 4 balancer routes on address and port without looking inside the request, while a layer 7 balancer reads the request and can route by path, so X is layer 4 and Y is layer 7.

questions.prompt: A team's target health check is a TCP connect to port 5432 on database replicas. Some replicas accept connections but return errors on every query. What is the consequence?
choices: Health checks are skipped for layer 4 targets, so the replicas stay in rotation untested.
The balancer detects the bad replicas within one probe, so the error rate stays low.
Failing replicas keep receiving traffic because they pass the check, so errors stay high while every target looks healthy.
The balancer removes all replicas at once, because a TCP check cannot report partial failure.
questions.why: A check that only confirms the port accepts connections passes even when real requests fail, so the balancer keeps sending traffic to the broken replicas and the error rate stays high while all targets appear healthy.

questions.prompt: A company puts a reverse proxy in front of three application servers. In the application logs, every request appears to come from the proxy's address, 10.0.4.9. Which is the most likely cause?
choices: The proxy does not pass the original client address in a forwarding header, so the servers only see the proxy's connection.
The health checks send all the traffic, so the logs record the probe source instead of clients.
The proxy performs TLS termination, which hides client addresses from every backend.
The application servers cache one client address and reuse it for every request.
questions.why: A reverse proxy opens its own connections to the backends, so the backends see the proxy's address unless the original client address is passed along in a header, which the proxy has not done here.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a load balancer and a reverse proxy, and name one limit or tradeoff of putting a layer 7 balancer in front of a service.
lessons.modelAnswer: A load balancer's main job is distribution. It takes incoming requests on a listener and spreads them across a group of identical targets, removing any that fail health checks. A reverse proxy is about position. It is the single address clients connect to, and it forwards to backends on their behalf, which lets it do things like terminate encryption or hide internal addresses. In practice one product often does both. The tradeoff of a layer 7 balancer is that it must read and interpret each request to route it by path or host name. That costs more CPU and adds latency compared with a layer 4 balancer that only looks at addresses and ports. It also takes on certificate handling and decides what client address the backend sees, so those choices need to be designed on purpose rather than left to defaults.
rubricPoints: Says a load balancer spreads requests across a group of identical targets.
Says a reverse proxy is the client-facing front that forwards requests to backends.
Explains that health checks remove failing targets from rotation.
Names a layer 7 cost or tradeoff, such as inspection overhead or certificate handling.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers load balancing, so an exam-style scenario to reason through is the best available practice.

lessons.plain: Imagine a company's network as a set of buildings connected by a central hub road. In AWS, Transit Gateway is that hub: it passes traffic between your virtual networks and your other connections. Some companies run their own traffic-steering software, called SD-WAN, which decides which connection carries each kind of traffic between sites. Transit Gateway Connect is a way to plug that software, running on a virtual server inside your AWS network, into the hub so the two can exchange route information automatically. Traffic management here means choosing which path traffic takes and having those paths update by themselves when a link fails, instead of someone editing settings by hand.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a branch office must reach your cloud VPCs through a company's own SD-WAN appliance, which piece should know the route to the branch, and what do you expect to happen to branch traffic if that appliance stops announcing the branch routes?
lessons.teach:
Transit Gateway is a managed routing hub in AWS. You attach VPCs, VPN connections and Direct Connect links to it, and it forwards packets between them using route tables. A route table is a list of destination ranges and the attachment to send each one to. Each attachment is associated with one route table, which decides where its traffic is looked up. Propagation lets an attachment advertise its routes into a table automatically.

Transit Gateway Connect is an attachment type for third-party SD-WAN appliances, which are virtual routers running on EC2 instances in a VPC. The appliance reaches the hub through a transport VPC attachment. On top of that you create a Connect attachment and one or more Connect peers. Each peer is a pair of inside addresses carried over a GRE tunnel (Generic Routing Encapsulation, which wraps packets inside another IP packet), with a BGP session (Border Gateway Protocol, which exchanges route announcements between routers) running across it. The appliance announces branch prefixes over BGP, and the hub learns them and propagates them into route tables. Nobody types those routes by hand.

Worked example: an appliance in a shared-services VPC announces 10.50.0.0/16, a branch network. The hub learns it and propagates it into the spoke route table. A spoke VPC sends traffic to 10.50.4.7.
