Traffic goes over the dedicated line to the public address and never enters the VPC. Option B: an interface endpoint exists at 10.0.5.12 in a VPC subnet. The on-premises routing sends 10.0.0.0/16 over the private virtual interface, and the service name resolves to 10.0.5.12. Traffic stays on private addresses end to end.

Common mistake: assuming a gateway endpoint can be reached from on-premises. It only serves resources in the VPC whose route tables point at it, so on-premises traffic needs an interface endpoint instead. In a running system, that mistake produces failed uploads or traffic that quietly takes the public path, which can break a policy that requires private access.

The private path is reachable only when routing, the endpoint type and name resolution all agree.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm has an on-premises warehouse server at 172.16.8.40. It must reach a key management service privately over a Direct Connect private virtual interface. The firm's VPC uses 10.40.0.0/16. An interface endpoint has been created in a subnet and given the private address 10.40.2.9. The on-premises network has a route sending 10.40.0.0/16 over the private virtual interface, so packets can reach that address. Step 1: the interface endpoint exists with address 10.40.2.9 in the VPC. Step 2: the on-premises route for 10.40.0.0/16 uses the private virtual interface. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the server connects to the service name and its traffic stays on private addresses. What belongs in the missing Step 3?
choices: Add a route for the service's public address over the public virtual interface so the server has a backup path.
Replace the interface endpoint with a gateway endpoint so on-premises traffic can use route table entries.
Set up a site-to-site VPN over the internet as a second path to the service.
Configure on-premises DNS so the service name resolves to 10.40.2.9 rather than a public address.
questions.why: Name resolution must return the endpoint's private address, otherwise the server uses the public address and the private path is not taken.

questions.prompt: Which kind of virtual interface on a dedicated line carries traffic to the public addresses of AWS services without that traffic entering your private virtual network?
choices: A public virtual interface
An interface endpoint with a private address
A VPN tunnel using IPsec over the internet
A private virtual interface attached to a transit gateway
questions.why: A public virtual interface carries traffic to public service addresses and keeps it out of the private network, which is the defining property asked about.

questions.prompt: A clinic's on-premises scheduling app at 192.168.44.10 connects over a VPN to a database service. The team created a gateway endpoint in the clinic's VPC and expects the app to reach the database through it. Uploads from the app fail. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The VPN tunnel uses IPsec, which blocks gateway endpoints.
The database service has no public address, so the app must use a public virtual interface.
The VPN bandwidth is too low for the app's traffic.
The gateway endpoint is only usable by resources in the VPC whose route tables point at it, so on-premises traffic cannot use it and an interface endpoint is needed.
questions.why: Gateway endpoints work through route table entries in the VPC and serve only resources there, so on-premises clients need an interface endpoint with a private address.

questions.prompt: A team runs a site-to-site VPN from its office to a cloud VPC. Users report that transfers are sometimes slow and sometimes fast. Which statement best explains this behavior?
choices: The VPN is an encrypted IPsec tunnel over the ordinary internet, so its bandwidth and latency depend on the internet path between the two sites.
Interface endpoints throttle VPN traffic whenever more than one user connects.
The VPN is a dedicated physical line, so its speed changes only when the hardware fails.
Speed changes because the VPN automatically switches between public and private virtual interfaces.
questions.why: A VPN runs over the public internet, so the path it takes determines its bandwidth and latency, which is why its performance varies.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether on-premises servers should reach an object storage service over a public virtual interface or through a private endpoint. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not choose by default.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start from the requirement. If the data must not cross public paths, I use a private route: a private virtual interface from the data centre into the VPC, plus an interface endpoint for the service, since a gateway endpoint cannot be reached from on-premises. The service name has to resolve to the endpoint's private address, or the traffic goes out the public path anyway. If the requirement only needs encryption in transit and not private addressing, a public virtual interface is simpler and avoids endpoint costs. The tradeoff with the public path is that traffic still leaves through the public address, so it is harder to prove privacy and data transfer charges may apply. The tradeoff with the endpoint path is that it adds per-hour and per-gigabyte costs and depends on correct DNS and route configuration, so I would verify it with a test upload before cutover.
rubricPoints: A public virtual interface reaches public service addresses and does not enter the VPC.
A private route to a VPC needs a private virtual interface or VPN plus routes for the VPC range.
A gateway endpoint works only for resources inside the VPC, while an interface endpoint has a private address reachable from on-premises.
Name resolution must return the private endpoint address, or traffic silently uses the public path.
Each option carries a tradeoff in privacy, cost, or configuration complexity.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between public and private paths across endpoint types is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario, since no current mission covers cloud networking.

lessons.plain: This is about where the two ends of a network conversation sit. Inside one Region, the parts of a system are spread across separate buildings called Availability Zones. These sit close together and talk quickly. Between Regions, the parts are far apart, sometimes thousands of kilometres, so every message takes longer and usually costs more to send. The pattern a system uses decides how fast it feels to users, what it costs, and what keeps working when one site fails. Think of a team in one office versus a team in another country: a quick hallway chat versus a long-distance call you try to make rarely.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app server in one city sends 20 small database requests one after another. Would the page feel faster if the database sat in the same building or on another continent, and why?
lessons.teach: A Region is a geographic area that contains several Availability Zones (AZs), which are separate data centre sites with their own power and cooling. Intra-Regional communication means traffic that stays inside one Region, usually between AZs. Inter-Regional communication means traffic that crosses from one Region to another. Latency is the delay before a message arrives. Round-trip latency is the time for a request and its reply to complete. Traffic between AZs in one Region typically has round-trip latency of a few milliseconds, while Regions can be tens or hundreds of milliseconds apart. Data transfer charges are the fees for moving bytes, and traffic crossing Regions is usually billed at a higher rate than traffic within one Region. Why it matters: each hop adds delay and cost, so the pattern you choose sets a floor on how fast a request can finish. Worked example: an order service in AZ-a calls a database in AZ-b of the same Region 20 times in sequence, each call taking 2 ms round trip, so the work takes about 40 ms. Move the same database to a second Region with an 80 ms round trip and the same 20 calls take about 1.6 seconds before any real work is done. To check a design, first count the sequential calls, then multiply by the round trip, then compare the result with the user's time budget. Common mistake: assuming a cross-Region link behaves like a local one, so a chatty design passes tests in one Region and then fails after a cross-Region failover. Consequence: during a regional outage, traffic redirected to a backup Region can turn a fast page into a slow one while also raising the bill. Keep chatty calls inside one Region and send across Regions only the data that truly must cross the distance.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company's seat-map service runs in Region North-1 and must read a seating table in Region South-2. A single seat-map page makes 8 sequential calls to that table, and each call has a 90 ms round trip. The page has a 500 ms budget. Step 1: count the sequential calls, which is 8. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: compare the total with the 500 ms budget. The design fails, because 720 ms is well over the budget.
choices: Add the 8 calls to the 90 ms round trip to get 98 ms, then compare that with the budget.
Divide the 90 ms round trip by 8 to find the average time each call spends waiting, which is about 11 ms.
Replace the 500 ms budget with the round trip, since the budget is the limit on each call rather than on the page.
Multiply the 8 sequential calls by the 90 ms round trip to get the total delay of 720 ms.
questions.why: Sequential calls add up, so the total delay is the number of calls times the round trip, which here is 8 times 90 ms, or 720 ms.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines intra-Regional communication?
choices: Any request that uses a cache, regardless of where the cache is located.
Traffic that is billed at the same rate as internet egress because it crosses a provider boundary.
Traffic that leaves a Region and returns through a different Region within the same hour.
Traffic that moves between two Availability Zones or resources that both sit inside the same Region.
questions.why: Intra-Regional means the traffic stays inside one Region, usually between its AZs, and the other options describe cross-Region traffic, caching, or billing rules that are not part of the definition.

questions.prompt: A booking app keeps its session store in Region East-A and its API in Region West-B. Each user action triggers 15 sequential reads of the session store, with a 70 ms round trip. A team argues that the app is fine because each read is fast. What is the flaw in that reasoning?
choices: Session stores should never be placed in a different Region, so the design is wrong no matter the latency.
The round trip only matters when the reads run in parallel, so sequential reads have no effect on speed.
Data transfer fees are the only real concern, so latency can be ignored when the bill is small.
The reads are fast individually, but the 15 sequential reads add up to about 1050 ms, so the page can still be slow.
questions.why: Sequential calls each pay the full round trip, so 15 calls at 70 ms take about 1.05 seconds, which is the key reason a fast single read can still produce a slow page.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm moves a reporting job from a database in its primary Region to a copy in a backup Region after an outage. The job used to finish in 3 seconds using only local calls. After the move, it makes the same number of cross-Region calls and the job takes 40 seconds. Which lesson from the pattern choice best explains the change?
choices: Backups should always be kept in the same Region as the primary, so the job was moved to the wrong place.
Cross-Region calls cost less than local calls, so the job should have finished faster.
The outage itself slowed the job, and latency is unrelated to where the calls go.
Every chatty call that crosses a Region pays a much longer round trip, so a design that was fast locally can become slow after failover.
questions.why: Cross-Region round trips are tens or hundreds of milliseconds, so a chatty pattern that was cheap inside one Region multiplies that delay after the job moves across Regions.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would keep a service's calls within one Region and when you would send them across Regions. Name one limit or tradeoff of the cross-Region choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I keep calls inside one Region by default, and spread the copies across Availability Zones there, because AZ-to-AZ round trips are a few milliseconds and transfer is cheaper. I only cross Regions when the goal needs it, such as disaster recovery or serving users far away. The main tradeoff is that every cross-Region call adds tens of milliseconds and a higher per-gigabyte charge, so a design that makes many sequential calls across the gap becomes slow and expensive. I would check the number of calls per user request, not just the average latency, and I would send only the data that must cross, often in batches or asynchronously. I would also test the design as it would run after a failover, because the slowdown often appears only then.
rubricPoints: Defines the same-Region pattern as traffic across Availability Zones with low latency and lower transfer cost
Defines the cross-Region pattern as traffic between Regions with higher latency and higher transfer cost
Explains that sequential calls multiply the round-trip delay, so chatty designs suffer most across Regions
Names a concrete tradeoff, such as resilience or user proximity gained versus latency and cost added

suggested.rationale: Choosing between same-Region and cross-Region patterns is best practised by reasoning through a realistic scenario with competing requirements.

lessons.plain: Network performance is how much data moves and how quickly, and reachability is whether one machine can reach another at all. Two things quietly limit both: the largest packet size every hop along a path will accept, and the routes and filters that decide where packets are allowed to go. When a link is slow or a host seems unreachable, these are the first places to look, before anyone buys a bigger connection or redesigns the network. Think of it like shipping boxes through a chain of depots: one depot with a smaller door forces everything through it, and a rule at the gate can turn traffic away without any error on the sender's side.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server in one network sends a large file to a server in another network. Small messages arrive fine, but the large transfer freezes partway through. What single property of the path would you check first, and why?
lessons.teach:
The maximum transmission unit (MTU) is the largest packet, in bytes, that a network link will carry without splitting it. The common Ethernet value is 1500 bytes. Jumbo frames are larger packets, often up to 9001 bytes, which carry more data per packet and so waste less effort on headers. They only help when every hop supports them. The path MTU is the smallest MTU along the whole route between two hosts, and that smallest value is the real ceiling. A sender can set the don't-fragment (DF) flag, which tells routers not to split its packets. If a router must forward a packet larger than its outgoing link allows, it drops the packet and returns an ICMP 'fragmentation needed' message reporting its limit, so the sender can shrink its packets. This process is called path MTU discovery.

Worked example. Host A sends 8000-byte packets with DF set toward host B across a VPN link with MTU 1500. Step 1: a small ping of 64 bytes succeeds. Step 2: a 1400-byte transfer succeeds. Step 3: an 8000-byte packet reaches the VPN router, which drops it and returns an ICMP message reporting 1500. Step 4: if a firewall blocks all ICMP, that message never arrives, so host A keeps resending large packets and the transfer stalls. The reachability test passed, but the large-packet path is broken.

Common mistake: treating a successful ping as proof that the full path works, or blocking all ICMP for security reasons without understanding what it carries. Consequence: connections open normally, then hang when a large response arrives, which looks like an application bug. Reachability asks whether a path exists under the route tables and filters, while performance depends on throughput, latency and packet loss, and packet size shapes all three. Check the smallest MTU on the path and whether the ICMP messages that report it are allowed through before blaming the application.

questions.prompt: A warehouse sensor uploads files to a server in another building. The path crosses three links: a local network with MTU 9000 bytes, a site-to-site tunnel with MTU 1472 bytes, and an uplink with MTU 1500 bytes. The maximum transmission unit (MTU) is the largest packet a link carries without splitting it. Step 1: list each link's MTU, which gives 9000, 1472 and 1500. Step 2: the path MTU is the smallest value on the route, and this is the real ceiling for packet size. Step 3 is missing: identify the path MTU, in bytes, that the sender must respect. Which completion is correct?
choices: The path MTU is 1472 bytes, because the tunnel is the smallest link and sets the ceiling.
The path MTU is 4236 bytes, because it is the average of the three link sizes.
The path MTU is 1500 bytes, because the uplink is the last hop before the server.
The path MTU is 9000 bytes, because the largest link sets the ceiling for the whole route.
questions.why: The path MTU is the smallest MTU along the whole route, and 1472 is the smallest of the three values, so it is the ceiling the sender must respect.

questions.prompt: A network path has three links with MTUs of 1500, 1400 and 9000 bytes. Which value is the path MTU for this route?
choices: 1500 bytes, because 1500 is the standard Ethernet value and the first hop uses it.
9000 bytes, because jumbo frames on the largest link define the route's capacity.
1450 bytes, because the path MTU is roughly the midpoint of the link sizes.
1400 bytes, because it is the smallest MTU along the route and sets the real ceiling.
questions.why: The path MTU is the smallest MTU on the whole route, which here is the 1400-byte link, regardless of the larger links elsewhere on the path.

questions.prompt: A branch office firewall drops all ICMP traffic to protect against scanning. Staff can ping the head office and small file lookups work, but large uploads to the same server start and then hang. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The head office DNS server is returning stale records for the upload hostname.
The TLS certificate on the upload server expired, which only affects large transfers.
The firewall drops the ICMP fragmentation-needed message, so the sender never learns the smaller limit and keeps sending packets that are too big.
The branch office LAN has jumbo frames enabled, so packets are always split at the firewall.
questions.why: When the don't-fragment flag is set, an oversized packet is dropped and the router returns an ICMP fragmentation-needed message; blocking that ICMP stops the sender from shrinking its packets, so large transfers stall while small ones succeed.

questions.prompt: A reachability check on a cloud route table reports that host X can reach host Y, and a monitoring graph shows that throughput between them is poor. Which statement correctly explains this?
choices: A reachability pass means every packet size works, so the throughput issue must be on host Y alone.
Throughput is determined only by the destination's link speed, so route and MTU details do not matter once reachability passes.

Reachability only shows that a path exists under the routes and filters, while throughput also depends on latency, packet loss and packet size, so a passed check does not rule out an MTU or loss problem.
The reachability check proves the application is healthy, so the poor throughput must come from the monitoring tool.
questions.why: Reachability answers whether a path exists under route tables and filters, but performance depends on throughput, latency, loss and packet size, so a reachability pass does not confirm that large packets can cross the path.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a file transfer can hang even though the two servers can ping each other, and name one limit or tradeoff of using jumbo frames across a mixed network.
lessons.modelAnswer: The ping works because small packets fit under every link's limit, so the path is reachable. The file transfer sends large packets with the don't-fragment flag set. At the first link with a smaller MTU, the router drops the packet and tries to send back an ICMP message saying what size it can accept. If a firewall blocks that ICMP message, the sender never learns the limit and keeps retrying large packets, so the transfer stalls after the connection opens. The fix is to allow that ICMP path, or to lower the MTU on the sending side or clamp the TCP segment size. A tradeoff of jumbo frames is that they only help when every hop supports them. If one link in the middle is 1500, the larger packets get dropped or fragmented, so you either match MTU across the whole path or accept the smaller limit.
rubricPoints: Reachability and performance are separate: a ping only proves that small packets pass.
MTU is the largest packet a link carries, and the path MTU is the smallest along the route.
With DF set, an oversize packet is dropped and an ICMP message should report the limit back to the sender.
Blocking ICMP can cause stalls on large transfers that look like application failures.
Jumbo frames only help when every hop supports them, so mixed paths need matching MTUs or a lower limit.

suggested.rationale: A planned virtual network path tracer would let the learner step a packet hop by hop and see where size or filter limits break it.

lessons.plain: When something on a cloud network is slow or unreachable, you need evidence. This objective covers three ways to gather it. CloudWatch is the general monitoring service that stores numbers over time, text logs, and alarms that trigger when a number goes past a limit. VPC flow logs are short summaries of which network connections happened, between which addresses and ports, and whether they were allowed. VPC Traffic Mirroring is a more expensive option that copies the actual packets so you can look inside them. Think of flow logs as a phone bill showing who called whom, and mirroring as recording the calls.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web server in one subnet cannot reach a database in another subnet, and nobody has changed any code. Which single record would you most want to see first, and why?
lessons.teach:
CloudWatch stores metrics (numbers sampled over time, such as bytes sent per minute or error counts), logs (text records collected into named log groups), and alarms (rules that fire when a metric crosses a threshold). A VPC flow log is a record of IP traffic seen at a network interface in your virtual network. Each record summarises packets that share the same source address, destination address, ports and protocol over a short capture window. Its fields include source and destination address, ports, protocol number, packet and byte counts, start and end times, and an action of ACCEPT or REJECT. A flow log never contains the payload. VPC Traffic Mirroring copies the real packets from a chosen network interface to a monitoring target, so you can inspect contents, but it costs more and adds load to the source.

Flow logs work because the network enforcement points, such as security groups and network ACLs, decide ACCEPT or REJECT for each connection, and the log records that decision.

Worked example: a record shows srcaddr 10.0.1.25, dstaddr 10.0.2.40, dstport 5432, protocol 6, action REJECT. Step 1: protocol 6 is TCP. Step 2: port 5432 is a common database port. Step 3: REJECT means a rule dropped the connection before it reached the database, so you check the security group or network ACL that guards the database side.

Common mistake: reading a flow log as proof that the application works, or expecting it to show what was in the request. It shows conversations and decisions, not content or latency.

In a running system, a steady stream of REJECT records on one port is often the first sign of a misconfigured rule, long before users report a fault.

questions.prompt: A flow log record from a different team's network shows srcaddr 172.16.3.14, dstaddr 172.16.8.20, dstport 6379, protocol 6, packets 4, action REJECT. Step 1: protocol 6 is TCP, the reliable transport protocol that a connection uses. Step 2: port 6379 is the default port for Redis, an in-memory cache service. Step 3 is missing: work out what the REJECT action tells you about where the connection was stopped, and which control to inspect first. A security group is a per-resource virtual firewall, and a network ACL is a subnet-level filter; both can drop traffic.
choices: The cache process has crashed, so restart the Redis service before checking any network rules.
The record shows the Redis commands were malformed, so enable Traffic Mirroring to read the payload.
The four packets show the connection succeeded, so the cache is healthy and the fault lies elsewhere in the application.
The REJECT means a rule dropped the connection before it reached Redis, so check the security group or network ACL guarding the cache side.
questions.why: REJECT is the enforcement decision recorded by a security group or network ACL, so the first place to look is the rule guarding the destination side, not the service itself.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what a VPC flow log record contains?
choices: Latency and response-time measurements for each connection, collected every few seconds.
Summaries of connections seen at a network interface, including addresses, ports, protocol, counts and an ACCEPT or REJECT action, but no payload.
Copies of the actual packets from a chosen interface, so you can read application data inside them.
A list of every security group rule and its last-modified date across the account.
questions.why: A flow log summarises traffic conversations and the enforcement decision, and it never includes packet contents or timing of application responses.

questions.prompt: A backup server at 192.168.50.7 sends nightly files over port 22 to 192.168.60.9. Flow logs show many ACCEPT records for that flow, yet the team says the backups are slow. What can the flow logs tell them?
choices: The logs confirm the connections are being accepted but cannot show why the transfer is slow, because they do not record latency.
The ACCEPT records prove the backup job finished successfully and the slowness is only a display issue.
The byte counts reveal exactly which files were corrupted during transfer.
The record shows the slowdown is caused by the destination disk, so restart that server.
questions.why: ACCEPT shows the decision was allowed, while flow logs carry no latency or content, so they cannot diagnose slowness on their own.

questions.prompt: A payments company wants to be warned early when a newly changed rule starts blocking traffic on port 8443, before customers report failures. Which approach fits the tools described for this objective?
choices: Wait for customer tickets, since flow logs only refresh once a month.
Set an alarm on the instance's CPU usage, because each REJECT action appears as a CPU spike.
Set a CloudWatch alarm on a metric that rises as REJECT records for that port accumulate, so the team is alerted when the count crosses a threshold.
Enable Traffic Mirroring on every interface and read the copied packets manually each morning.
questions.why: CloudWatch alarms fire when a metric crosses a threshold, and a rising REJECT count on one port is the early warning the teaching text describes, without the cost of mirroring.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between CloudWatch metrics, VPC flow logs and VPC Traffic Mirroring when a service reports that a link is slow. Name one limit or tradeoff of the tool you would pick first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with CloudWatch metrics for the affected interface or load balancer, because they are cheap and show whether bytes, errors or retransmissions changed and when. If the metrics show traffic is being blocked or behaving oddly between two specific addresses, I would turn to VPC flow logs, which tell me which connections were accepted or rejected and how many packets and bytes moved, without the cost of capturing content. Only if I still cannot explain the slowness, for example to see packet sizes, retransmissions or odd flags, would I use Traffic Mirroring to copy packets to an inspection target. The limit I would state is that flow logs sample conversations over a capture window and omit payloads and detailed timing, so they can show that traffic moved but not exactly why it was slow. Traffic Mirroring carries its own cost and load, so I would enable it briefly and with narrow filters.
rubricPoints: CloudWatch metrics give cheap, time-based evidence of change first
VPC flow logs show accepted or rejected connections between addresses and ports, not payloads
Traffic Mirroring copies packets, gives deepest detail, and costs more
Names a concrete limit, such as flow logs lacking payload and precise latency

suggested.rationale: Choosing which evidence source to trust for a slow or unreachable path is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario, which the course's existing missions do not provide for AWS networking.

lessons.plain: A transit gateway is a central hub that connects many private networks, such as your cloud virtual networks and your office network, so they can reach each other through one place instead of a tangle of direct links. As the hub grows, it gets hard to see which networks plug into which, or which routes lead where. Mapping the topology means drawing that picture from the live setup: the hubs, the connections that plug into them, the route tables that steer traffic, and the links out to offices. Network Manager is the tool that builds this picture from the service's own records, so you can answer 'what connects to what' before you change anything.
lessons.guessPrompt: Three cloud networks and an office all connect through one central hub, and one cloud network cannot reach another. What is the first picture you would want to see before changing any setting, and why?
lessons.teach:
A transit gateway is a regional router hub. Each network or site that connects to it is called an attachment. Attachments can be a virtual private cloud (an isolated network inside your cloud account), a VPN (an encrypted tunnel over the internet), a Direct Connect gateway (a dedicated private line into the cloud), or another transit gateway. Each hub has route tables, which are lists saying which destination ranges go to which attachment. An association links an attachment to the table used for its outbound traffic. Propagation means the hub learns a network's address range automatically and adds it to a table, instead of you typing it in. A topology is the map of nodes (hubs, attachments, sites) and the links between them. Network Manager gathers these records into one view, and you can register your office sites and devices so they appear on the same map.

Worked example. Hub H has attachments A (production VPC), B (shared services VPC) and C (analytics VPC), plus a VPN to the office. A and B use table P. Analytics team says A cannot reach C. Step 1: open the topology and select attachment C. Step 2: check its association and propagation settings. Step 3: note C is not propagated into table P, so table P has no route to C's address range. Step 4: the map now shows the gap as a missing link, which tells you where to look next.

Common mistake: treating the map as proof that traffic flows. A topology shows what is configured, not what packets actually do. Use flow logs or Reachability Analyzer to test real paths.

Consequence: if a site or device is not registered, the map has a hole in it, so an outage can look like it sits in the wrong place. A complete, current map is the starting point for every fix in this unit.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Logistics runs a hub with three attachments: a web VPC (attachment W), a reporting VPC (attachment R), and a Direct Connect gateway to the head office (attachment D). Table T1 is the route table used for W's outbound traffic, and table T2 is used for D's. The web team says W cannot reach R. Worked steps: Step 1: open the topology and select attachment W. Step 2: [MISSING: this is the step you must work out]. Step 3: confirm that R is propagated into table T1, and see that it is not, so T1 has no route to R's range. Step 4: the map shows the gap as a missing link, which tells you where to look next.
choices: Delete and recreate the hub so that propagation resets on every table
Register the head office on the map so the topology has no hole in it
Run a flow log query on R to measure how many packets it drops
Check that W is associated with table T1, the table its outbound traffic uses
questions.why: Step 2 is to confirm the association between W and the table its outbound traffic uses, because that table is the one that must contain a route to R.

questions.prompt: At Corvid Labs, a new VPC is attached to the hub and its address range appears in a route table without an engineer typing it in. Which term describes this process?
choices: Propagation, where the hub learns a network's address range automatically and adds it to a table
Attachment, a connected network such as a VPN or a Direct Connect gateway
Topology, the map of hubs, attachments, sites and the links between them
Association, which links an attachment to the table used for its outbound traffic
questions.why: Propagation is defined in the teaching text as the hub learning an address range automatically and adding it to a table, which is exactly what happened here.

questions.prompt: Ferncliff's Network Manager map shows every attachment and link as configured, yet its payment service cannot reach the fraud service. Which conclusion is best supported by the teaching text?
choices: The fraud service is at fault alone, because a complete map rules out every network path
The payment service is in another Region, which the map cannot show, so no testing is needed
The map records configuration only, so the real path must be tested with flow logs or Reachability Analyzer
The hub must be rebuilt, because a map that shows links is always wrong about the real paths
questions.why: The teaching text says a topology shows what is configured, not what packets actually do, so real paths must be tested with flow logs or Reachability Analyzer.

questions.prompt: Harlow Dental connects a branch office over a VPN, but the branch device was never registered in Network Manager. During an outage at the branch, the team sees the fault shown at the hub. What is the main risk the teaching text points to?
choices: Traffic from the branch is rerouted through the analytics VPC without any configuration change
The map has a hole where the branch should be, so an outage can appear to sit in the wrong place
The VPN is disabled automatically until the branch is registered on the map
The hub deletes the branch's propagated routes on its own when the site is unregistered
questions.why: The teaching text warns that an unregistered site leaves a hole in the map, so an outage can look like it sits in the wrong place.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a transit gateway topology map in Network Manager shows you that a single route table does not, and name one thing the map cannot prove on its own.
lessons.modelAnswer: A route table only lists the destinations one hub table knows about, so it cannot show how the whole setup fits together. The topology map draws every hub, attachment, and office site as nodes with links between them, so you can see which networks connect and which tables they use. That lets you spot a missing link, like a network that never propagated into the table its peers use, before you read any single table line by line. The limit is that the map shows configuration, not traffic. A link can look correct on the map and still drop packets because of a security rule or a wrong address range. To prove a path works, you need a reachability test or flow logs, and you should say so in any report that relies on the map.
rubricPoints: Describes the topology as a whole-network view of hubs, attachments, and sites, unlike one route table
Explains how the map helps locate a missing or wrong link, such as a missing propagation
States that the map shows configuration, not live traffic
Names a tool that proves actual reachability, such as Reachability Analyzer or flow logs

suggested.rationale: The planned virtual network path tracer would let the learner follow a path across hubs and attachments, which practises the same reading of a multi-hop network map.

lessons.plain: Think of a busy road where you want to watch every car without stopping any of them. Traffic mirroring is like a camera that photographs a copy of each vehicle passing a point, while the originals keep moving. In cloud networks, the vehicles are packets, small chunks of data that carry messages between computers. Packet-shaping problems are issues with how big packets are, how they are split, or how often they are resent, such as packets too large for part of the route. Looking at copies of real packets lets an engineer see these problems directly instead of guessing from averages.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web app loads small pages fine, but large downloads from a cloud server hang partway through. What would you suspect about packet size, and how could you look at the actual packets without slowing the app down?
lessons.teach:
A packet is one small unit of data sent across a network, with a header that says where it is going and how big it is. Packet size matters because every link on a route has a maximum transmission unit (MTU), the largest packet it will carry without splitting. A packet larger than a link's MTU is either split into fragments or dropped, and both slow traffic down. VPC Traffic Mirroring is an AWS feature that copies packets from a chosen elastic network interface (ENI, a virtual network card attached to a virtual machine) and sends the copies to a monitoring target, such as an ENI running a capture tool or a Network Load Balancer in front of several tools. The original packets keep their normal path, so the copy does not slow the application. A mirror session ties together a source, a target, a filter that selects traffic by protocol, address range or port, and an optional limit on how many bytes of each packet are copied.

Worked example: a server's large responses time out, but small ones work. You mirror the server's ENI with a filter for TCP on the application port. Step one: the capture shows 1500-byte packets marked 'do not fragment'. Step two: a router further along the route has a smaller MTU, so it cannot forward them and sends no usable reply. Step three: the sender times out and resends the same size, so the same loss repeats. The fix is correcting the path or its MTU settings, not adding capacity to the server.

Common mistake: assuming the mirror shows what the application experienced. It shows only what crossed that one interface, and filters or truncation can hide the rest. Mirrored traffic also adds load and cost, so filter narrowly.

Consequence in a running system: a mirror target that cannot keep up drops copies, so a capture can look clean when packets were in fact lost.

questions.prompt: Scenario: a retailer's checkout API runs on a server whose ENI is mirrored with a filter for TCP port 8443. Step one: the capture shows 1460-byte packets with the do-not-fragment flag set, and client responses above that size stall while small responses succeed. Step two: ___. Step three: the server's TCP stack resends the same 1460-byte packets, and the same stall repeats. Which choice correctly fills step two?
choices: The mirror target's load balancer dropped copies, so the capture itself is incomplete.
The checkout server's CPU is saturated, so it builds the responses too slowly.
A router on the route has an MTU below 1460, so it cannot forward those packets and sends no usable reply.
The filter excluded UDP traffic, so the stall must come from a different protocol.
questions.why: Loss that depends on packet size and repeats at the same size points to a link further along the route with a smaller MTU, which the do-not-fragment flag prevents from being split.

questions.prompt: A mirror session's filter is set to TCP port 443 only. Which statement describes what happens to traffic that does not match the filter?
choices: It keeps its normal path and is not copied to the monitoring target.
It is dropped by the mirror session so the application never receives it.
It is copied to the target at a reduced rate.
It is held at the source interface until the filter is changed.
questions.why: A filter only selects which packets are copied; unmatched packets are not copied, and the original packets always keep their normal path.

questions.prompt: A network team mirrors a payment server's ENI and sees a clean capture with no retransmissions. They conclude the application saw no packet loss. Their monitoring target is a small capture instance that has been running near its limit all day. What is the main flaw in their conclusion?
choices: The mirror shows only what crossed that interface, and a target that cannot keep up may have dropped copies.
Clean captures are always a sign of a filter that is too broad.
Mirroring only shows inbound traffic, so outbound loss is never visible.
The capture tool cannot read packets larger than its own MTU.
questions.why: A mirror reflects only one interface, and an overloaded target can silently drop copies, so a clean capture does not prove the application experienced no loss.

questions.prompt: A team mirrors a busy web tier to diagnose one slow API call. They want to keep the monitoring cost and extra load low. Which setup best follows good practice for VPC Traffic Mirroring?
choices: Set the filter to all protocols and all ports so the capture is complete.
Mirror every ENI in the VPC so that no traffic pattern is missed.
Remove the filter and rely on the target to discard unwanted packets.
Use a filter limited to the API's protocol, port and address range, so only the relevant copies are sent.
questions.why: Mirrored traffic adds load and cost, so narrow filters that select only the relevant protocol, port and address range are the recommended approach.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how VPC Traffic Mirroring helps find a packet size problem, and name one limit or tradeoff of using it.
lessons.modelAnswer: VPC Traffic Mirroring copies packets from one network interface to a monitoring target while the originals keep flowing normally. If large responses hang, we set up a mirror session with a filter for that application's traffic, then read the copies. We look for big packets marked do-not-fragment, and for the same segment being sent again and again, which points to a packet too large for part of the route. That tells us where to look, usually the path MTU, rather than the server's CPU or memory. One limit is that a mirror only sees the interface it is attached to, so anything beyond that point is invisible to it. Another is that copies add load and cost, and a target that cannot keep up will drop copies, so a clean capture does not prove nothing was lost. Truncating packets also hides the payload, so the capture confirms sizes and timing but not the content.
rubricPoints: Mirroring copies traffic from a chosen interface without interrupting the original flow.
Large packets with do-not-fragment set and repeated retransmissions indicate a size mismatch.
The mirror sees only one interface, so the view is partial.
Copies add load and cost, and a saturated target can drop copies, so captures must be interpreted carefully.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a capture scenario like the one above adds the most, since the skill is interpreting what the copied packets show.

lessons.plain: When a computer cannot reach another one, the cause is often a setting rather than a broken machine: a rule that blocks the traffic, a missing route, or a gate that is closed. Checking every setting by hand across many places is slow and easy to get wrong. A reachability check works like a planner that reads the settings, walks the path a request would take from the starting point to the target, and says whether that path is open. If it is not, it names the exact setting that stops the traffic, so you can fix one rule instead of guessing.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web server in one private network cannot be reached on port 443 from a second network, yet the server is running and healthy. Without looking at any settings, list three places along the path where a setting could block the request, and say which one you would check first and why.
lessons.teach:
Reachability means whether one network endpoint can send packets to another over the path that the network settings define. A source is where traffic starts, and a destination is where it should arrive. Several components decide the path. A route table lists where traffic for each address range should go. A security group is a stateful firewall attached to a single resource, so if an inbound connection is allowed, its replies are allowed automatically. A network access control list (NACL) is a stateless rule set applied at the subnet boundary, so the request and the reply must each be explicitly allowed. A reachability analyzer reads these settings and walks the path on paper, without sending real packets. It reports either reachable, or unreachable together with the first component that blocks the path.

Why it works: the settings are what decide whether traffic flows, so a careful walk through them answers the question for the configuration as written.

Worked example. A load balancer in subnet A must reach an app server in subnet B on port 443. Step 1: the analyzer checks the source route table, finds a route to subnet B's address range, and continues. Step 2: it checks the app server's security group, finds inbound 443 allowed from the load balancer, and continues. Step 3: it checks subnet B's NACL, finds an inbound deny for 443 placed above the allow, and stops. The result names that NACL rule. You change that rule, rerun the check, and see reachable.

Common mistake: adding a security group rule and expecting it to fix everything, while a NACL deny still blocks the path. Another is forgetting that NACLs are stateless, so reply traffic on temporary ports must be allowed as well.

Consequence: a single NACL change during a deploy can break an API path while every service still looks healthy. The analysis points at the blocking component, so the team fixes one rule instead of redesigning the network. The check covers configuration only, not whether the application is listening or whether a firewall on the host itself drops packets.

questions.prompt: Tidewater Dental runs a reporting tool in subnet C (10.20.3.0/24) that must reach a reporting database in subnet D (10.20.4.0/24) on port 5432. The reachability analyzer, which walks the configured settings on paper without sending packets, checks components in order. Step 1: the route table for subnet C has a route to 10.20.4.0/24, so the check continues. Step 3: the network access control list (NACL, a stateless rule set at the subnet boundary) for subnet D allows inbound 5432 and allows outbound ephemeral ports for replies, so the check continues. Step 2 is not written out here: the database's security group (a stateful firewall attached to the resource) allows inbound 5432 only from 10.20.9.0/24, and the reporting tool's address is 10.20.3.15. Which result does the analyzer report?
choices: Unreachable, blocked at subnet D's NACL, because the outbound reply rule is missing.
Reachable, because security groups only check replies, so the source address is ignored.
Unreachable, blocked at the database security group, because 10.20.3.15 is outside the allowed source range.
Reachable, because the NACL check at step 3 passed and that is the last check that matters.
questions.why: The analyzer stops at the first blocking component, and the security group's inbound rule does not match the reporting tool's address, so that group is the blocker.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does a reachability analyzer do, and what does it report when a path is blocked?
choices: It sends test packets through the network and reports latency for each hop along the path.
It edits route tables and NACLs until the path works, then lists the changes it made.
It reads the configured settings, walks the path without sending real packets, and reports reachable or unreachable with the first blocking component.
It checks whether the application on the destination is listening and reports the process name.
questions.why: The analyzer evaluates the configuration on paper and names the first component that stops traffic, without sending packets or changing anything.

questions.prompt: Northwind Logistics has a webhook sender in subnet 10.40.1.0/24 that calls an order service in subnet 10.40.2.0/24 on port 8443. The analyzer reports unreachable at subnet 10.40.2.0/24's NACL, where an inbound deny for 8443 sits above an inbound allow for 8443. The team adds an inbound allow for 8443 to the order service's security group and reruns the analysis. What happens?
choices: Reachable, because a security group allow overrides a NACL deny when both are present.
Unreachable, but the fault moves to the route table, because the analyzer checks routes last.
Still unreachable, reported at the same NACL, because the NACL deny at the subnet boundary still blocks the path.
Reachable, because adding a security group rule resets the order in which the NACL is evaluated.
questions.why: A security group change does not alter a NACL rule, and the NACL deny sits above the allow, so the analyzer still stops there.

questions.prompt: A batch worker in subnet 10.60.5.0/24 is shown as reachable by the analyzer to a metrics agent on port 9100, yet its connections time out. Which explanation fits the scope of the check?
choices: The analyzer is wrong and should be rerun with real packets sent through the network.
The route table must be missing a default route, which the analyzer failed to report.
The check reads configuration only, so a firewall on the host itself or a process not listening on port 9100 would not show up.
The NACL is stateful, so the reply traffic is being dropped at the subnet boundary.
questions.why: The analyzer covers configuration only, so host-level firewalls and whether the application is listening lie outside what it can detect.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use a reachability check to find out why a service cannot be reached after a configuration change. Name one thing the check cannot tell you.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by naming the exact source and destination, then run the check for the protocol and port that fails. The check walks the route tables, security groups and network ACLs along the path without sending real traffic. If it reports unreachable, it names the first component that blocks the path, such as a deny rule in a network ACL. I would change only that rule, rerun the check, and then send real traffic to confirm. The limit is that it only checks configuration as written. It cannot tell me whether the application is listening on the port, or whether a firewall on the host drops packets, so a passing check does not prove the service works.
rubricPoints: Describes the check as a walk through configuration from source to destination, not a test of live traffic.
Explains that the result names the blocking component so only that setting needs changing.
Names a limit: it does not confirm the application is listening or that host firewalls allow traffic.
Notes that a passing check should be followed by a real connectivity test.

suggested.rationale: A virtual network path tracer lets the learner walk a simulated path hop by hop and find the blocking rule, which is the skill this objective tests.

lessons.plain: A design document says which systems must be able to talk to each other, which must stay apart, and how fast or safe things must be. Verifying a configuration means checking that the live or proposed setup actually does this, not just that someone typed it in. Automating that check means writing these expectations down as tests that a machine runs every time the network changes, so a change that quietly breaks a requirement is caught before it reaches users. Think of a building inspector who runs the same checklist after every renovation instead of trusting the builder's memory.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team's design says the payments service must reach the database and must never be reachable directly from the internet. On Friday someone edits a route table and a security rule. Without running any tool, what could go wrong, and how would you find out it had happened?
lessons.teach:
A requirement, sometimes called intent, is a statement of what must be true about a network: which sources may reach which destinations, on which ports, and which paths must be blocked. Verification is the act of checking a configuration against those statements. Drift is what happens when the real configuration slowly departs from the design, usually through manual edits. Automated verification means writing each requirement as a test that runs without a person, often in the same pipeline that deploys infrastructure, so every proposed change is checked before it is applied.

Why it works: a network's behaviour comes from several pieces together, including route tables, filtering rules and gateways. A single rule can look correct while a route elsewhere still exposes or blocks traffic. A path-level test asks the real question, whether a packet from A can reach B, and answers it by reading all the pieces that could affect the path.

Worked example. Requirement one: the web tier may reach the app tier on port 8080. Requirement two: the database tier must not accept traffic from the internet. Step 1: write each as a record with source, destination, port and expected result (allowed or denied). Step 2: before merging a change, the check evaluates the proposed configuration for each path. Step 3: web to app on 8080 is allowed, so the check passes. Step 4: internet to database on 5432 is denied, so it passes. Step 5: a later edit opens 5432 to all addresses. The second check now fails, and the pipeline blocks the change.

Common mistake: testing one component, such as only the security rule, and treating it as proof of the whole path. This misses routes and filters elsewhere.

Consequence: a passing check on one piece can hide an outage or an exposure. A path-level test that re-runs on every change catches both before they reach users.

questions.prompt: A reporting service in one subnet must reach a metrics store on port 9090 in another subnet, so its expected result is allowed. The analytics subnet must not reach the payroll database on port 3306, so its expected result is denied. Step 1: each requirement is written as a record with source, destination, port and expected result. Step 2: before a change merges, the check evaluates the proposed configuration for each path. Step 3: reporting to metrics on 9090 is allowed, which matches its record, so that check passes. Step 4: the check finds that analytics to payroll on 3306 is allowed, but its record expects denied. What should the pipeline do with the proposed change?
choices: Pass the change, because one path already passed
Block the change, because the observed result contradicts the expected denied result
Change the payroll record's expected result to allowed so the check passes
Pass the change but add a warning that the record may be out of date
questions.why: A requirement check fails whenever the observed result on a path differs from the expected result in its record, and a passing check on another path does not offset that.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is drift in a network that is managed with a design document?
choices: The delay between a requirement being written and the first test run
A planned, reviewed change that updates the design document first
The gradual departure of the live configuration from the design, often through manual edits
A temporary route that a cloud provider adds during maintenance
questions.why: Drift is defined as the real configuration slowly departing from the design, usually through manual edits, so the last option matches that definition.

questions.prompt: A team's test for a path from a partner network to an order API checks only that a security rule allows port 443. The route table for that path has no route back to the partner network. What does the test show?
choices: The test fails, because the route table is part of the same rule
The test passes, but a path-level test would be needed to expose the missing route
The path is verified, because the security rule that matters is present
The test is invalid, because security rules should never be tested alone
questions.why: A rule-only check passes while a route elsewhere is missing, which is why a path-level test that reads all the pieces is needed to catch it.

questions.prompt: A requirement states that a partner network may reach an order API on port 443 and nothing else. A later change opens port 8443 as well. The automated check runs on the proposed change. What is the expected outcome?
choices: The check fails, because port 8443 is now reachable though the requirement says it must be denied
The check is skipped, because it only tests ports named in the requirement
The check passes, because the change only adds a port and does not remove one
The check passes, since 443 is still allowed
questions.why: The requirement says nothing else may be reached, so an allowed result on 8443 differs from the expected denied result and the check must fail and block the change.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would turn a design requirement such as 'the app tier can reach the database on one port only' into an automated check that runs on every network change. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would write the requirement as a record: source tier, destination tier, port, and whether it must be allowed or denied. Then I would have a check run on every proposed change that evaluates each path against the real configuration, including route tables and filtering rules, not just one rule. The check runs in the deployment pipeline, so a change that breaks the requirement fails before it is applied. The main limit is that the check only tests the paths I wrote down. If a requirement is missing from the list, a bad change can pass silently, so the list of intents has to be reviewed when the design changes. Also, a path test can say a route exists but not prove that the application behind it works, so I still rely on separate health checks.
rubricPoints: Defines a requirement as a checkable record with source, destination, port and expected result
Explains that the check runs automatically on each change, before it is applied
Notes that a path-level test reads all the pieces that affect traffic, not one rule
Names a limit, such as only covering the requirements that were written down

suggested.rationale: The planned virtual network path tracer would let the learner evaluate paths against intent records, which is the core skill of this objective.

lessons.plain: When data travels between two computers, each network link has a largest packet it can carry in one piece, called its maximum transmission unit or MTU. Think of a box that must fit through a doorway: if the box is bigger than the door, it has to be cut down or the sender has to be told to pack smaller. Inside a cloud network (a VPC, which is a private section of a cloud provider's network that you control), some links allow much bigger boxes than the public internet or a VPN tunnel does. A mismatch shows up as a strange failure: small messages get through, but large file transfers or web responses hang. This lesson covers how to recognise that pattern and find where the size limit is being broken.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two servers in the same cloud network can ping each other and open a connection, but downloading a 2 MB file between them stalls partway through. What is the first size-related explanation you would test, and why would small messages still work?
lessons.teach: An MTU is the largest packet a link will carry without splitting it. A packet is one unit of data sent over the network, made of a payload plus headers. Some links allow jumbo frames, which are packets much larger than the usual 1500 bytes. Inside a VPC, instances can often use a larger MTU than traffic that leaves through an internet gateway, a VPN, or a Direct Connect path, so a large packet can be accepted at the source and then meet a smaller link. Normally the router at the smaller link either splits the packet (fragmentation) or refuses it and sends back an ICMP message, a control message from the network layer, saying the packet is too big. The sender then lowers its size. This process is called path MTU discovery. Worked example: instance A sends an 8000-byte TCP segment with the do-not-fragment flag set toward instance B across a VPN path with a 1500-byte MTU. The VPN edge drops it and returns an ICMP fragmentation-needed message to A. A should shrink its segments. If a security group or network ACL blocks that ICMP message, A never learns the limit, keeps sending 8000-byte segments, and they vanish. Small packets, such as the TCP handshake and pings, succeed, so the connection looks open while the first large response stalls. Common mistake: concluding the application or the route is broken, or allowing ICMP only from the internet while the VPN peer range is blocked. Flow logs record accepted and rejected traffic counts and bytes, but they do not state the MTU cause, so you confirm with a packet capture. The consequence is intermittent hangs and repeated retransmissions that look like random slowness. The fix is to allow the needed ICMP on every path or to set a consistent MTU, for example by clamping TCP segment size at the edge.

questions.prompt: A payments service in a VPC in ap-southeast-2 sends a 4200-byte UDP datagram with the do-not-fragment flag set to a partner's server over a site-to-site VPN whose path MTU is 1400 bytes. Here is the trace so far. Step 1: the VPN edge cannot forward the datagram and sends an ICMP fragmentation-needed message back toward the sender. Step 2: a network ACL on the sender's subnet denies inbound ICMP from the partner's address range, so the message never arrives. Step 3: (missing). Step 4: the sender keeps retransmitting the same oversized datagram, and the partner never receives it. Which completion correctly fills in step 3?
choices: Flow logs report an MTU mismatch directly, so the team skips any further checks and changes the sender's instance type.
The VPN edge silently splits the datagram and the partner reassembles it, so the ACL block has no effect on delivery.
The team concludes the partner's DNS record is stale and changes the record's time-to-live value, which leaves the datagram size unchanged.
The team confirms the cause with a packet capture, because flow logs show only accepted and rejected counts and bytes, not the MTU reason.
questions.why: Flow logs record traffic counts but do not name an MTU cause, so a packet capture is the step that confirms the mismatch.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is the MTU of a link?
choices: The largest packet a link will carry without splitting it, counting the headers as part of the packet.
The smallest packet a link will accept, used to decide when a sender should pad its data.
The total bandwidth a link can carry in one second, measured in megabits.
The number of routers a packet passes through before it reaches its destination subnet.
questions.why: An MTU is defined as the largest packet a link carries without splitting it, and the packet includes its headers.

questions.prompt: A client in a VPC completes a TCP handshake and gets replies to small pings from a partner across a VPN. The first large response then hangs, and the client keeps retrying. Which explanation best fits the failure pattern?
choices: The VPN path has a smaller MTU than the sender uses, and the ICMP message telling the sender to shrink its packets is blocked, so it keeps sending packets that are too large and they are dropped.
Security groups allow the TCP handshake on port 443 but block the ping, so the handshake never completes and the large response is never sent.
The VPC route table is missing a route for the partner's CIDR range, so the handshake packets never reach the partner at all.
The partner's application has a bug that only affects requests from the client's specific operating system version.
questions.why: Small packets succeed while large ones vanish, and a blocked ICMP fragmentation-needed message stops the sender from learning the smaller limit.

questions.prompt: A team wants to fix an MTU mismatch between a VPC and a Direct Connect path without redesigning the network. Which action addresses the cause?
choices: Move the workload to a larger instance type so that its outbound packets are always split before they leave the VPC.
Open an additional inbound TCP port on the security group so that retransmitted segments are accepted sooner.
Replace the Direct Connect link with a public internet path so every packet uses the standard 1500-byte size.
Allow the needed ICMP messages on every path between the two sides, and clamp TCP segment size at the edge to a value that fits the smaller link.
questions.why: Allowing ICMP on every path lets senders learn the limit, and clamping TCP segment size at the edge makes segments fit the smaller link, which is the fix named in the teaching text.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says the health checks pass but a large file download between two instances in our VPC, and between our VPC and an on-premises site over VPN, hangs halfway. Explain to them how a packet size mismatch could cause this, what you would check first, and one limit of that check.
lessons.modelAnswer: Small packets like health checks and handshakes fit through every link, but a large download sends full-size packets. Inside the VPC the path can carry jumbo frames, while the VPN path carries about 1500 bytes. When a large packet with the do-not-fragment flag hits the VPN edge, it is dropped and the router should send back an ICMP fragmentation-needed message so the sender shrinks its packets. If a security group, network ACL, or firewall on the VPN side blocks that ICMP, the sender never adjusts and the transfer stalls. What I would check first is whether ICMP type 3 code 4 is allowed on both sides and whether the size can be tested with a do-not-fragment ping at increasing sizes. The limit is that this test shows the symptom and the likely size boundary, but a packet capture is needed to confirm the returned message or its absence.
rubricPoints: Explains that the MTU differs between the VPC path and the VPN or internet path.
Identifies that large packets are dropped while small ones succeed, the symptom of a size mismatch.
Names path MTU discovery and the ICMP fragmentation-needed message as the mechanism that should fix it.
States that blocking that ICMP message causes the stall, and that a packet capture confirms it.

suggested.rationale: A virtual network path tracer would let the learner walk each hop and see where a large packet is dropped, which practices this objective directly.

lessons.plain: When two or more private networks in the cloud need to talk, you have several ways to connect them. The three common options differ in how many networks they link and how traffic moves between them. A direct link between two networks is simple but gets messy as the count grows. A hub that every network connects to is easier to manage at scale. A proxy is a middleman that accepts requests for one service and forwards them on, which can hide details and control what gets through. Choosing well means reading the requirements first: how many networks there are, whether traffic must pass through to networks beyond the next one, and whether only one service needs exposing.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have three office networks, A, B and C, and every office must be able to reach every other one. Before reading on, would you connect each pair directly, or put one central hub in the middle? Which would you pick, and what would worry you about that choice?
lessons.teach:
Three patterns cover most cases. VPC peering is a direct, private connection between exactly two virtual networks (a VPC is an isolated virtual network inside a cloud account). Peering is not transitive: if A peers with B and B peers with C, A cannot reach C through B, because traffic does not pass through a network that sits in the middle. Each pair needs its own peering link, so the number of links grows quickly with the number of networks.

A Transit Gateway is a regional routing hub. Each network attaches to it once, and the hub routes traffic between all attachments, including networks in other accounts or on-premises when those are attached. Routing through the hub is transitive, so adding a network means one new attachment rather than one new link per existing network. It costs more per attachment and per unit of data, but it scales.

A proxy pattern puts an intermediary in front of a service. It accepts connections on behalf of clients and opens its own connection to the backend. The client only sees the proxy, so the backend's network does not need to be reachable in general, and the proxy can filter or log requests. A proxy only carries the protocols it understands, so it suits specific application traffic, not general network reachability.

Worked example: three VPCs, A, B and C, all must talk. Peering needs three links (A-B, B-C, A-C). A hub needs three attachments and route entries so each attachment can reach the others. If only C's API must be reached by A and B, a proxy or a single exposed endpoint may be enough, and general reachability is not needed.

Common mistake: assuming peering is transitive and building a chain of peerings. Traffic from A to C is then dropped with no error from the application, and the fix is either a direct peering or a hub.

questions.prompt: A team runs four VPCs (isolated virtual networks inside a cloud account) named Pine, Oak, Birch and Cedar. All four must reach each other, so they use direct peering links, where each link joins exactly two VPCs. Step 1: list every pair that needs a link: Pine-Oak, Pine-Birch, Pine-Cedar, Oak-Birch, Oak-Cedar and Birch-Cedar, which is 6 links. Step 2: a fifth VPC, Maple, must reach all four existing VPCs, so it needs one new peering link to each of them, which is 4 new links. Step 3: the team wants the total number of peering links across all five VPCs. Step 4: total peering links after Maple joins = ?
questions.why: Five VPCs in a full set of pairwise links need 10 links (6 existing plus 4 new), since each pair needs its own link and the pairs are not transitive.

questions.prompt: A retail company has VPC Lark peered with VPC Heron, and VPC Heron peered with VPC Finch. Instances in Lark try to reach Finch and the connection fails with no error from the application. What is the most accurate explanation?
choices: Peering is not transitive, so Lark cannot reach Finch through Heron and needs its own direct peering or a hub
Heron must be in the same Region as Finch for the chain to carry traffic
Lark's peering link has expired because it was made through an intermediate VPC
Peering is transitive, so the link is still working but the security group blocks the traffic
questions.why: Peering links only join two VPCs directly, and traffic does not pass through a middle network, so Lark needs a direct link to Finch or a hub.

questions.prompt: A payments firm has three client VPCs that must call one HTTPS API running in a partner account's VPC. The clients need no other access to the partner network. Which pattern fits these requirements best?
choices: Chain peering links from each client VPC through an extra VPC to reach the partner VPC
Peer every client VPC with the partner VPC and route the entire partner address range to each one
Put a proxy in front of the partner API so clients reach only the proxy and no general network reachability is granted
Attach all four VPCs to a Transit Gateway and open routes between every attachment
questions.why: A proxy carries only the application protocol the clients need, so it meets the single-API requirement without opening general reachability into the partner network.

questions.prompt: Two VPCs, one in each of two accounts, exchange data with each other only. The team does not expect to add any more networks. Which choice is most sensible based on the requirements?
choices: A proxy pattern, because a proxy is the only way to connect two accounts
A Transit Gateway, because a hub is always cheaper once any two networks exist
A direct peering link, because two networks need only one link and a hub adds per-attachment and per-data cost
A chain of two peering links through a third VPC, because peering is transitive
questions.why: A single direct peering link is the simplest and cheapest option for two networks, while a hub's extra cost pays off only when many networks need to be connected.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate proposes connecting our five VPCs with a full mesh of VPC peering links because it seems cheaper and simpler than a hub. Explain to them, in your own words, how you would decide between peering, a hub and a proxy, and name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would recommend.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from the requirements rather than the tool. First I count the networks and check whether they all need to reach each other. Five VPCs in a full mesh means ten peering links, each managed separately, and peering does not pass traffic through a middle network, so any missing pair fails silently. A hub with five attachments needs one attachment per network and routes between them, which is easier to audit as the estate grows. The tradeoff is cost: a hub charges per attachment and per unit of data processed, so for two networks with one traffic flow, peering is cheaper and simpler. If only one service must be reached, a proxy gives narrower access and better logging. For our five VPCs I would recommend the hub, and I would name its per-attachment cost and note that its route tables still need regular review.
rubricPoints: Peering is a direct link between two networks and is not transitive
A hub scales by adding one attachment per network and routes between all of them
A proxy exposes one service through an intermediary and only carries the protocols it understands
The choice depends on how many networks there are, whether they all need to reach each other, and the cost of each option

suggested.rationale: Choosing between these patterns from a scenario is best practised by reasoning through a realistic requirement set, which no current mission covers directly.

lessons.plain: Bandwidth is how much data a connection can carry each second, and sending fewer copies of the same bytes makes a slow link faster and a large bill smaller. This lesson covers two ways to do that. The first is choosing how a sender delivers the same content: one separate copy to each receiver, called unicast, or one copy shared by everyone who asked for it, called multicast. The second is placing copies of popular content close to users with a content delivery network, which in AWS is CloudFront, so the same file does not travel the long path again and again. Both ideas answer one question: how many times does the same data travel?
lessons.guessPrompt: If 500 phones all want the same live video at the same moment, would you rather have the server send 500 separate copies, or send one copy that the network shares? Which option uses less bandwidth at the server's link, and why do you think so?
lessons.teach:
Unicast means one sender talks to one receiver. If a server streams a live video to 1,000 viewers using unicast, it makes 1,000 separate copies, so its outbound link carries the stream 1,000 times. Multicast means one sender transmits once to a group address, and the network copies packets only where group members exist. Multicast saves bandwidth when many receivers want the same data at the same time, but it needs network devices and paths that support group membership, and not every cloud network path does. In AWS, multicast inside a VPC or across a Transit Gateway works only under specific conditions, so check the current rules before designing around it.

A content delivery network, or CDN, is a set of servers spread across many locations that keep copies of content close to users. In CloudFront, those locations are called edge locations. The server that holds the original content is the origin. The first request for an object goes to the origin, and the edge keeps a copy for a period set by its time-to-live, or TTL. Later requests that the edge can answer from its copy are cache hits, and they never reach the origin.

Worked example: 10,000 requests for the same 2 MB image arrive in one hour. Step one, the cache hit ratio is 99 percent, so 9,900 requests are served from the edge. Step two, 100 requests reach the origin. Step three, the origin sends 100 times 2 MB, which is 200 MB. Without caching it would send 10,000 times 2 MB, about 20 GB.

Common mistake: caching responses that are personalized for each user, or setting a TTL so long that users keep seeing old content. Consequence in a running system: a low hit ratio sends nearly every request to the origin, so the origin's link and CPU saturate during a traffic surge, while a long TTL on an updated file keeps serving the old version until the cache expires or is invalidated.

Cached delivery moves load off the origin, and multicast carries one stream where unicast would carry many copies.

questions.prompt: A software vendor serves a 500 KB product thumbnail from its origin. In one hour, 50,000 requests arrive for it and the CloudFront cache hit ratio is 98 percent. Step one: 2 percent of 50,000 requests miss the cache, so 1,000 requests reach the origin. Step two is missing. Step three: the origin therefore sends 500 MB in that hour. What is the missing step two?
choices: Multiply 50,000 by 500 KB to get 25 GB, which is the origin load.
Divide 500 KB by 2 percent to get the cost of each cache miss.
Multiply the 1,000 origin requests by the 500 KB object size to get the bytes the origin sends.
Add the 98 percent hit ratio to the 1,000 misses to get the origin load.
questions.why: Origin bytes equal the number of requests that miss the edge cache multiplied by the size of each object, which gives 1,000 times 500 KB, or 500 MB.

questions.prompt: A online training platform streams one live lecture to 800 students at the same moment. Its network path supports multicast group membership. Which sending method sends the lecture stream from the server the fewest times?
