choices: Multicast, sending one transmission to a group address that the network copies only where members exist.
Unicast, but only for the first 100 students who join.
Unicast, creating a separate stream for each of the 800 students.
Multicast, sending one transmission per student group of 10 people.
questions.why: Multicast sends one transmission to a group address, and the network copies it only where members exist, while unicast would send 800 separate copies from the server.

questions.prompt: A retailer caches its logged-in account dashboard pages at CloudFront edge locations with a one-hour TTL. Which outcome is the most serious risk of this setup?
choices: The cache hit ratio will rise to nearly 100 percent, overloading the origin with cache refills.
The edge locations will store the pages in a different format than the origin.
The origin will receive more requests because CloudFront checks for updates on every visit.
Personalized pages may be stored and then served to a different user, and per-user pages rarely produce cache hits anyway.
questions.why: Personalized responses should not be cached and shared, because one user's copy could reach another user, and per-user content seldom gets reused, so caching it gives little benefit.

questions.prompt: A company publishes a policy PDF through CloudFront with a 24-hour TTL. It replaces the PDF at the origin, but does not invalidate the cache. What do readers in a region with an edge location see after the update?
choices: The new PDF immediately, because the origin pushes updates to all edge locations.
The old PDF, served from the edge copy until the TTL expires or the object is invalidated.
The new PDF only after the origin's CPU load drops below its normal level.
An error, because the edge cannot compare the old and new versions.
questions.why: An edge keeps its copy for the TTL period, so until that period ends or the object is invalidated, cache hits return the old version even though the origin has the new one.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never worked with networks when you would choose CloudFront or multicast over simply adding more bandwidth to the origin server. Name at least one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use CloudFront when many users fetch the same content from one origin, because the edge answers repeat requests and the origin only sends each object on a cache miss. The limit is the cache hit ratio: personalized, uncacheable, or constantly changing content gets few hits, so it still loads the origin and adds a hop. A long TTL keeps load low but serves old versions until expiry, so I would set TTLs per path and use invalidation for urgent changes. For multicast, I would only use it when many receivers on the same network need the same stream at the same time, and only after confirming the VPC or Transit Gateway path supports it. Otherwise unicast with caching is simpler. Before claiming either one helps, I would measure the bytes leaving the origin, the cache hit ratio, and the data transfer bill, because bandwidth saved on one link can move the cost somewhere else.
rubricPoints: Explains that CloudFront serves repeat requests from edge caches so the origin sends each object only on a miss
Explains that multicast sends one copy shared by group members, while unicast sends a copy per receiver
Names a limit of caching, such as low hit ratio for personalized content or stale content from a long TTL
Notes that multicast depends on network support and that the team should measure hit ratio and transfer cost before deciding

suggested.rationale: The objective is mostly facts about how CloudFront caching and multicast support work, which are best read and then checked against the current AWS documentation.

lessons.plain: When data moves between your cloud network and your own offices or data center, you pay for that movement, and the route you choose changes the bill. Some routes charge per gigabyte, some charge a flat monthly fee for a line, and some charge both. The cheapest-looking option is not always the cheapest overall, because a fixed-fee private line only saves money once you send enough data to cover its monthly cost. The skill is comparing the routes at your real monthly volume, and remembering that data leaving the cloud usually costs more than data arriving.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team moves about 500 GB a month from their cloud network to their data center. Would a dedicated private line with a monthly port fee likely be cheaper than sending the same traffic over the public internet, and why?
lessons.teach:
Connectivity options for data transfer are the routes traffic can take between a VPC (an isolated virtual network you define in the cloud) and your on-premises network (your own offices and data center). Three common routes are an encrypted tunnel over the public internet (a Site-to-Site VPN), a dedicated private line into the cloud (Direct Connect), and plain internet traffic. Charges differ. A VPN bills an hourly fee per connection plus data transfer out. Direct Connect bills a monthly port fee plus a lower per-gigabyte rate for data transfer out, meaning data leaving the cloud (egress), while inbound data is generally not charged on that path. Why it works: a dedicated line carries traffic over the provider's own links, so its per-gigabyte rate can be lower, but its fixed fee must be covered by enough volume.

Worked example, using illustrative credits rather than real rates. Suppose internet egress costs 9 credits per GB, and a private line costs 20,000 credits a month plus 2 credits per GB out. Step 1: at 10,000 GB a month over the internet, 10,000 times 9 gives 90,000 credits. Step 2: over the private line, 20,000 plus (10,000 times 2) gives 40,000 credits. Step 3: the saving is 7 credits per GB, so the private line only wins once volume passes 20,000 divided by 7, about 2,857 GB a month.

Common mistake: comparing only per-gigabyte rates and ignoring fixed fees, or forgetting that a managed gateway in the path, such as a NAT gateway, adds its own per-gigabyte processing charge. Consequence: a nightly sync routed through such a gateway can cost more than the transfer itself, and the bill rises with every byte moved.

The cheapest route is the one whose fixed and per-gigabyte costs, added up at your real monthly volume, come out lowest.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm sends backup copies from its office data center into a VPC each night. Traffic that leaves the cloud back to the office is billed at 8 credits per GB over the internet. A private line costs 15,000 credits a month plus 3 credits per GB out. Step 1: at 6,000 GB a month over the internet, 6,000 times 8 gives 48,000 credits. Step 2: over the private line, 15,000 plus (6,000 times 3) gives 33,000 credits. Step 3: the break-even volume is missing. Which completes step 3?
choices: About 1,875 GB, the fixed fee divided by the 8 credit internet rate
About 2,000 GB, the 6,000 GB volume divided by 3
3,000 GB, the 15,000 credit fixed fee divided by the 5 credit per-GB saving
15,000 GB, the monthly fixed fee read as a volume
questions.why: The private line wins once the per-GB saving (8 minus 3, which is 5) has covered the fixed fee of 15,000, so break-even is 15,000 divided by 5, or 3,000 GB.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does egress mean in the cloud billing described in this unit?
choices: A monthly port charge on a dedicated line
Traffic that stays inside one VPC
Data leaving the cloud, billed per gigabyte
The hourly fee for keeping a VPN connection up, charged per connection and per tunnel
questions.why: The teaching text defines egress as data leaving the cloud, and says that path carries a per-gigabyte charge.

questions.prompt: A team's nightly sync to its on-premises network moves 4,000 GB, and the traffic passes through a managed gateway that charges per gigabyte processed. Why can the bill end up higher than the transfer cost itself?
choices: A private line has no per-gigabyte rate, so the gateway is forced onto a more expensive public route
Inbound data is billed at the egress rate on every path, including the gateway path
Each byte also pays a per-gigabyte processing charge at the gateway, so cost rises with every byte moved
The hourly VPN fee falls as traffic rises, so the gateway makes the sync more expensive over time
questions.why: The teaching text warns that a managed gateway such as a NAT gateway adds its own per-gigabyte processing charge, so the bill grows with every byte moved.

questions.prompt: A small team moves 300 GB a month to its on-premises network. Plain internet traffic costs 5 credits per GB. A private line costs 4,000 credits a month plus 1 credit per GB out. Which route is cheapest at this volume, and why?
choices: The private line, at 1,300 credits, because the fixed fee is spread across the 300 GB
Both routes cost the same, because the per-gigabyte rates and fixed fees always balance out
Plain internet traffic, at 1,500 credits, because the private line's 4,300 credit fixed-plus-volume total is higher
The private line, at 4,300 credits, because its per-gigabyte rate is lower than the internet rate
questions.why: At 300 GB the internet route costs 1,500 credits while the private line costs 4,000 plus 300 credits, or 4,300, so the internet route is cheapest at this volume.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between an internet-based VPN and a dedicated private line for moving data from a VPC to on-premises. Name one limit or tradeoff of the cheaper option.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would compare total monthly cost at our real volume, not the per-gigabyte rate alone. A VPN has a low fixed cost: an hourly charge per connection plus data transfer out at internet-style rates, so it suits small or occasional transfers. A dedicated line adds a monthly port fee but charges less per gigabyte leaving the cloud, so it wins above a break-even volume, which is the fixed fee divided by the per-gigabyte saving. The tradeoff with the VPN is that it runs over the public internet, so throughput and latency vary, and a large steady transfer may be slower and more expensive over time. The tradeoff with the dedicated line is the fixed commitment and setup time, which is wasted if we move little data. I would also check any gateways in the path, since they add per-gigabyte charges of their own.
rubricPoints: Compares fixed fees and per-gigabyte charges together at the expected monthly volume
Explains that a dedicated line becomes cheaper only above a break-even volume
Names a limit of the VPN, such as variable performance over the public internet
Notes that gateways in the path add their own processing charges

suggested.rationale: A cost model in fictional credits would let the learner vary volume and fixed fees to find the break-even point, which is the core skill of this objective.

lessons.plain: A network interface is the virtual network card a cloud server uses to send and receive traffic. Each card has its own addresses and can carry firewall rules. Cloud providers offer cards at different performance levels. The basic card handles everyday traffic. An enhanced card, which uses a faster driver path, lets a server move far more data with less delay. A specialised card is built for tightly coupled work, such as scientific or machine-learning clusters where many servers must exchange messages constantly. Choosing the right card means matching it to how much data moves and how sensitive the work is to delay.
lessons.guessPrompt: A website handles a few small requests per second, while a physics simulation runs on 64 servers that exchange small messages thousands of times per second and must wait for each other before each step. Which kind of network card would you expect the simulation to need, and why might the simple card that works for the website make the simulation slow even though nothing is broken?
lessons.teach:
A network interface, in AWS called an elastic network interface (ENI), is the logical object that gives an instance a network identity: a private address, a hardware address, and attached security rules. An ENI on its own says nothing about speed. The Elastic Network Adapter (ENA) is the enhanced hardware and driver path behind that interface. It offers higher packet rates, higher bandwidth and lower, steadier latency than a basic path. The Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) is an ENA-style device with one extra capability: it lets applications send messages without every message passing through the operating system's network stack, a technique called OS-bypass. Every message that goes through the kernel costs processor time and adds delay, so skipping that step matters when thousands of messages are exchanged per second between nodes that wait on each other.

Worked example. A 16-node simulation runs in steps. In each step every node sends small boundary values to its neighbours, then waits for all replies before continuing. Step 1: identify the traffic pattern, which is many small messages with a synchronisation point. Step 2: a plain ENI gives the nodes addresses but ordinary network speed, so each step waits on slow message handling. Step 3: an ENA-capable instance type improves throughput and reduces jitter for general traffic. Step 4: if the messages are sent through an MPI library that supports the EFA provider, on EFA-capable instances placed together in one subnet and one Availability Zone, the messages bypass the kernel and the wait per step drops.

Common mistake: treating EFA as a general speed upgrade for any workload, such as a website or a database. Most applications gain little from it, and it only helps when the software is written or configured to use it.

Consequence: the card is tied to the instance type and to placement, so an EFA cluster spread across zones or launched on an unsupported type either fails to start or quietly runs on ordinary networking. The job then completes more slowly with no error message to explain why. Selecting the network card is therefore a decision made at design time, when the instance type and placement are chosen.

questions.prompt: A fraud-scoring team runs a Monte Carlo risk job on 24 worker instances. In each iteration, every worker sends small partial totals to its neighbours and waits for all replies before starting the next iteration. Step 1: the traffic is many small messages with a synchronisation point at every iteration. Step 2: the team chooses an EFA-capable instance type, so the adapter can support OS-bypass. Step 3: the messaging library is configured to use the EFA provider, so messages can skip the operating system's network stack. Step 4 is not yet done: decide where the workers are launched. Which action completes Step 4 so the placement requirement is met?
choices: Launch all workers in one subnet within a single Availability Zone, so they share the EFA placement.
Move the partial totals into a managed queue so that workers no longer wait on each other.
Spread the 24 workers across three Availability Zones so that one zone outage cannot stop the job.
Attach a second ENI to each worker to double the bandwidth available to the job.
questions.why: EFA's OS-bypass benefit depends on EFA-capable instances being placed together in one subnet and one Availability Zone, so the placement must be chosen at launch.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does an elastic network interface (ENI) give an instance, and what does it not tell you?
choices: A logical network identity with a private address, a hardware address and attached security rules, but no promise of speed.
A messaging technique that lets applications skip the operating system's network stack.
A load balancer that spreads incoming traffic evenly across Availability Zones.
A faster hardware path that guarantees lower latency to every other instance in the region.
questions.why: An ENI is the logical object that provides identity and security attachments, and the text says it says nothing about speed on its own.

questions.prompt: A media company moves its ordinary web front end to EFA-capable instances and expects much faster page responses. What is the most likely result?
choices: Little gain, since the benefit comes only from software that uses OS-bypass.
Responses get slower because OS-bypass adds a second network stack to every request.
The instances fail to start because web servers cannot attach an EFA device.
Responses get faster in proportion to the advertised bandwidth of the instance type.
questions.why: EFA helps when software sends many messages that skip the kernel, and ordinary web traffic typically gains little from it.

questions.prompt: A research team launches an EFA-capable cluster with nodes split across two Availability Zones to get more capacity. The job runs much slower than expected, and the logs show no error. Which explanation fits the teaching?
choices: The ENA driver was disabled, so the job lost its bandwidth allocation and no error was written.
The security rules on the ENI blocked the messages silently, and the logs did not record the drops.
Splitting nodes across zones adds a managed queue delay that cannot be seen in the job logs.
Cross-zone placement breaks the EFA requirement, so the job may quietly run on ordinary networking with no error.
questions.why: EFA depends on instances being placed together in one subnet and one Availability Zone, and when that is not met the job can silently fall back to ordinary networking.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between an elastic network interface, the Elastic Network Adapter and the Elastic Fabric Adapter, then name one limit or tradeoff you would check before choosing the Elastic Fabric Adapter for a workload.
lessons.modelAnswer: An elastic network interface is the virtual network card that gives an instance its addresses and security rules, but it says nothing about how fast traffic moves. The Elastic Network Adapter is the enhanced path behind that card, giving higher throughput, more packets per second and steadier latency for ordinary traffic. The Elastic Fabric Adapter adds the ability for an application to send messages around the operating system, which helps tightly coupled jobs where many nodes exchange small messages and wait on each other. The main tradeoff is that it only pays off when the software uses the matching messaging library, and it is limited to supported instance types, usually placed together in one subnet and one Availability Zone. Before choosing it, I would check that the instance type supports it and that the cluster can be placed as required, because a mismatch can silently fall back to ordinary networking.
rubricPoints: An elastic network interface is the logical network card carrying addresses and security rules, separate from performance.
The Elastic Network Adapter is the enhanced path that improves throughput, packet rate and latency for general traffic.
The Elastic Fabric Adapter adds OS-bypass messaging for tightly coupled workloads that exchange many small messages.
A limit to check is that EFA needs supported instance types, software that uses it, and placement in one subnet and Availability Zone.

suggested.rationale: Which instance types support each adapter and the placement rules are catalogue-style facts best learned by reading, and no listed mission or planned engine covers network interfaces.

lessons.plain: Multicast is a way to send one copy of a message from one sender to a group of receivers who have asked to hear it. Normally a network sends a separate copy for every receiver, which wastes bandwidth when a price feed or video stream goes to dozens of machines. With multicast, the sender transmits once to a special group address, and the network copies the message only where interested receivers sit. In a cloud network this is not the default behaviour. You have to check which parts of the network support it, how receivers announce that they want the group's traffic, and whether the link to the office carries that traffic at all.
lessons.guessPrompt: If one sender must deliver the same update to 50 receivers, roughly how many copies of that update should the sender's own network link need to carry under unicast, and how would that change under multicast?
lessons.teach:
Multicast means one packet addressed to a group address, delivered to every member who has joined that group. A group address is a special IP address that names a group rather than one host. For IPv4, the multicast range is 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255. Receivers join a group by telling their network, typically with the Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP), which is the protocol hosts use to announce group membership. Multicast saves bandwidth because the sender transmits once and the network duplicates the packet only toward branches that have interested receivers.

A cloud VPC, which is a private virtual network, is built mainly for unicast, meaning one-to-one traffic. Multicast needs extra support. A multicast domain is a logical grouping of network attachments on a transit or overlay device that lets group traffic flow between members. Group traffic reaches only the members of that domain, and each attachment must be enabled for it. A hybrid link to on-premises, such as a VPN or a Direct Connect path, carries multicast only if the routers at both ends are configured to pass it.

Worked example: a sender at 10.0.1.10 sends one market update to group 239.1.1.1. Three receivers in two subnets have joined that group through IGMP. Step one, the sender transmits one packet. Step two, the multicast domain copies it once for each receiving attachment, so the sender link carries one copy no matter how many receivers exist. Step three, a host that never joined the group receives nothing.

Common mistake: assuming multicast works because the instances share a subnet and the application uses a group address. Without an enabled domain and correct membership, packets are dropped, and receivers see silence rather than an error.

Consequence in a running system: a missing join or a disabled domain looks like a receiver that never gets updates while the sender reports success, so verify group membership and domain attachment before blaming the application.

questions.prompt: A manufacturing firm runs a telemetry publisher at 10.60.1.20 inside its VPC, a private virtual network. The publisher sends sensor readings to the group address 226.4.7.9, where a group address is a special IP address that names a set of receivers rather than one host. Two plant servers on premises are meant to receive the readings over a hybrid link, meaning a connection between the cloud network and the company's own site. Both servers have joined the group using IGMP, the protocol hosts use to announce group membership. Step one: the publisher transmits one packet to 226.4.7.9. Step two: [missing]. Step three: each plant server receives one copy of the reading.
choices: The on-premises router floods the copy to every host in the plant subnet, whether or not that host joined the group.
The VPC unicasts the packet to each server's private address, so the link carries one copy per server.
The plant servers send IGMP joins back to the publisher before the link forwards any data.
The on-premises routers at both ends of the link are configured to pass multicast, so the copy crosses the hybrid path to the servers.
questions.why: A hybrid link carries multicast only when the routers at both ends are configured to pass it, so that configuration is the step that lets the copy reach the plant servers.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a multicast group address?
choices: It is the address of one specific host that receives all traffic sent by the group's members.
It is any private address shared by instances in the same subnet, so they can talk to each other directly.
It is the address of the gateway that copies packets to every host attached to the VPC.
It names a group rather than one host, and for IPv4 it falls in the range 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255.
questions.why: A group address names a set of receivers, and for IPv4 multicast it sits inside the 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255 range.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's ticket-feed sender in one subnet reports that every packet was sent successfully. Two receivers in the same subnet, which run the same application, never show the feed. Which check should come first?
choices: Replace the group address with a unicast address for each receiver.
Restart the application on the sender, since the sender's success report proves the network is fine.
Confirm that the receivers have joined the group and that their attachments are enabled on the multicast domain.
Increase the sender's bandwidth allocation so that the packets arrive faster.
questions.why: Shared subnets and a group address are not enough, because packets are dropped without correct membership and an enabled domain, and receivers show silence rather than an error.

questions.prompt: A company wants to send one market update to ten receivers across a VPN to its office. Which statement about multicast over that hybrid link is correct?
choices: The link carries multicast only if the routers at both ends are configured to pass it, and then the sender transmits a single packet.
The sender must transmit ten separate copies, one for each receiver, because multicast cannot cross a hybrid link.
The link carries multicast automatically because the VPN encrypts every packet.
Multicast works across the VPN only if every receiver sends a unicast request to the sender first.
questions.why: A hybrid link needs both end routers configured to pass multicast, and once they are, the sender still transmits one packet that the network duplicates toward interested receivers.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what multicast is, how it differs from sending a separate unicast copy to each receiver, and name one limit or tradeoff you would check before relying on it across a VPC and an on-premises link.
lessons.modelAnswer: Multicast sends one packet to a group address, and the network delivers a copy only to hosts that have joined that group, usually through IGMP. The sender's link carries one copy regardless of how many receivers there are, which is the bandwidth win over unicast, where the sender would transmit one copy per receiver. The catch is that a VPC is built for unicast, so group traffic only flows where a multicast domain is enabled and the members are attached to it. Before relying on it, I would check that every attachment is in the domain, that receivers have actually joined, and that the on-premises link and routers at both ends pass multicast. If any of those is missing, the failure is silent: the sender looks healthy while receivers get nothing, so I would test membership first.
rubricPoints: Defines multicast as one packet to a group address delivered only to joined receivers
Contrasts the single sender transmission with one unicast copy per receiver and the bandwidth saving
Notes that VPC networks are unicast by default and need an enabled multicast domain with attached members
Names a limit: hybrid links and routers must also support multicast, and missing membership fails silently

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining how group delivery differs from unicast and where it breaks across a VPC and on-premises links, which an explain exercise tests directly.

lessons.plain: DNS is the phone book of the internet: it turns a name like shop.example.com into the address of a server. Route 53 is AWS's DNS service, and its high-availability features let that phone book give different answers depending on which servers are healthy, how far away the visitor is, or what share of traffic each server should get. Health checks are regular probes that watch each server, and if one stops answering, the phone book stops listing it. This keeps users away from broken servers without anyone changing the name they type. Think of a restaurant host who seats guests only at tables that are free and close to them.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your website runs on two servers in different cities. One server crashes at night. Without anyone touching the system, how could the name you type still reach a working server, and what would have to notice that the first server was down?
lessons.teach:
A DNS record is a single entry that maps a name to a value, such as an IP address. A record set is a group of records with the same name and type, and a routing policy decides which member of that group a resolver receives. The TTL, or time to live, is how many seconds a resolver may keep an answer before asking again. A health check is a regular probe that Route 53 sends to an endpoint, such as an HTTP request to a path, and it marks the endpoint healthy or unhealthy based on the response.

Three routing choices matter here. Weighted routing gives each record a number, and each query is answered with one record picked in proportion to those numbers, which is useful for splitting traffic or trying out a new version. Latency routing answers with the record for the AWS Region measured as fastest from the requester's network. Health checks can be attached to records so that an unhealthy record is withheld from answers, which provides the failover behaviour that high availability depends on.

Worked example: a name has two weighted records, A with weight 70 and B with weight 30, each with a health check. Step one, a resolver asks for the name. Step two, Route 53 finds both records healthy. Step three, it returns A for about 70 of every 100 queries and B for 30. Step four, if B's health check fails, B is dropped from answers, so every query gets A until B recovers.

Common mistake: assuming the change takes effect instantly. Resolvers cache answers for the TTL, so a client that cached B keeps trying it until its cache expires. A long TTL means slow failover, while a very short TTL means more queries and higher cost.

Consequence in a running system: during an outage, some users reach the dead server for up to one TTL, so the TTL is a deliberate choice between failover speed and query volume. Route 53 cannot redirect clients that have already cached an old answer.

questions.prompt: A name has three weighted records: X with weight 50, Y with weight 25, and Z with weight 25. Each has a health check. Step one: a resolver asks for the name. Step two: Route 53 sees that Z's health check has failed, so Z is withheld from answers. Step three (missing from this trace): Route 53 works out how the remaining queries are shared between the records that are still answering. Step four: the share is applied to each new query. Which statement correctly completes step three?
choices: Queries are still split three ways until the cached answers for Z expire, then X and Y share them equally.
X and Y share queries in proportion to their remaining weights, 50 to 25, so X gets about 2 of every 3 queries and Y about 1 of every 3.
X and Y each get half of the queries, because weights only matter when all three records are healthy.
X keeps its weight of 50 out of 100, so about half of queries go to X and the rest to nobody until Z recovers.
questions.why: Once an unhealthy record is withheld, the weights of the healthy records are compared with each other, so 50 to 25 gives X two thirds and Y one third.

questions.prompt: In Route 53, what does a health check do to a record that has one attached?
choices: It marks the endpoint healthy or unhealthy from the probe responses, and an unhealthy record is withheld from answers.
It deletes the record from the hosted zone after three failed probes.
It forces every resolver to refetch the answer immediately.
It sets the record's weight to zero and the weight of its partner to one hundred.
questions.why: A health check is a regular probe whose result marks the endpoint healthy or unhealthy, and unhealthy records are left out of answers.

questions.prompt: A team sets the TTL on a record to 3600 seconds to reduce query charges. Their endpoint fails just after resolvers have cached its address. What is the most accurate expectation?
choices: Route 53 immediately stops returning the failed address, so no user is affected.
Clients keep trying the cached address until the health check passes again, because the TTL is ignored once a check fails.
Resolvers refetch after 60 seconds because Route 53 pushes updates to them.
Some clients may keep reaching the failed address for up to 3600 seconds, because cached answers last for the TTL even though the health check has already marked it unhealthy.
questions.why: Resolvers hold a cached answer for the full TTL, so a long TTL slows failover for those clients regardless of the health check result.

questions.prompt: A record set has three weighted records with weights 5, 15 and 80. Over 1000 queries, about how many should go to the record with weight 5?
questions.why: The total weight is 100, so the weight-5 record gets 5 out of every 100 queries, which is 50 out of 1000.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Route 53 can keep a website available when one of two regional servers fails, and name one limit of DNS-based failover that they should plan around.
lessons.modelAnswer: Route 53 holds one name with a record for each regional server, and each record has a health check that keeps probing its server. When a check fails, Route 53 stops returning that server's address, so new lookups go to the healthy region. The main limit is caching: resolvers and client devices keep answers for the record's TTL, so some users keep reaching the dead server until their cached copy expires. A short TTL speeds failover but increases query volume and cost, so the value has to fit the recovery goal. DNS also only steers where a name points. It does not fix a broken application behind the address, and an existing long-lived connection may stay on the failed server until it times out.
rubricPoints: Health checks detect a failed endpoint and remove its record from answers
Routing policies such as weighted or latency decide which healthy record is returned
Resolver caching governed by the TTL delays how quickly clients stop using the failed endpoint
Shorter TTLs speed failover but increase query volume and cost

suggested.rationale: Choosing between latency, weighted and failover routing from a stated requirement is an exam-style reasoning task that no listed mission or planned engine covers directly.

lessons.plain: Route 53 is AWS's managed DNS service. It turns names like orders.corp.internal into the network addresses a program should connect to. A hosted zone is the container that holds the name rules for one domain. A private hosted zone answers only for computers inside the networks you link to it, so internal names stay internal. You can give one name several answers, one per data centre location, and have the service stop offering any answer whose location has failed. That lets an application keep working through a single location failure, using a few DNS settings rather than a redesign.
lessons.guessPrompt: If an internal service name points to one server, and that server's data centre location fails, what could you change in the name's settings so clients get another working address without changing their code?
lessons.teach:
A hosted zone is the container in Route 53, AWS's DNS service, that holds the records for one domain. DNS is the system that maps a name to the address a client should use. A public hosted zone answers queries from anywhere. A private hosted zone answers only queries from the virtual networks (VPCs) associated with it. A record is one rule inside a zone: a name, a record type such as A for an IPv4 address, a time to live (TTL) in seconds that tells resolvers how long they may cache the answer, and one or more values. An Availability Zone (AZ) is an isolated data centre location inside a Region.

Why it works: give one name a primary record tied to one AZ and a secondary record tied to another, and add a health check to each. When the primary is unhealthy, the service stops returning it and returns the secondary instead. Clients keep using the same name.

Worked example. The private zone corp.internal is associated with the production VPC. You create api.corp.internal with a primary A record for 10.0.1.10 in AZ a and a secondary A record for 10.0.2.10 in AZ b, both with a TTL of 30. Step 1: a service asks for api.corp.internal. Step 2: the VPC resolver queries the private zone. Step 3: the primary is healthy, so 10.0.1.10 is returned. Step 4: AZ a fails and the health check goes unhealthy. Step 5: new lookups return 10.0.2.10. Step 6: clients that cached the old answer keep it until the TTL expires, at most 30 seconds later.

Common mistake: creating the private zone but not associating it with the VPC, or leaving DNS resolution off on the VPC. Queries then miss the zone, return no such name, and the team blames the application. A second mistake is a TTL of 3600 seconds on a record meant to fail over, which can turn a short outage into an hour of errors.

In a running system the TTL sets the failover speed limit, because recovery can be no faster than caches expire.

questions.prompt: Northwind Freight has the private zone hub.freight.internal associated with its analytics VPC. It creates tracker.hub.freight.internal with a primary A record for 172.16.5.40 in AZ b and a secondary A record for 172.16.6.40 in AZ c, both with a TTL of 60 seconds, and a health check on each. Here is the failure, with one step left for you to fill in. Step 1: a dashboard asks for tracker.hub.freight.internal. Step 2: the VPC resolver queries the private zone. Step 3: the primary is healthy, so 172.16.5.40 is returned. Step 4: AZ b fails and the primary's health check goes unhealthy. Step 5: this step is missing and you must supply it. Step 6: a dashboard that cached 172.16.5.40 keeps using it until the 60-second TTL expires. What belongs in Step 5?
choices: Route 53 rewrites the cached answer inside every dashboard so they all switch at once.
The private zone is moved into AZ c and its TTL is raised to 3600 seconds.
New lookups for tracker.hub.freight.internal return 172.16.6.40, the secondary.
The service keeps querying the primary until someone deletes its record by hand.
questions.why: Once the primary is unhealthy the service stops returning it and answers new lookups with the secondary, while caches are not edited and only expire by TTL.

questions.prompt: In Route 53, what is the defining difference between a public hosted zone and a private hosted zone?
choices: A private zone holds only A records, while a public zone can hold every record type.
A public zone answers queries from anywhere; a private zone answers only queries from associated VPCs.
A private zone is stored in one AZ, while a public zone is spread across several Regions.
A public zone needs a health check on every record, while a private zone never uses one.
questions.why: A hosted zone's visibility is set by whether it is public (answers anyone) or private (answers only the VPCs associated with it).

questions.prompt: A team created the private zone billing.internal and associated it with VPC A. A service in VPC B asks for ledger.billing.internal and gets a no-such-name answer. Which explanation fits the teaching text?
choices: The TTL on the record is too long, so the missing answer is cached for an hour.
The record type must be AAAA for queries that cross VPCs, so the A record is ignored.
The zone is not associated with VPC B, so queries from VPC B never reach it.
Route 53 has to be turned off in VPC B so that its own resolver can take over the name.
questions.why: A private zone only answers queries from VPCs associated with it, so a VPC outside the association gets no-such-name, which is the missing-association mistake described in the text.

questions.prompt: A record for status.shop.example is part of a failover pair and has a TTL of 900 seconds. A client looked up the name one second before the primary's AZ failed. What is the longest that client can keep sending traffic to the failed address?
choices: Indefinitely, because caches are only cleared when the record itself is deleted.
Only 1 second, because the answer is refreshed on the client's next query.
Until the next health check runs, which is usually within a few seconds.
About 900 seconds after its lookup, until its cached answer expires.
questions.why: Recovery can be no faster than caches expire, so a client that cached the answer keeps it for up to the full TTL after its lookup.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a private hosted zone with primary and secondary records keeps an internal service name working when one Availability Zone fails. Name one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: A private hosted zone is a set of DNS rules that only answers for the VPCs linked to it, so the internal name resolves inside our network and nowhere else. For api.corp.internal we create one record for each AZ, a primary and a secondary, and attach a health check to each. When the primary AZ's endpoint is marked unhealthy, the DNS service stops returning its address and gives the secondary address instead, so callers keep using the same name without any code change. The limit is timing: clients and resolvers cache answers for the record's TTL, so a failover can only take effect as fast as those caches expire. A long TTL slows failover, and a very short one means more DNS queries. We should set the TTL deliberately and test the failover path rather than assume it is instant.
rubricPoints: A private hosted zone answers only for associated VPCs, which keeps internal names internal.
Records in different AZs plus health checks let DNS return only healthy addresses.
The record TTL limits how fast clients see a failover because of caching.
The zone must be associated with the VPC, or queries will not resolve.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers DNS hosted zones and records, so this is best learned by reading the teaching text and checking the console steps yourself.

lessons.plain: Your servers live on a network with a fixed pool of addresses, like seats in a hall. An auto scaling group adds servers when traffic rises and removes them when it falls. Each new server needs a free address in the subnet it lands in. If a subnet is too small, or fills up, the group cannot launch the server it needs at the moment it most needs capacity. This objective is about sizing subnets so there is room to grow, and about adding a second address block to a network that has run out, without rebuilding it.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your subnet is a /26. How many addresses can servers actually use from it, and could it hold a group that grows to 200 servers?
lessons.teach:
A subnet is a slice of a virtual network (a VPC) that sits in one Availability Zone, which is one isolated data centre within a Region. Its size is set by a CIDR block, a notation such as 10.0.1.0/24, where the number after the slash is the prefix length. A longer prefix means fewer addresses: a /24 holds 256 addresses, a /26 holds 64 and a /28 holds 16. The cloud platform keeps five addresses in every subnet for its own use: the network address, the router, the DNS service, one reserved slot and the broadcast address. So a /24 leaves 251 usable addresses and a /26 leaves 59.

An auto scaling group is a managed set of servers that grows and shrinks between a minimum and a maximum count. Every server it launches takes one free address from its subnet, and so do load balancers and other attached network interfaces. Auto scaling therefore needs headroom: the subnet must hold the group's maximum size plus everything else that lives there, in every Availability Zone the group spans.

A secondary CIDR is an extra address block added to an existing network after it was created. It lets you create new subnets when the original block is used up. You cannot grow an existing subnet; you create a new one inside the added block and place new capacity there.

Worked example. A group with a maximum of 200 servers, plus a load balancer using about 8 addresses, needs 208 addresses per zone. Take a /24: it has 251 usable, and 251 minus 208 leaves 43 spare, so it fits. Take a /26: it has 59 usable, so the group fails on its 60th launch.

Common mistake: sizing the subnet for today's server count rather than the maximum. In a running system the group reaches its limit during a traffic peak, and the launch fails with an insufficient-address error exactly when capacity is most needed. Size for the maximum, and keep a secondary block ready as the escape route.

questions.prompt:
A payments team has a private subnet of /25 in one Availability Zone. Its auto scaling group has a maximum of 110 servers, and four other network interfaces also live in that subnet. Work it through:

Step 1: A /25 holds 128 addresses.
Step 2: (missing step)
Step 3: The group needs 110 plus 4 other interfaces, which is 114 addresses.
Step 4: 123 minus 114 leaves 9 spare, so the subnet fits the group at its maximum.

Which statement correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: Subtract 5 reserved addresses, giving 123 usable addresses.
Subtract the group's minimum size of 20 from 128.
Divide 128 by 2 to get 64 usable addresses.
Add 5 reserved addresses to 128, giving 133 usable addresses.
questions.why: Every subnet keeps five addresses for the platform, so usable addresses are the total minus 5, which is 123, and that is the figure Step 4 relies on.

questions.prompt: A team's subnet is a /27 in one Availability Zone. How many addresses can the platform actually assign to servers and interfaces in that subnet?
questions.why: A /27 holds 32 addresses, and the platform keeps 5 of them for its own use, leaving 27 assignable.

questions.prompt: An auto scaling group has a maximum of 100 servers in a /25 subnet, which has 123 usable addresses. A load balancer in the same zone uses 25 addresses. A colleague says the subnet is fine because the group only runs at 100 most of the time. What is the correct conclusion?
choices: The subnet fits with 3 addresses spare, because the group's typical count is what matters.
The subnet fits, because the load balancer does not take addresses from the subnet.
The subnet fails at peak, because the group needs 125 addresses and only 123 are usable.
The subnet fits with 18 addresses spare, because the five reserved addresses are not counted.
questions.why: Sizing must use the group's maximum plus everything else in the subnet, so 100 plus 25 is 125, which exceeds the 123 usable addresses and the launch fails at peak.

questions.prompt: A group spans two Availability Zones with a maximum of 60 servers, so each zone must hold up to 60 servers. Each zone has a /26 subnet with 59 usable addresses and 3 other interfaces. The subnet is already full at its current size and cannot be enlarged in place. Which remedy fits the platform's rules?
choices: Add a secondary CIDR block to the network and create a new subnet inside it for the new capacity.
Resize the existing /26 to a /25 in place so it grows to fit the group.
Lower the group's minimum size to 0 so the subnet no longer needs headroom.
Move all of the group's servers into a single zone to avoid the second subnet.
questions.why: An existing subnet cannot be grown, so the correct approach is adding a secondary CIDR block and creating a new subnet in it to hold new capacity.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would size a subnet for an auto scaling group and what you would do if the subnet runs out of addresses. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I size the subnet for the group's maximum size, not its current count, and I count the other things that take addresses in the same subnet, such as load balancer interfaces. I also leave spare room for growth, because the subnet's addresses are fixed once created. Each Availability Zone needs this headroom, since the group launches into whichever zone has space. If a subnet runs out, I cannot resize it. I would add a secondary CIDR block to the VPC, create a new subnet in that block, and add it to the group, so new capacity has somewhere to go. The tradeoff is that a larger subnet uses more of the address plan up front and makes it harder to fit other networks, so I balance generous sizing against the risk of overlapping ranges I might need later.
rubricPoints: Size the subnet for the group's maximum, not its current count, in every Availability Zone it spans
Count other address consumers such as load balancer interfaces and remember the platform reserves five addresses per subnet
An existing subnet cannot be resized, so depletion is fixed by adding a secondary CIDR and a new subnet
Naming a real tradeoff: oversized subnets waste the address plan, undersized ones fail at peak

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning about address headroom and explaining the sizing tradeoff back, which no listed mission or planned engine directly covers.

lessons.plain: Normally a network sends data in chunks of about 1500 bytes. A jumbo frame is a bigger chunk, often around 9000 bytes, so each chunk carries more data and the computer spends less effort per byte moved. The catch is that every piece of the route between two machines has to accept the bigger size. When one link in the middle only takes small chunks, the big ones get lost. This lesson covers how to set the size on the parts of a cloud network and why the smallest size on the whole path decides what works, much like a route that is only as wide as its narrowest doorway.
lessons.guessPrompt: If your server can send 9000-byte chunks but the only link to an office across a VPN accepts 1500-byte chunks, what do you think happens to a 9000-byte chunk, and why might small requests still work?
lessons.teach:
A jumbo frame is an Ethernet frame larger than the usual 1500-byte limit, so one packet can carry more data. Ethernet is the standard framing used on local links, and a frame is one unit of data sent across a single link. The largest frame a link accepts is its maximum transmission unit, or MTU, measured in bytes. Why it works: every packet carries a fixed amount of header overhead, so a larger payload per packet means fewer packets and less per-packet processing for the same data. The number that actually governs a conversation is the path MTU, the smallest MTU on every hop between the two endpoints. Inside a VPC, instances commonly support about 9001 bytes. Traffic that leaves through an internet gateway, a VPN, or some gateway attachments is capped lower, often at 1500 or a gateway-specific value, so check the current limit for each connection type.

Worked example: instance A (MTU 9001) sends 8000 bytes to an on-premises server through a VPN (MTU 1500). Step 1: the sender uses its own MTU and sends one 8000-byte packet with the do-not-fragment flag set. Step 2: the packet reaches the VPN, whose limit is 1500, so it cannot pass. Step 3: the router drops it and should return an ICMP 'fragmentation needed' message stating 1500. Step 4: the sender shrinks its packets to fit. If that message is blocked by a filter, the sender never learns the limit and the transfer stalls.

Common mistake: enabling jumbo frames on the instances and assuming the whole path follows. In a running system this means small requests and pings succeed, while large API responses or file copies hang, which looks like an application bug rather than a size mismatch.

Jumbo frames help only when every hop on the path accepts them, so the path MTU, not the instance setting, decides what works.

questions.prompt: A build server in a private subnet with an MTU of 9001 bytes sends a 7000-byte transfer to a partner's API over a tunnel whose MTU is 1400 bytes. The sender sets the do-not-fragment flag. Step 1: the server sends one 7000-byte packet, since its own MTU allows it. Step 2: the packet reaches the tunnel, whose limit is 1400, so the packet cannot pass. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the server shrinks its packets to 1400 bytes or less and the transfer completes. Which choice correctly fills the missing step?
choices: The tunnel router splits the packet into smaller pieces and forwards them, so the sender never needs to change anything.
The tunnel router drops the oversized packet and returns an ICMP fragmentation-needed message stating 1400 bytes.
The partner's API returns a 1400-byte error response, which tells the server to retry the same 7000-byte packet.
The tunnel router raises its MTU to 7000 bytes so the packet passes without any message back to the sender.
questions.why: With the do-not-fragment flag set, the router must not split the packet, so it drops it and reports the limit back so the sender can shrink its packets.

questions.prompt: What is the path MTU between two endpoints?
choices: The MTU of the receiving endpoint, which sets the size of every reply.
The smallest MTU on every hop between the two endpoints.
The average MTU across all hops on the route.
The MTU of the sending interface only, since that is where packets start.
questions.why: The path MTU is defined as the smallest MTU on every hop, because one small link on the route limits every packet that crosses it.

questions.prompt: A team enables jumbo frame support on every instance in their VPC. Short health checks and pings to an office across a VPN succeed, but a large file upload to that office hangs. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The file upload is being encrypted twice, which adds too much overhead.
The VPN hop has a lower MTU, so large packets are dropped on that path while small ones pass.
Ping and health checks use a different protocol that always ignores MTU limits.
The instances' jumbo setting is too large and the operating system has crashed.
questions.why: Jumbo frames only help when every hop accepts them, and a lower-capped VPN hop drops large packets while small ones still get through.

questions.prompt: A firewall on the route between a sender and a receiver blocks all ICMP messages. A hop on the path has an MTU of 1400 bytes. The sender uses 8000-byte packets with the do-not-fragment flag set. Why does the transfer stall while small requests still work?
choices: The firewall fragments the large packets, which slows them until they time out.
Small requests use a different route that bypasses the 1400-byte hop.
The receiver rejects large packets on purpose to protect its own memory.
The sender never receives the fragmentation-needed message, so it keeps sending packets that the 1400-byte hop drops.
questions.why: Without the ICMP message the sender cannot learn the smaller limit, so oversized packets keep being dropped while packets under the limit pass.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why enabling jumbo frames on two instances in the same VPC may not speed up a large transfer to an on-premises server over VPN. Name the limit that matters and one tradeoff of raising the frame size.
lessons.modelAnswer: The two instances can use large frames between themselves, but the transfer to the on-premises server crosses a VPN, and that path has a smaller MTU, usually 1500 bytes. The effective size is the path MTU, the smallest limit on every hop, so the instance setting does not decide anything once traffic leaves the VPC. If a large packet is sent, the router must drop it and report the limit back. If that report is filtered, the transfer hangs even though small requests work. So before changing anything, I would verify the MTU at each hop and confirm that ICMP fragmentation-needed messages are allowed. A tradeoff of raising the size is that every device on the path must support it, so a mixed path can break in ways that only show up with large transfers.
rubricPoints: The effective size is the path MTU, the smallest MTU on every hop, not the instance setting.
A VPN or internet path usually caps traffic at about 1500 bytes.
Oversized packets with the do-not-fragment flag are dropped, and the failure can look like a stalled transfer.
Blocking ICMP fragmentation-needed messages prevents the sender from discovering the smaller limit.

suggested.rationale: A virtual network path tracer would let the learner walk each hop and see where the packet size drops, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Imagine a chain of shops that gives every customer one fixed front door close to where they live, then moves their order along the chain's own private roads to whichever warehouse is working. AWS Global Accelerator does this for internet traffic to your application. You get two fixed IP addresses that never change. Users connect to the AWS entry point nearest them, and their traffic travels over AWS's own global network instead of many unpredictable public internet hops. If a server or a whole Region stops responding, the service notices through health checks and sends new traffic to healthy places. The usual result is a steadier connection and faster recovery when something fails.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app runs in one Region, and users in Asia and Europe report slow connections and long outages whenever that Region has trouble. Without changing the app code, what would you want to add in front of it, and why might a fixed IP address for users matter?
lessons.teach:
AWS Global Accelerator is a managed service that gives your application two static IP addresses. Static means they never change. Both addresses are announced from many edge locations at once, which is called anycast: the same address is reachable from many places, and internet routing sends each user toward the closest one. An edge location is a point of presence where AWS connects to internet providers. A listener is the rule set that says which protocol and ports to accept, such as TCP on port 443. An endpoint group is a set of endpoints in one Region, and each endpoint is a load balancer, instance, or Elastic IP that receives a share of traffic through a weight. A health check decides whether an endpoint is usable. A traffic dial lets you reduce the share of traffic one Region receives, which is handy for planned maintenance.

Why it works: public internet routing is decided by many networks in between, and the path is often long and variable. Global Accelerator brings the user onto AWS's backbone at the nearest edge and carries traffic across it to your endpoint. Because the client keeps the same IP address, failover does not depend on DNS caches expiring.

Worked example: a game server runs in Region A and Region B, and players are in Europe. Step 1: you create an accelerator with a TCP listener on port 7777. Step 2: you add an endpoint group for Region A and one for Region B, each with its load balancer as an endpoint. Step 3: a European player connects to the static IP and enters the network at the nearest edge, which forwards them to the healthy Region A endpoint. Step 4: Region A's health check fails. New connections now go to Region B, and the player's address stays the same. Existing sessions may drop, so the client must reconnect.

Common mistake: treating Global Accelerator as a cache or a content delivery network. It does not store content. For cacheable web content, CloudFront is usually the better fit. Another mistake is expecting failover from a single endpoint that has no second place to go.

Consequence: if health checks are set to the wrong path or port, healthy endpoints can look dead and traffic is moved for no reason, or a broken endpoint keeps receiving traffic. Watch the health check status as part of normal operation.

questions.prompt: A ticketing firm, Harbourline Tickets, runs its booking API behind a load balancer in North Region and another in South Region. Its accelerator has a TCP listener on port 443, and each Region is an endpoint group holding its load balancer. The steps for a planned North Region maintenance window are: Step 1: create the accelerator with the TCP listener on port 443. Step 2: add an endpoint group for North Region and one for South Region, each with its load balancer as an endpoint. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: when maintenance ends, set North Region's traffic dial back to 100 so new connections return to North Region.
choices: Delete the North Region endpoint group so the static IP addresses are released for South Region
Update the DNS records to point at South Region's load balancer address so clients stop using the static IPs
Set North Region's traffic dial to 0 so new connections are sent to South Region before maintenance starts
Change the listener from TCP to UDP on port 443 so the clients reconnect faster
questions.why: A traffic dial reduces the share of traffic a Region receives, so setting North Region's dial to 0 before maintenance moves new connections to South Region while the static IPs stay unchanged.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does it mean that a Global Accelerator accelerator gives you two static IP addresses that are announced from many edge locations at once?
choices: The addresses are copies of each endpoint's private address, so traffic is delivered without leaving the customer's network
The addresses are assigned to one Region, and clients are always routed to that Region regardless of where they are
The addresses change every time an endpoint fails, so clients must refresh their DNS cache to find the new one
The addresses never change, and the same address is reachable from many places so internet routing sends each user toward a nearby edge
questions.why: Static means the addresses never change, and anycast means the same address is reachable from many edge locations so routing picks a nearby one.

questions.prompt: A logistics company, Coastwater Freight, has one load balancer in a single Region with one endpoint group and an accelerator in front of it. That Region has an outage. What is the most accurate expectation?
choices: The accelerator automatically copies the load balancer's data to another Region within seconds
Clients are not moved anywhere useful, because there is no second healthy endpoint to send traffic to, so the accelerator alone does not give failover
Clients are moved to a healthy Region immediately because the accelerator always has a backup
The static IP addresses switch to a cached copy of the application stored at the edge
questions.why: Failover needs a second healthy endpoint in another Region; with only one endpoint, the accelerator has nowhere else to send traffic.

questions.prompt: A media company, Brightreel Studio, added a health check path to its accelerator endpoint, but the path it configured returns an error for every request even though the application is working. What is the likely consequence for the running system?
choices: The endpoint is judged unusable even though it is healthy, so traffic may be moved away from it for no good reason
The accelerator stops accepting connections on its static IP addresses until the health check path is fixed
The endpoint becomes a cache for the failing path, so users still receive stored responses
Nothing changes, because health checks only affect monitoring dashboards and never affect routing
questions.why: A health check decides whether an endpoint is usable, so a wrong path can make a healthy endpoint look dead and cause traffic to be moved unnecessarily.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we would put Global Accelerator in front of our TCP game service instead of using a DNS record with latency routing. Explain to them what Global Accelerator changes about how clients reach the service, and name one limit or tradeoff of using it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Latency-based DNS sends each user to the lowest-latency Region, but the user still travels over the public internet to that Region's address, and when a Region fails, clients keep resolving old addresses until DNS caches expire. Global Accelerator gives clients two static anycast IPs, so they enter AWS's network at a nearby edge and cross AWS's backbone to the endpoint. Health checks can move new traffic to another Region within seconds without the client changing anything. The tradeoff is cost: you pay for the accelerator and for data transfer through it, and it only helps if you have more than one healthy endpoint to fail over to. It also does not cache anything, so a service that needs content caching should look at CloudFront instead. Existing connections may still drop during failover, so the game client needs reconnect logic.
rubricPoints: Explains that static anycast IPs let clients enter AWS's network at a nearby edge rather than relying on public internet routing
Contrasts failover speed with DNS-based routing, where cached records delay the switch
Names a concrete limit or tradeoff, such as cost or the need for multiple healthy endpoints
Notes that Global Accelerator does not cache content, so CloudFront is the better fit for cacheable web traffic

suggested.rationale: The core skill is choosing and explaining the tradeoff between Global Accelerator, DNS routing, and CloudFront, which is best shown by explaining it back.

lessons.plain: A threat model is a structured way to ask, before you build or change a system, who might want to harm it, how they could get in, and what you would do about it. It starts from the shape of the application: where data enters, where it is stored, and which parts of the system trust each other. For each place where data crosses from one part to another, you list the likely attacks and choose a protection. It is like studying a building's floor plan to find where a thief could get in, rather than locking the front door only after construction is finished.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web app has a public load balancer, a web server, and a database in a private network. Before you read further, name two places where you think an attacker could cause damage, and say why those places and not others.
lessons.teach:
A threat model starts from the application's architecture, not from a list of attacks. First, draw the data flows: which component sends what to which other component, and where data is stored. Second, mark the trust boundaries, which are the lines where the level of trust changes, such as the internet meeting your load balancer, or a web server calling a database. Third, for each flow that crosses a boundary, ask which threats apply. A common checklist covers spoofing (pretending to be someone else), tampering (changing data in transit or at rest), repudiation (denying an action with no record of it), information disclosure (data leaking to the wrong party), denial of service (making a service unavailable), and elevation of privilege (gaining more access than allowed). Fourth, record a mitigation for each threat that matters, and state any risk you accept.

Worked example: a public web app has a load balancer, a web tier, an application tier, a managed database, and an admin API reachable from a corporate network. Trace the flows. Internet to load balancer crosses the outermost boundary; the main threats are flooding and malicious requests, so you assign edge filtering and rate limits. Web tier to application tier is an internal flow; a forged or unencrypted call could be altered, so you require encrypted connections and authenticated callers. Application tier to database crosses another boundary; if its credentials leak, the database exposes every record, so you give it a least-privilege account and encrypt the stored data. The admin API is a separate entry point and the usual route for privilege escalation, so it needs its own identity checks.

Common mistake: modelling only the internet-facing edge because it looks most dangerous. An attacker who gets past one tier moves sideways, so internal boundaries need threats too. Consequence: if the web tier is compromised and the database flow was never considered, the whole customer dataset can be read from inside the network.

A threat model is only useful when it is revisited each time the architecture changes, because every new connection creates new flows and new boundaries.

questions.prompt: Ana is building a threat model for a payroll SaaS. It has a file-ingest service that receives payslip files pushed by partner SFTP servers on the public internet, an object store that holds the uploaded files, and a reporting service on the private network. She has drawn three data flows: partner server to ingest, ingest to object store, and object store to reporting. She has marked a trust boundary between the internet and the ingest service, and another between the ingest service and the object store. For the partner-to-ingest flow, which crosses the internet boundary, she listed the threats of flooding and forged uploads, and recorded edge rate limits and partner authentication as mitigations. For the store-to-reporting flow, which crosses the boundary into the private reporting tier, she has written 'require encrypted connections' as its mitigation. What step has she skipped?
choices: Add a trust boundary between the reporting service and the object store
Accept the risk of that flow without recording it, since the flow is internal
List the threats that apply to the store-to-reporting flow before choosing a mitigation for it
Redraw the data flows from scratch before doing anything else
questions.why: Each flow that crosses a boundary needs its applicable threats identified first, and only then a mitigation chosen for each threat that matters, so Ana has jumped to a mitigation without identifying the threats.

questions.prompt: In a threat model, what is a trust boundary?
choices: The encryption key that protects data at rest in a storage service
A line where the level of trust changes between two components, such as the internet meeting a load balancer
The maximum number of requests a service will accept per minute
A list of the threats that apply to a single component
questions.why: A trust boundary is defined as a line where the level of trust changes, and the other options describe a rate limit, a key, and a threat list, which are different things.

questions.prompt: A team runs a ticketing platform. An administrator deletes a customer's support ticket, and the platform has no audit record of the deletion, so the administrator later claims they never did it. Which threat category from the common checklist does this case best match?
choices: Information disclosure
Repudiation
Denial of service
Spoofing
questions.why: Repudiation is denying an action when there is no record of it, and here the missing audit record lets the administrator deny the deletion.

questions.prompt: A logistics company models only the internet-facing API of its shipment system and considers that review complete. An attacker who never touches the API instead compromises a reporting worker and then uses that worker's service account to read every row of the shipments database, because the account has full rights to all tables. Which two gaps in the model best explain this outcome?
choices: No threats were assessed for the internal worker-to-database flow, and the service account has more privilege than the flow needs
The shipments database was not given a public IP address, so it could only be reached from inside the network
The company did not rename the reporting worker, so the attacker could guess its name
The API was not protected by a rate limit, so the attacker had free access to the worker
questions.why: Modelling only the internet edge leaves the internal database flow without threats or mitigations, and a service account with full rights turns one compromised tier into a full data leak.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only built single-server apps what a threat model is for a multi-tier application, how you derive the threats from the architecture, and one limit of the method.
lessons.modelAnswer: A threat model is a working map of how a system can be attacked, built from its architecture rather than from a generic checklist. You start by sketching the data flows between components and marking the trust boundaries, the points where the level of trust changes, like the internet edge or the link from the app tier to the database. For each flow that crosses a boundary, you ask which threats apply, such as forged requests, data leaking, or someone gaining more privilege than they should. Then you pick a mitigation for each serious threat and note what risk remains. The main limit is that the model is only as good as the diagram: if the diagram does not match what is actually deployed, or nobody updates it after a change, the threats you list will miss the new paths. It also cannot tell you how likely an attack is, only where the exposure is.
rubricPoints: A threat model is derived from the architecture: data flows and trust boundaries come first.
Threats are assessed for each flow that crosses a boundary, including internal ones.
Each serious threat gets a mitigation, and any accepted residual risk is stated.
The method depends on an accurate, up-to-date diagram and does not measure likelihood.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a multi-tier architecture and deciding which boundaries carry which threats is best practised as an exam-style scenario.

lessons.plain: Inbound traffic is anything that arrives at your cloud network from outside, such as customers' web requests or an attacker's probes. Securing it means deciding which arrivals to let through, which to block, and how to survive when someone floods you. On AWS, three managed services cover different layers of that job. One inspects web requests for attack patterns, one absorbs denial-of-service floods, and one filters network traffic by address, port and protocol. Choosing the right one depends on what kind of traffic you are stopping and at which layer it shows up.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web application is receiving thousands of requests a second that all try to log in with random passwords, and a separate flood is simply filling the network link with junk packets. Which layer of protection would you expect to handle each one, and why might a single tool not cover both?
lessons.teach: A layer is a level of how traffic is built. The network layer is about addresses, ports and protocols. The application layer is about the content of a request, such as its URL, headers and body. A denial-of-service (DoS) attack tries to exhaust capacity so real users cannot get through. A distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack does this from many sources at once. AWS WAF is a web application firewall. It sits in front of supported resources, such as load balancers and content delivery networks, and checks each HTTP request against rules. Rules can match paths, headers, body text, or the rate of requests from one source over a time window. Each matching request is allowed, blocked, or counted. AWS Shield provides DDoS protection. Shield Standard is included for all accounts and absorbs common volumetric floods. Shield Advanced adds stronger protection, a response team and cost protection. AWS Network Firewall is a managed stateful firewall that you place inside a VPC. It inspects packets by address, port and protocol, and it tracks connections so it can judge whether a packet belongs to an allowed conversation. Worked example: an address sends 3,000 login requests in five minutes. The request reaches a load balancer protected by WAF. A rate rule counts requests per address, sees the limit exceeded, and blocks that address. A separate flood of junk packets is absorbed by Shield before it consumes your capacity. Common mistake: expecting WAF to stop volumetric floods or expecting Shield to read request content. Each tool works at its own layer. In a running system, a rate limit set too high lets the brute-force attempts through, and a Network Firewall placed in a single subnet becomes a single point of failure.

questions.prompt: A ticket shop puts AWS WAF in front of its Application Load Balancer. One bot sends 600 requests to the /checkout path from a single address within five minutes. Step 1: this is application-layer traffic, because the requests are HTTP requests to a URL path. Step 2: a rate rule counts requests per address over the five-minute window, finds 600, and the limit is 500, so the limit is exceeded. Step 3 is missing: the rule's action is set to block. What happens to the bot's next request to /checkout from that address?
choices: It is absorbed by Shield Standard before it reaches the load balancer.
It is passed to AWS Network Firewall, which inspects the packet headers.
It is blocked, because the matching rule's action is block.
It is allowed, because rate rules only count requests and never change the result.
questions.why: A rate rule that exceeds its limit with a block action causes WAF to block the next matching request from that source, while Shield and Network Firewall do not inspect HTTP paths.

questions.prompt: A media company wants a control that can look inside the body of each HTTP POST and block requests whose text contains a specific injected string. Which AWS service fits this need?
choices: Amazon VPC route tables, because they filter traffic by application content
AWS Shield Advanced, because it reads request bodies during a DDoS event
AWS Network Firewall, because it inspects packet payloads by address and port
AWS WAF, because it checks request content such as body text against rules
questions.why: AWS WAF is the web application firewall that matches HTTP request content such as body text, whereas Shield and Network Firewall operate on other layers.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's public load balancer receives a sudden flood of UDP packets that is large enough to saturate the link before any request reaches a web server. Which protection is designed to absorb common volumetric floods of this kind without any action by the firm?
choices: A custom route table with a blackhole route for the load balancer
A Network Firewall stateful rule group in a single subnet
A WAF rate rule set to 100 requests per minute
AWS Shield Standard, which is included for all accounts
questions.why: Shield Standard is included automatically and absorbs common volumetric DDoS floods, while WAF rules act on HTTP requests and Network Firewall does not stop floods at the edge.

questions.prompt: A freight company places an AWS Network Firewall inside its VPC. Outbound connections from its servers are allowed, and the return packets for those connections are also let through without a separate inbound allow rule. What property of the firewall explains this behaviour?
choices: It is stateless, so it judges each packet alone against a list of rules
It is a DDoS scrubber that trusts all traffic from known address ranges
It is stateful, so it tracks connections and recognises return packets that belong to an allowed conversation
It is a web application firewall that rewrites response headers
questions.why: Network Firewall is stateful: it tracks connections so it can recognise that a return packet belongs to a conversation already allowed, rather than judging every packet in isolation.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between AWS WAF, AWS Shield and AWS Network Firewall for a public web API, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you would pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking what kind of traffic I am stopping. Malicious web requests, such as credential stuffing or injected query text, are visible in the HTTP content, so they belong to WAF, which can block by pattern, path or request rate.
