choices: It sets how many evaluation periods an alarm must see before it changes state.
It names the container that groups all related metrics for one team.
It splits one metric into separate series by a label such as a tunnel identifier.
It records the timestamp that each reading was taken at.
questions.why: A dimension is a key-value label that divides one metric into separate series, such as one series per VPN tunnel.

questions.prompt: A script on a NAT instance publishes a custom metric every minute, and the publisher crashes overnight. The alarm on that metric is set so that missing data is treated as not breaching. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: The alarm reports OK all night even though the NAT instance is unmonitored.
The metric automatically falls back to the platform's built-in copy of the same measurement.
The alarm sits in ALARM all night because silence is treated as a fault.
The alarm switches to INSUFFICIENT_DATA and a notification is sent to the on-call engineer.
questions.why: Treating missing data as not breaching makes silence look healthy, so the alarm shows OK while nothing is being measured.

questions.prompt: A team publishes a custom metric for DNS resolution time, recorded once per query, and wants an alarm that catches the slowest 1 percent of lookups without being dominated by a few long-tail spikes. Which statistic should the alarm use?
choices: The average, because it is the most stable value over a period.
A high percentile such as p99, because it reflects the tail of slow results.
The minimum, because it shows the best case lookup time.
The sum, because it adds up every lookup in the window.
questions.why: A high percentile reports the slow tail of the distribution, which an average would hide and a sum or minimum would not describe.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use a custom metric and an alarm to detect a burst of rejected connections from a blocked source. Name one limit or tradeoff in your design.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would have a small script count rejected connection attempts from the blocked source and publish that count as a custom metric every minute, using the sum statistic so bursts are not averaged away. The alarm would evaluate 5-minute sums and require two consecutive breaching windows before entering ALARM, so a single noisy minute does not page anyone. I would set the threshold from a week of normal traffic. The main tradeoff is between speed and noise: a lower threshold or a single evaluation period catches attacks sooner but causes more false alarms. The other limit is that the alarm only sees what the script publishes. If the script stops, the metric goes silent, so I would configure missing data to alarm rather than report OK, and I would also alarm on the publisher itself.
rubricPoints: Defines a metric, a custom metric, and an alarm in plain terms
Explains why the statistic (sum versus average) must match the question being asked
Explains evaluation periods as a way to avoid false alarms from single noisy windows
Names a tradeoff or limit, such as speed versus noise, or silent failure when data stops arriving

suggested.rationale: A planned metric alarm builder engine would let the learner configure statistics, thresholds, and missing-data handling and see the resulting state changes.

lessons.plain: When something goes wrong on a network, the evidence is scattered across several record-keeping systems. One logs network traffic, another logs who changed which settings, and another logs the web requests a load balancer handled. Correlating means lining those records up so they tell one story, by matching them on time, on the addresses involved, and on the resource they touched. Analyzing means asking what the combined picture shows, such as whether a settings change happened just before traffic began to be blocked. A single log rarely answers the question alone. The skill is knowing which sources to open, how to join them, and how far to trust the join.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose traffic from one client suddenly starts failing at 10:03, and a log shows someone edited a firewall rule at 10:02. What would you check before deciding the edit caused the failures?
lessons.teach:
A log source is any system that writes timestamped records of what happened. On AWS, examples include VPC flow logs, which record metadata about IP traffic (source and destination addresses, ports, protocol, packet and byte counts, and whether traffic was accepted or rejected), and AWS CloudTrail, which records API calls, meaning who asked for what change and when. Load balancer access logs record each request a load balancer handled. Correlation is joining records from two or more sources that refer to the same event. Flow log records cover a capture window of minutes rather than a single instant, so their timestamps are approximate.

Why it works: each source shares a few keys, namely time (ideally in UTC), addresses, network interface IDs, and resource IDs. A change in a configuration log explains a traffic change in a flow log only when the times line up and the affected resource appears in both.

Worked example. Step 1: flow logs show REJECT records from 203.0.113.50 to port 443 on interface eni-0abc starting at 10:03 UTC. Step 2: CloudTrail shows a call at 10:02 UTC that changed a security group. Step 3: confirm that group is the one attached to eni-0abc, not to a neighboring resource. Step 4: check in CloudTrail whether the rejects stop after a rollback at 10:20 UTC.

Common mistake: joining on IP address alone, or mixing local time with UTC. Address translation can rewrite source addresses, and a clock offset of a few minutes can make a cause appear to come after its effect.

Consequence: if you blame the wrong change, you may revert something innocent while the real cause keeps blocking traffic. Correlation narrows the search; it does not replace checking the resource itself.

questions.prompt: A retail company's payments team sees REJECT records in flow logs from 198.51.100.7 to port 5432 on network interface eni-0f19, starting at 14:40 UTC. CloudTrail shows a call at 14:37 UTC that changed the rules of security group sg-0b7e. Step 1 is the flow log observation and step 2 is the CloudTrail call. Step 3 is left for you to complete, and step 4 checks whether the rejects stop after a rollback at 14:55 UTC. Which action fills step 3?
choices: Confirm that sg-0b7e is attached to eni-0f19 and not to a neighbouring resource
Join the two sources on source IP 198.51.100.7 alone, since that address identifies the change
Disable the flow log for eni-0f19 so the rejects stop appearing in the record
Treat the 14:37 call as the cause because it happened before the rejects were logged
questions.why: Correlation links a change to traffic only when the affected resource appears in both sources, so checking that the group is attached to the same interface is the required step.

questions.prompt: Which combination of shared keys is the strongest basis for linking a flow log record to a configuration change?
choices: The time aligned in UTC, together with a resource ID or network interface ID that appears in both sources
The log file name, because files are grouped by hour
The packet byte count, because matching counts prove the same traffic
The IP address alone, because every change names the address it affects
questions.why: The teaching text says a change explains a traffic change only when the times line up and the affected resource appears in both records, so time plus a shared resource or interface ID is the basis.

questions.prompt: An engineer compares a load balancer entry stamped 22:10 local time (UTC minus five hours) with a CloudTrail entry stamped 03:05 UTC on the following day. The engineer concludes the configuration change came after the request. What is the most likely error in that conclusion?
choices: The load balancer log is missing its resource ID, so the entry cannot be matched to any change at all
Local time was compared with UTC without conversion, so the two timestamps sit on different clocks
The security group was attached to the load balancer only after the CloudTrail call was made
The flow log capture window was too long to support any comparison between the two records
questions.why: 22:10 local at UTC minus five is 03:10 UTC, which is after the 03:05 UTC change, so the apparent order reverses once both times are expressed in UTC.

questions.prompt: A team sees REJECT records from 10.20.4.9 to an instance port in flow logs and proposes linking them to a change by matching only that source address in CloudTrail. Why is this risky?
choices: Addresses are always unique within a single hour, so any match is safe to act on
Flow logs never record source addresses, so the match cannot be made at all
The match is pointless because CloudTrail only records calls made from the console
Translation can rewrite the source address, and a shared address proves little on its own
questions.why: Address translation can change the source address in a record, and one address can recur across resources, so an address match alone does not establish that a change caused the traffic.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would work out whether a configuration change caused a traffic problem, using flow logs and a change log. Name one limit of the method.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the time the traffic problem began, taken from the flow logs, and filter for the affected interface and the rejected records. Then I would pull the change log for the same window and look for edits to the security group or network ACL attached to that interface, comparing timestamps in UTC. If a change lands just before the first rejects and touches the same resource, that is a strong lead. I would confirm it by checking that rejects stop after rollback, or by testing in a safe environment. The main limit is that flow logs are aggregated over a capture window and do not explain why a packet was rejected, so the correlation suggests a cause rather than proving it. Address translation and clock skew can also mislead the join, so I would verify the resource identity before acting.
rubricPoints: Names at least two sources and what each one records.
Aligns events by time in a common time zone, allowing for capture windows and clock skew.
Joins records on shared keys such as interface or resource IDs, not on IP address alone.
States a limit: correlation suggests cause, so confirm with a rollback or controlled test.

suggested.rationale: That mission trains reading log records and building a timeline of events from one source, which is the core of this skill, though it does not require joining two sources.

lessons.plain: Logs are the written record a system keeps of what happened. In cloud networking, several services can write down the traffic they handle: a record of each network conversation through your virtual network, each request a load balancer forwards, and each request a content delivery network serves. Each record is a line of metadata, such as who talked to whom, on which port, when, and whether it was allowed. Creating these logs means switching them on for the right resource and choosing where they land, such as cheap object storage, a searchable log store, or a streaming pipe that feeds other tools. If the switch is never flipped, the traffic still happened, but nobody can prove it later.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a security group blocks an incoming connection attempt to a server, would you expect the flow log for that server's network interface to record the attempt? What would you look for in the record to tell it was blocked?
lessons.teach:
A flow log is a record of IP traffic metadata captured at a VPC, a subnet, or a single network interface. It does not hold packet contents. It holds facts about each conversation: source and destination addresses, ports, protocol, packet and byte counts, start and end times, and whether the traffic was accepted or rejected. Records are not written per packet. The service groups packets that share the same source, destination, ports and protocol (often called the five-tuple) into one flow, then writes the flow out at the end of an aggregation interval, commonly one or ten minutes. The delay is by design. Load balancer access logs and CloudFront access logs work differently: each record describes one request or connection the service handled, including status and timing, and the files are written on a schedule to an object storage bucket whose policy must allow the service to write. Delivery destinations are the places records go: object storage for cheap archive, CloudWatch Logs for searching and alarms, and Kinesis Data Firehose or Kinesis Data Streams for streaming to other tools.

Worked example: a client at 203.0.113.10 opens an HTTPS connection (TCP port 443) to a web server at 10.0.1.25 in a subnet with flow logs enabled. During the ten-minute window the service counts 12 packets and 6,400 bytes, marks the action ACCEPT, and writes one record with start and end timestamps. A blocked attempt from the same client to port 22 appears as a separate record with action REJECT, which is how you spot a scan.

Common mistake: assuming a flow log shows what was inside a request, or that it shows results immediately. It shows metadata only, and a connection that a rule allowed looks the same as any other accepted connection, so the log proves what got through, not whether it was wise.

In a running system the consequence is timing and coverage. During an incident the record you need may still be arriving minutes later, and logs switched on today give you no history for yesterday. Logs only help when they are enabled, sent to a destination that exists and accepts writes, and read with the delay in mind.

questions.prompt: A payments team at a regional retailer wants to know whether their checkout service at 172.16.8.14 reached the orders database at 172.16.20.5 on TCP port 5432 during the last hour. Their procedure has three steps. Step 1: confirm that flow logs are enabled on the database subnet and were already on for the whole hour. Step 2 is missing from the procedure below and you must supply it. Step 3: filter the records to source 172.16.8.14, destination 172.16.20.5, port 5432, then read the action field, where ACCEPT means the connection got through and REJECT means it was blocked. Which step 2 completes the procedure correctly?
choices: Ask the database administrator to report the connection count from the database engine's own status page.
Wait until the aggregation window covering the hour has closed and the records have been delivered, because flow records are written at the end of each window and are not available immediately.
Decode the packet payload to read the SQL statements the checkout service sent to the database.
Check the load balancer access log for the HTTP status code returned to the checkout service.
questions.why: Flow records are written only when an aggregation window ends, so the records for the hour are not complete or visible until after that window closes and delivery finishes.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines a flow log record?
choices: A copy of every packet's payload, saved in the order the packets arrived at the network interface.
A per-request record that includes the HTTP method, path and response code for each call made to a web application.
A live stream of firewall rule changes that shows which security group rules were edited and by whom.
A metadata record for a group of packets sharing the same source, destination, ports and protocol, including the counts and whether the traffic was accepted or rejected.
questions.why: A flow log record summarises a conversation as metadata grouped by the five-tuple, without holding packet contents, and marks whether it was accepted or rejected.

questions.prompt: A media company runs an image resizing API behind a load balancer. The operations team wants real-time alarms when rejected traffic spikes, and also wants a cheap long-term archive of all network records for later audits. Which pairing of delivery destinations fits these two needs best?
choices: CloudWatch Logs for searching and alarms, and object storage for the cheap archive.
A single object storage bucket for both, because it can trigger alarms on new files as they arrive.
Kinesis Data Streams for the archive, and the load balancer's own access log bucket for alarms.
Object storage for the real-time alarms and CloudWatch Logs for the long-term archive.
questions.why: CloudWatch Logs suits searching and alarms, while object storage is the cheap archive destination, so the two needs map to two different destinations.

questions.prompt: On a Monday, a security engineer enables flow logs on a VPC that has been running for two years. On Friday, a port scan against that VPC is discovered. What can the engineer expect to find in the logs for the scan?
choices: The full history of the scan, because flow logs for the VPC were stored from the time the VPC was created.
Nothing from before Monday, because flow logs only capture traffic from the time they were enabled, so the Friday scan may appear if it occurred after Monday.
The complete set of rejected packets, because enabling flow logs replays earlier traffic from the network interfaces.
Full packet contents for the scan, because flow logs switch to packet capture when a scan is detected.
questions.why: Flow logs record only traffic from the moment they are enabled, so history from before that point does not exist in the logs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a VPC flow log records and what it cannot tell you, and name one limit or tradeoff in choosing where the logs are delivered.
lessons.modelAnswer: A VPC flow log records metadata about network traffic for a VPC, subnet, or network interface: source and destination addresses, ports, protocol, packet and byte counts, and whether each flow was accepted or rejected. It does not record payloads, so it cannot show what a request contained or whether an attacker's data was malicious. Flows are aggregated over an interval of one or ten minutes, so the records arrive late, and short bursts can be merged or hidden inside a larger window. The tradeoff with delivery is cost and speed: object storage is cheap for long retention but slow to query, while CloudWatch Logs is searchable and can drive alarms but costs more at high volume, and streaming through Kinesis suits real-time tools but needs a consumer. Choosing the destination is a decision about how quickly you need to act versus how long you must keep the data.
rubricPoints: Flow logs capture connection metadata such as addresses, ports, protocol, counts and accept or reject action, not payloads.
Records are aggregated over an interval, so they arrive with delay and may merge short events.
Each delivery destination trades cost, query speed, and real-time capability against retention needs.
Logs are only useful if they are enabled ahead of time and the destination allows writes.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly configuration facts and delivery options that are best learned from reading, and no current OpsForge mission practices creating AWS log delivery.

lessons.plain: Auditing network security configuration means checking, on a schedule and on demand, that the rules protecting your network still say what you intended. Think of a building inspector who walks every floor with a checklist, rather than trusting that the locks were fine on the day they were installed. In AWS, three tools help with this: security groups are the per-resource gatekeepers whose rules get checked, Firewall Manager applies one rule set across many accounts and reports which resources drift from it, and Trusted Advisor compares the account against common best practices and flags risky settings. The goal is evidence that the controls exist and still work, not just a belief that they do.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web server should accept HTTPS from anywhere on the internet and SSH only from your office address range. Later someone adds a rule allowing SSH from anywhere. How would you find that change, and how often would you need to look for it?
lessons.teach:
A security group is a stateful virtual firewall attached to a resource such as a server's network interface. Stateful means that if an inbound connection is allowed, the reply traffic is allowed automatically. Its rules only allow traffic: each rule names a direction (inbound or outbound), a protocol and port range, and a source or destination, which is an address range such as 0.0.0.0/0, meaning every IPv4 address on the internet. Anything not explicitly allowed is dropped.

An audit asks whether the set of rules matches a baseline your organisation has written down. A baseline is the list of rules you have agreed are required. Firewall Manager is the AWS service that lets you define such a baseline once for an entire AWS Organization, which is the group of accounts you manage together, and then reports resources that drift from it. Trusted Advisor is a separate service that checks an account against general best practices and raises warnings, including on security groups that leave sensitive ports open to the world. Which checks you see in full depends on your AWS support plan.

Worked example. The baseline says SSH (TCP port 22) must never be open to 0.0.0.0/0. Step 1: the audit reads each inbound rule on each security group. Step 2: it finds a rule with protocol TCP, port 22, source 0.0.0.0/0. Step 3: the rule violates the baseline, so the resource is recorded as non-compliant. Step 4: someone narrows the source to the office range, and the finding clears on the next evaluation.

Common mistake: treating a clean audit as proof of security. An audit only checks what it was told to check, so a port missing from the baseline passes silently, and a check that runs once a day can miss a rule that was opened and closed in between.

Consequence: while a rule open to the world exists, every resource it is attached to is reachable on that port by anyone, and attackers scan for exactly these ports continuously. Auditing exists to shrink that window and to leave a record of when it opened and closed.

questions.prompt: Your organisation's baseline says inbound access to the payments service on TCP port 8443 may come only from the approved range 203.0.113.0/24. An audit reads the rules on the security group sg-payments-api in a different account. Step 1: it finds an inbound rule for TCP 8443 with source 198.51.100.0/24. Step 2: it compares that source with the approved range and finds no match, so the rule breaks the baseline. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: an engineer changes the source to 203.0.113.0/24, and the finding clears on the next evaluation.
choices: The resource is recorded as non-compliant, which keeps a record of when the gap was open.
The finding is held back until the next day's scan, because audits can only run once every 24 hours.
The audit deletes the rule itself, so the security group is never out of line with the baseline.
The rule is ignored, because security groups are stateful and the reply traffic is already covered.
questions.why: A rule that breaks the baseline causes the audit to record the resource as non-compliant, and that record is what later shows when the rule was open.

questions.prompt: A security group allows inbound TCP 443 from 192.0.2.0/24 and has no matching outbound rule. A client in that range sends a request and receives a reply. What explains whether the reply is allowed?
choices: The reply is blocked unless the source range is widened to 0.0.0.0/0 first.
The reply is blocked, because every reply needs a separate outbound rule on the same group before it can leave.
The reply is allowed only if Trusted Advisor has marked the group as compliant.
The reply is allowed automatically, because a security group is stateful and tracks the allowed connection.
questions.why: A security group is stateful, so once an inbound connection is allowed, its reply traffic is allowed automatically without a separate outbound rule.

questions.prompt: A team's baseline says SSH on TCP 22 and RDP on TCP 3389 must never be open to 0.0.0.0/0. An account has a rule allowing TCP 2222 from 0.0.0.0/0, and TCP 2222 is not in the baseline. The latest audit reports the account as clean. What is the correct conclusion?
choices: The account is secure, because the audit passed and an audit is proof of security.
Firewall Manager flags every open port automatically, so the clean result must include TCP 2222.
Trusted Advisor will flag TCP 2222 on any support plan, so the account is covered either way.
The clean result says nothing about TCP 2222, because an audit only checks what the baseline tells it to check.
questions.why: An audit only checks the rules named in the baseline, so a port missing from the baseline passes silently and the clean result does not prove that port is safe.

questions.prompt: An engineer asks what Trusted Advisor is and how it differs from a baseline audit. Which answer is accurate?
choices: It compares every security group against a baseline you wrote and reports drift, in the same way as Firewall Manager, under another name.
It is a separate service that checks an account against general best practices and can warn about sensitive ports left open to the world.
It only runs when someone starts a manual review, so it cannot raise any warning by itself at any time.
It is the Organisation-wide tool that stores your agreed baseline, enforces it across every linked account, and blocks any rule that drifts from it.
questions.why: Trusted Advisor is a separate service that checks general best practices, including warnings on security groups with sensitive ports open to the world, and which checks are visible depends on the support plan.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would audit whether security groups across a multi-account organisation stay within policy, and name one limit of that approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by agreeing a baseline written as concrete, testable rules, such as no inbound SSH from the whole internet and no database ports open outside private subnets. Firewall Manager can hold that baseline as a policy across the accounts in our organisation, and it reports each security group that does not match, so nobody has to check accounts by hand. Trusted Advisor runs alongside as a second opinion against general best practices, which can catch things our baseline forgot. I would export those findings on a schedule and keep them, because an audit is only useful as evidence if it shows dates and results over time. The limit is that every check only covers what someone wrote into the baseline or what the service already knows to test. A rule for a new risky port passes until we add it, and a rule opened and closed between two runs leaves no finding unless logs record it. So the audit is strong on drift from what we decided, and weak on what we never thought to decide.
rubricPoints: Names the baseline as explicit, testable rules agreed in advance.
Explains that Firewall Manager applies the baseline and reports drift across accounts, while Trusted Advisor gives a best-practice cross-check.
Notes that audit results must be kept over time to serve as evidence.
States a limit: audits only catch what the baseline or checks cover, and changes between runs can be missed.

suggested.rationale: Working through an exam-style situation with a drifted security group and conflicting findings adds the most here, since no current mission or planned engine teaches configuration auditing directly.

lessons.plain: Encryption in transit means scrambling data while it travels between two machines, so anyone who copies the traffic cannot read it. On AWS you have several ways to do this. TLS is a protocol you already meet as the lock icon in a web browser. IPsec wraps whole network packets in an encrypted tunnel, often used for a private link between an office network and a cloud network. AWS builds and runs the underlying network and services, but you decide which hops get encrypted, which certificates and keys they use, and whether a plain-text hop is left somewhere in the middle. It is like sealing an envelope: the postal service carries it, but you choose whether it is sealed.
lessons.guessPrompt: A phone app calls your API through a load balancer, and the load balancer forwards the request to a server inside your private network. Which of those two hops is your responsibility to encrypt, and could a hop inside your private network still be readable?
lessons.teach:
Encryption in transit protects data while it moves across a network. TLS (Transport Layer Security) is a protocol that runs on top of TCP, the reliable connection protocol that carries most web traffic. A client and server perform a handshake, agree on keys, and then encrypt the application's bytes. The server proves its identity with a certificate, a signed document that binds a name such as api.example.com to a public key, issued by a certificate authority. IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) works lower down, at the IP packet level. It encrypts and authenticates packets inside a tunnel between two gateways, so the applications on either side need no changes. Encryption at rest, which protects stored data, is a separate topic.

Why it works: public-key cryptography is used only during the handshake to agree on a shared symmetric key, because symmetric encryption is fast enough to carry bulk traffic. The certificate or pre-shared key proves the other end is who it claims to be.

Worked example: a mobile app calls https://api.example.com, served by an Application Load Balancer. Step 1: the app opens a TCP connection to the load balancer on port 443. Step 2: the load balancer presents its certificate. Step 3: the app checks the signature and the name, and both sides derive a session key. Step 4: the request is encrypted on the phone. Step 5: the load balancer decrypts it and forwards it to a target. If that last hop is plain HTTP inside the VPC, the request is readable on that segment.

Common mistake: assuming traffic is encrypted because it stays inside a private network or AWS's own backbone. AWS encrypts much of its backbone, but you cannot verify that as your control, so configure each hop yourself.

Shared responsibility: AWS secures the physical facilities, hardware and operation of its services. You choose protocols and cipher settings, install and renew certificates, manage keys, and decide which hops are encrypted. If a certificate expires, that failure is yours.

Consequence: one plain-text hop lets anyone who can capture traffic there read session tokens, so a strong edge can still leak credentials.

questions.prompt: Lantern Dental runs a site-to-site VPN so its clinic router can reach a database in a VPC. The sequence is: Step 1: the clinic router starts an IPsec negotiation with the VPC gateway. Step 2: both ends prove their identity using a pre-shared key. Step 3: both ends agree on symmetric session keys. Step 4: [missing]. Step 5: the VPC gateway decrypts the packet and delivers it to the database server on port 5432. Which choice fills Step 4?
choices: The clinic router sends every packet to the database server unencrypted and relies on the tunnel to hide it later
The clinic router encrypts and authenticates each outgoing packet before it enters the tunnel
Both gateways renew the pre-shared key before each packet is sent
The database server installs a public certificate so the clinic router can verify its name
questions.why: Once session keys are agreed, the sending gateway must encrypt and authenticate each packet before it enters the tunnel, which is what the decryption in Step 5 reverses.

questions.prompt: Which description of IPsec is accurate?
choices: A certificate authority that signs names so browsers can trust web servers during every handshake
A replacement for TCP that gives faster reliable delivery of web requests to load balancers
Encrypts and authenticates IP packets inside a tunnel between two gateways, so applications need no changes
Encrypts files stored in object storage when they are written to disk, leaving network traffic alone
questions.why: IPsec works at the IP packet level inside a tunnel between two gateways, which is why the applications on either side need no changes.

questions.prompt: A retailer terminates TLS at its load balancer for shoppers, then forwards requests to app instances over plain HTTP inside the same VPC. Which statement is true?
choices: Shoppers' connections are encrypted only if the app instances also hold the public certificate
Traffic is safe because it never leaves the private network and AWS encrypts the backbone
The hop from the load balancer to the app instances is unencrypted, so anyone capturing traffic there can read session tokens
The hop to the app instances is protected by the shoppers' TLS session, so no further change is needed
questions.why: TLS protects only the hop it runs on, so the plain HTTP hop inside the VPC is readable by anyone who can capture traffic there, and you must configure that hop yourself.

questions.prompt: A team's public API certificate expired at midnight and clients began failing the TLS handshake. Under the shared responsibility model, who owns the fix?
choices: The certificate authority, which must automatically reissue certificates to all customers
Nobody, because a handshake failure is a transient network issue that resolves itself
The team, because installing and renewing certificates is a customer task
AWS, because it operates the load balancer hardware that presented the certificate
questions.why: Under the shared responsibility model AWS secures the facilities and hardware, while the customer installs, renews and manages certificates, so an expired certificate is the team's failure to fix.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what encryption in transit covers on AWS, what AWS handles and what you still have to configure yourself, and name one limit or tradeoff of terminating TLS at a load balancer rather than on each backend server.
lessons.modelAnswer: Encryption in transit means data is encrypted while it moves between two points, so someone capturing the traffic cannot read it. On AWS the main options are TLS, which encrypts application connections and needs a certificate, and IPsec, which encrypts packets inside a tunnel, for example a VPN over a Direct Connect link. AWS is responsible for the physical network, the hardware, and running its services securely. We are responsible for choosing the protocol, setting the cipher policy, installing and renewing certificates and keys, and making sure every hop is encrypted, including the hop from the load balancer to the backend. One tradeoff of terminating TLS at the load balancer is that traffic between the load balancer and the backend may be plain text unless we re-encrypt it, and we give up end-to-end encryption to that server. We have to decide whether that hop is acceptable for our data.
rubricPoints: Defines encryption in transit as protecting data while it moves between points
Names TLS as an application-level option and IPsec as a network-level tunnel option
States what AWS handles versus what the customer must configure, including certificates and keys
Identifies a concrete limit, such as plain-text hops after TLS termination at a load balancer

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining who secures what and where encryption must be configured, which is best checked by explaining it back.

lessons.plain: Encryption in transit means scrambling data while it moves between two points, so anyone who captures the traffic on the way sees only noise. In the cloud, data travels across the public internet, across private links from a data center, and between parts of your own network. Two common methods do the scrambling. TLS wraps a single application connection, the kind your browser uses when it shows a padlock. IPsec wraps everything passing between two network gateways, so whole networks can talk privately. This objective is about knowing which method applies at each hop of a cloud setup and where you must switch it on yourself.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company sends customer records from its office data center to a cloud database over a dedicated fiber link it rents from a telecom provider. Before reading any further, would you assume that link is already encrypted, and why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Encryption in transit protects data while it is moving. TLS (Transport Layer Security) sets up an encrypted session between a client and a server. The server proves its identity with a certificate, which is a signed document binding a name such as shop.example to a public key, issued by an authority the client trusts. IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) is a set of protocols that encrypts and authenticates IP packets between two gateways, forming a tunnel. A listener is the port and protocol a load balancer accepts. Termination is the point where an encrypted session ends and the traffic is decrypted.

It works because only the two endpoints hold the keys needed to decrypt the traffic. Every hop is a separate connection, so each hop needs its own protection.

Worked example: a shopper opens a CloudFront distribution over HTTPS. Step 1: the browser starts a TLS handshake with the CloudFront edge and names the site. Step 2: CloudFront presents its certificate, and the browser checks the name and the issuer. Step 3: both sides agree on session keys. Step 4: the request travels encrypted. Step 5: CloudFront opens a second, separate connection to an Application Load Balancer origin. If that origin listener accepts only plain HTTP, the second hop is unencrypted, even though the first one was not.

Common mistake: assuming a private or dedicated path is encrypted. A Direct Connect link is private but not encrypted, so an IPsec VPN must run over it to protect the data.

Consequence: one plaintext hop lets anyone on that path read session cookies or credentials, so a secure front door does not protect the traffic behind it.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs a mobile tracking API at track.parcel-co.test behind a Network Load Balancer with a TLS listener on port 8443. The walkthrough: Step 1: the app starts a TLS handshake with the load balancer and names track.parcel-co.test. Step 2: the load balancer presents a certificate for that name, and the app checks the name and the issuer. Step 3: both sides agree on session keys. Step 4: the load balancer decrypts the request at its termination point. Step 5: [MISSING - to be chosen]. Step 6: the target in a private subnet receives and processes the request.
choices: The load balancer reuses the client's session keys from Step 3 to protect the connection to the target
The load balancer forwards the decrypted request over the private VPC network, which needs no further encryption because the network is internal
The load balancer opens a separate connection to the target and encrypts that connection with TLS, so the target has its own termination point
The load balancer sends the request to the target over a Direct Connect link, which is already private and therefore safe
questions.why: Each hop is a separate connection that needs its own protection, so the load balancer must open a new TLS connection to the target, making the second hop encrypted as well.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what IPsec does?
choices: It encrypts and authenticates IP packets between two gateways, forming a tunnel
It decides which port and protocol a load balancer accepts from clients
It removes encryption at the point where a session ends so the traffic can be inspected
It binds a domain name to a public key with a certificate signed by a trusted issuer
questions.why: IPsec is a set of protocols that encrypts and authenticates IP packets between two gateways, forming a tunnel, which is the definition given in the teaching text.

questions.prompt: A bank connects its head office to its cloud network over a dedicated private circuit. An engineer says the circuit is private, so the bank's payment data is already encrypted in transit and no extra step is needed. What is the error in that reasoning?
choices: A private circuit is encrypted only when it carries TLS, so the bank must enable TLS on every application instead
A private circuit does not need protection because the bank's own gateways hold the keys at both ends
A private circuit is encrypted by the provider, but only for traffic that is smaller than the maximum packet size
A private circuit is not encrypted by being private, so an IPsec VPN must run over it to protect the data
questions.why: Privacy of a path does not mean encryption, so the data needs an IPsec tunnel running over the circuit to be protected in transit.

questions.prompt: A client connects to the name reports.lakeside.test. The certificate it receives names a different host, and it is signed by an issuer the client trusts. What should the client do, and why?
choices: Reject the session only if the issuer is unknown, since the name in the certificate does not matter
Accept the session, because a certificate from a trusted issuer is always valid for any name
Accept the session, because the public key inside the certificate still proves the server's identity
Reject the session, because the certificate does not bind the name the client connected to, so the server's identity is not proven
questions.why: A certificate must bind the name the client is trying to reach to a public key; if the name does not match, the server has not proven it is the host the client intended, so the client should reject it even though the issuer is trusted.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says our Direct Connect link to the data center is private, so we do not need encryption on it. Explain to them, in your own words, why that is incomplete, how you would encrypt that path, and one limit or tradeoff of your fix.
lessons.modelAnswer: Direct Connect gives a private, dedicated path, but private is not the same as encrypted. Anyone with access to the physical path or carrier equipment could in principle read the packets, and compliance rules often require encryption regardless. To encrypt it, we build an IPsec VPN tunnel from the on-premises router to a cloud VPN endpoint, running across a private virtual interface attached to a Transit Gateway, so the traffic inside the tunnel is encrypted. The tradeoff is that the tunnel adds per-packet overhead, reduces the usable packet size, and is bounded by the throughput limits of each tunnel, so higher bandwidth needs multiple tunnels or a different design.
rubricPoints: A private path does not mean the data is encrypted.
Encryption is added by running an IPsec tunnel over the link.
Both sides need tunnel endpoints and managed keys or certificates.
The fix adds overhead, smaller packets, and per-tunnel throughput limits.

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right protection at each hop of a traffic path is a reasoning task best practised by working through an exam-style situation.

lessons.plain: Imagine a company that rents a dedicated private road from its office to a cloud data center, instead of sending its traffic over public streets. That road is Direct Connect. A private road is not automatically sealed, though, because the road only controls who can reach it, not what is written on the packages inside. So engineers often run a scrambled, sealed tunnel inside that road. The tunnel is a VPN, and the scrambling is done by a set of rules called IPsec. Running a VPN over Direct Connect gives you a private path and encryption on that path, both at once.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company already pays for a private dedicated link into AWS. Why might its security team still ask for an encrypted VPN to run across that same link, and what could go wrong if the team skipped it?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. Direct Connect is an AWS service that provides a dedicated physical network connection between your site, such as an office or data center, and AWS, so traffic does not have to cross the public internet. A virtual interface, or VIF, is a logical channel carried on that connection, with its own routing purpose. A Site-to-Site VPN is a pair of tunnel endpoints, one on the AWS side and one on your router, that protect traffic passing between them. IPsec is a set of protocols that authenticates the two ends and encrypts each IP packet, then wraps the encrypted packet in a new outer packet addressed from one tunnel endpoint to the other. A transit gateway is a regional routing hub that connects many VPCs and VPNs.

Why it works: the private link controls which path the traffic takes, but a circuit does not encrypt the bits it carries. Putting IPsec inside the link means that anyone who can see the physical path sees only ciphertext. The outer packet still rides the Direct Connect virtual interface, so you keep the predictable private path and add encryption on top.

Worked example. An on-premises router at 192.168.10.1 serves 192.168.10.0/24. A VPC uses 10.20.0.0/16. Step 1: an application at 10.20.5.9 sends a packet to 192.168.10.50. Step 2: the route table sends that prefix to the VPN attachment on the transit gateway. Step 3: AWS encrypts the packet with IPsec and wraps it in an outer packet addressed to the tunnel endpoint on the router. Step 4: the outer packet crosses the Direct Connect virtual interface. Step 5: the router authenticates and decrypts the packet, then delivers the inner packet to 192.168.10.50.

Common mistake: treating the Direct Connect link as encrypted because it is private, and leaving the VPN off to save setup effort. A single tunnel also has a throughput ceiling far below the port speed of the link, and a tunnel fault stops traffic unless a second path exists. In a running system, a regulated data flow can look private on a diagram while being sent unencrypted across the circuit, which is the kind of gap an audit finds.

A private link and an encrypted tunnel answer different questions, and in regulated designs you usually need both.

questions.prompt: A payments firm has an on-premises router at 172.20.30.1 serving 172.20.30.0/24. Its VPC uses 10.70.0.0/16 and reaches the router over a dedicated Direct Connect link with a virtual interface, with a Site-to-Site VPN running across that link. Step 1: an application at 10.70.8.44 sends a packet to 172.20.30.99. Step 2: the route table sends 172.20.30.0/24 to the VPN attachment on a transit gateway. Step 3: AWS encrypts the packet with IPsec and wraps it in an outer packet addressed to the tunnel endpoint on the router. Step 4: [missing]. Step 5: the router authenticates and decrypts the packet and delivers the inner packet to 172.20.30.99. Which choice correctly fills in Step 4?
choices: The transit gateway decrypts the packet before it reaches the Direct Connect link, so the link carries plain IP traffic.
The packet is sent over the public internet because a virtual interface cannot carry IPsec traffic.
The inner packet is sent unencrypted across the virtual interface so the router can read the destination address.
The outer packet crosses the Direct Connect virtual interface, keeping the predictable private path while staying encrypted.
questions.why: Step 4 is the outer encrypted packet crossing the Direct Connect virtual interface, which keeps the private path while the IPsec wrapping protects the contents.

questions.prompt: A logistics company describes its Direct Connect virtual interface as its secure channel for customer records. In plain terms, what is a virtual interface (VIF) on that connection?
choices: An encrypted tunnel endpoint that AWS operates on its own side.
A transit gateway attachment that hosts the route tables for a VPC.
A physical fiber strand reserved only for that company's traffic.
A logical channel carried on the connection that has its own routing purpose.
questions.why: A VIF is a logical channel carried on the Direct Connect connection with its own routing purpose, and it does not by itself encrypt traffic.

questions.prompt: A bank runs one Site-to-Site VPN tunnel across its Direct Connect link to protect card data. The router at one tunnel endpoint fails overnight and no second path exists. What happens to the traffic?
choices: It keeps flowing on the bare Direct Connect link without encryption, because the link is private.
It is queued at the transit gateway and sent later with the same encryption once the tunnel returns.
It reroutes over the public internet automatically, because Direct Connect always has an internet fallback.
It stops until the tunnel is restored, because a tunnel fault halts traffic when no second path exists.
questions.why: With a single tunnel and no second path, a tunnel fault stops the traffic, and the private link alone does not carry it unencrypted in its place.

questions.prompt: A retailer's architecture diagram labels its Direct Connect link as the private path for customer data. An auditor asks for evidence that the data is protected in transit. Which response is strongest?
choices: The diagram shows the link is private, and a private path is enough protection.
The dedicated port speed of the link is high enough to make interception impractical.
The link is in a single Region, so the data never leaves that Region.
An IPsec tunnel on that path with the route table pointing traffic to it, shown in the configuration.
questions.why: A private link does not encrypt the bits it carries, so the defensible evidence is the IPsec tunnel itself and the route that sends traffic through it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we run a Site-to-Site VPN over a Direct Connect link instead of relying on the link alone, and name one limit or tradeoff of doing it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Direct Connect gives us a dedicated private path from our data center to AWS, but a private circuit does not encrypt the bits on it, so anyone with access to the physical path could in principle read the traffic. We add a Site-to-Site VPN, which builds IPsec tunnels between a tunnel endpoint on AWS and our router. IPsec authenticates both ends and encrypts each packet, and the encrypted packet still travels over the Direct Connect path. The main tradeoff is throughput: each tunnel has a ceiling well below the link's port speed, so high bandwidth needs several tunnels, and the encryption plus tunnel management adds configuration and operational work. We also need a backup path, so a tunnel failure does not cut traffic.
rubricPoints: A private Direct Connect circuit does not by itself encrypt traffic.
A Site-to-Site VPN runs IPsec tunnels that authenticate and encrypt packets across the link.
The encrypted packets still use the private Direct Connect path.
A tradeoff such as per-tunnel throughput limits, added configuration, or the need for a backup path.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a compliance scenario about what a private link does and does not protect adds the most, and no listed mission or planned engine covers this objective directly.

lessons.plain: A certificate is a small digital ID card for a server. It states which name the server answers to, such as shop.example.com, and carries a public key that visitors use to set up an encrypted connection. A trusted authority signs the card, so a visitor's software can check that it is genuine. AWS Certificate Manager issues, stores and renews these cards so you do not handle key files yourself. AWS Private Certificate Authority lets your organization run its own signing authority for internal names and devices that only your company needs to trust. Both exist to prevent the manual renewal mistakes that cause outages.
lessons.guessPrompt: A website's certificate expired at midnight. Visitors see a security warning and the site stops loading in their browsers, though the servers themselves are running. Before reading on, what do you think the browser is checking, and who has to act to fix it?
lessons.teach:
A certificate binds a domain name to a public key and carries a digital signature from a certificate authority (CA), an organization whose signatures software is configured to trust. A public key is the half of a key pair that may be shared openly; its matching private key must stay secret. The validity window is the start and end dates between which the certificate is accepted.

Why it works: when a browser connects over TLS, the protocol behind HTTPS, the server presents its certificate. The browser checks that the signature chains back to a trusted CA, that the name matches the address requested, and that the current time falls inside the validity window. If all three pass, both sides agree on session keys and encrypt the traffic. AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) issues public certificates from a public CA and handles renewal. For ACM public certificates the private key stays inside AWS and cannot be exported, which is why they attach to managed services such as load balancers rather than being copied onto your own machines. AWS Private Certificate Authority (Private CA) is a CA you create in your own account. Its certificates are trusted only where you install your private root, which suits internal services and devices.

Worked example: a team requests a certificate for api.internal.example.com from a Private CA. Step 1: the CA signs the certificate with its private signing key. Step 2: the service presents it to clients. Step 3: a client that has the private root installed checks the signature, the name and the dates, and accepts it. Step 4: thirty days before expiry, the team issues a replacement and deploys it.

Common mistake: treating renewal as set-and-forget. ACM renews public certificates automatically only while the domain validation records you chose remain in place. If those records are removed, renewal fails and nobody notices until expiry.

Consequence: an expired certificate makes every client reject the connection at once, so a healthy service looks down, often at peak hours. Certificate expiry must be monitored as a production risk.

questions.prompt: A kiosk company, Brightwater Transit, issues a certificate from its own AWS Private CA for the name gateway.fares.brightwater.example for its ticket gateway. Step 1: the Private CA signs the certificate with its private signing key. Step 2: the gateway presents the certificate when a kiosk connects over TLS. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the kiosk refuses the connection and shows a certificate warning, because the chain never reaches a root it trusts. Which step 3 completes the trace?
choices: Kiosks compare the name and dates, then accept the certificate even without a root installed, because a valid-looking signature is enough.
Kiosks copy the gateway's private key so they can verify the signature themselves before connecting.
Kiosks send the certificate to AWS Certificate Manager, which re-signs it with a public CA so the chain succeeds.
Kiosks check the signature against the private root they have installed; that root is absent on these kiosks, so the chain cannot be built and the connection is rejected.
questions.why: A client can only confirm the signature chain if it holds the private root that the Private CA signed under, and the missing root is what makes the chain fail.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the public key and private key inside a certificate's key pair?
choices: The public key may be shared openly, and its matching private key must stay secret.
The private key is embedded in the certificate so that browsers can verify the domain name.
Both keys are published in the certificate so that clients can sign their own traffic.
The public key is kept secret on the server, and the private key is sent to every client.
questions.why: The public key is the shareable half of the pair and the private key is the secret half that must never be exposed.

questions.prompt: A team has an AWS Certificate Manager public certificate attached to a load balancer. They want to copy the certificate's private key into a container image so the app can terminate TLS itself. What is the correct response?
choices: Copy the key, since ACM keeps a second exportable copy for exactly this use.
Export the key from the load balancer's console settings, since the load balancer owns the certificate and can hand it over.
ACM public certificate private keys cannot be exported, so the key cannot be copied; keep the certificate on the managed load balancer or use a different certificate source the team controls.
Request the same domain again from the public CA and paste the new private key into the image.
questions.why: ACM keeps public certificate private keys inside AWS, which is why such certificates attach to managed services rather than being copied to your own machines.

questions.prompt: An ACM public certificate for a payments domain expires in 10 days. Last month a DNS cleanup removed the validation records that were used when the certificate was issued. What should the team do first?
choices: Request a new certificate from a Private CA and attach it, because public certificates cannot be renewed.
Restore the domain validation records so ACM can renew the public certificate, and set up expiry monitoring.
Do nothing until the expiry date, then let clients fall back to plain HTTP.
Delete the validation records and wait, since ACM renews automatically regardless of them.
questions.why: Automatic renewal of a public certificate depends on the validation records staying in place, so restoring them is the step that lets renewal succeed before expiry.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only run a web server before: what problem a certificate solves, how ACM differs from a Private CA, and one limit or tradeoff of using a private authority for internal services.
lessons.modelAnswer: A certificate lets a visitor's software confirm that a server is who it claims to be and then encrypt the connection with it. The certificate ties a name to a public key and carries a signature from an authority the client trusts. ACM is the managed service that issues and renews public certificates for us, and it keeps the private key inside AWS so it can attach to load balancers. Private CA is an authority we run ourselves, so its certificates work only on devices where we have installed our private root. The tradeoff is that internal clients must all trust that root, and if the root's private key were compromised, we would have to rebuild trust across every device. We also must monitor expiry dates, because an expired certificate breaks every client at once.
rubricPoints: A certificate binds a name to a public key and is signed by a trusted authority.
ACM issues and renews public certificates, and the private key stays inside AWS.
Private CA certificates are trusted only where the private root is installed.
Expiry or failed renewal breaks clients all at once, so it must be monitored.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers certificate issuance, trust chains or renewal, so this is best learned from facts and console concepts.

lessons.plain: DNS is the internet's phone book: it turns a name such as shop.example.com into a numeric address. The weakness is that an answer can be forged or altered on its way back, sending people to a fake site. DNSSEC is an add-on that signs DNS answers with digital signatures, so a receiving resolver can check that the answer really came from the owner of the name and was not changed. It proves who vouched for the answer and that it is intact, but it does not hide the question from anyone watching the network.
lessons.guessPrompt: If an attacker can slip a fake answer into a DNS reply, what would a resolver need in order to notice the answer is fake, and where could it get the proof from?
lessons.teach: DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions) adds signature records to a DNS zone, which is the set of records one organisation controls under a domain. Each record set gets an RRSIG record, a signature made with a private key. The matching public key is published as a DNSKEY record. Two keys are used. The zone signing key (ZSK) signs the everyday records. The key signing key (KSK) signs the DNSKEY set, and a hash of the KSK, called a DS record, is published in the parent zone, such as .com, through the domain registrar. That link is the chain of trust: each parent vouches for its child's key, all the way up to the root, which resolvers trust as an anchor. A validating resolver fetches the answer and its RRSIG, fetches the DNSKEY, checks the DS at the parent, and walks upward until it reaches the root. If every link checks out, the answer is accepted. If a check fails, the resolver rejects the answer and returns SERVFAIL. Worked example: a resolver asks for www.example.com and receives an A record plus its RRSIG. It fetches the DNSKEY set, confirms the KSK matches the DS published at the .com parent, then verifies the signature on the A record. All checks pass, so the answer is accepted. On AWS, Route 53 can sign a public hosted zone. It keeps the KSK private key in a customer managed AWS KMS key, an asymmetric key that must be created in us-east-1, and it handles signing-key rotation. You then copy the DS record it generates into the registrar. Common mistake: enabling signing without publishing the DS record at the registrar, or changing the KSK without updating the DS. The chain breaks, validating resolvers refuse the zone, and users see an outage even though the records themselves are correct. DNSSEC gives integrity and authenticity, not confidentiality: queries and answers stay readable on the wire unless they travel over an encrypted DNS transport.

questions.prompt: A new example in a different zone. A validating resolver is checking mail.bluefinch.net, which sits in a zone signed with DNSSEC, and the parent zone is .net. Work through the chain of checks. Step 1: the resolver receives the MX record for mail.bluefinch.net together with its RRSIG, a signature made with a private key. Step 2: the resolver fetches the DNSKEY set for bluefinch.net. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the resolver checks the RRSIG on the MX record against the zone signing key in the DNSKEY set. All checks pass, so the answer is accepted. Which choice correctly completes step 3?
choices: The resolver checks the RRSIG on the DNSKEY set using the zone signing key, then accepts the MX record without looking at the parent zone at all, since the parent has no role in verifying everyday records.
The resolver asks the bluefinch.net registrar to sign the MX record with its own key so the parent can vouch for it.
The resolver compares the DS record directly with the zone signing key, since the DS record is a hash of the ZSK.
The resolver hashes the key signing key from the DNSKEY set and compares it with the DS record at the .net parent, then climbs toward the root anchor.
questions.why: The DS record is a hash of the key signing key published at the parent, so the resolver must hash the KSK and match it to the DS before climbing the chain toward the root.

questions.prompt: The logistics firm parcelcrate.io is setting up DNSSEC for a public zone. Which record is the hash of the key signing key that must be published at the parent zone through the registrar?
choices: A record
RRSIG record
DNSKEY record
DS record
questions.why: The DS record is a hash of the key signing key and is published in the parent zone, while the RRSIG is a signature and the DNSKEY is the public key itself.

questions.prompt: parcelcrate.io rotated its key signing key last night, generated a new KSK, and left the old DS record at the registrar. A user then queries www.parcelcrate.io through a validating resolver. What does the resolver do?
choices: It falls back to an unsigned answer and returns it silently.
It accepts the answer, because the A record and its RRSIG are still correctly signed.
It returns NXDOMAIN, meaning the name does not exist.
It rejects the zone and returns SERVFAIL, because the new KSK no longer matches the DS at the parent, even though the A record is correct.
questions.why: A broken link in the chain of trust makes a validating resolver reject the zone and return SERVFAIL, even when the records themselves are fine.

questions.prompt: A company enables DNSSEC on its zone and tells its security staff that DNS lookups are now hidden from the local network operator. Which statement is accurate?
choices: DNSSEC hides only the answer, while the queried name stays visible to everyone on the path.
DNSSEC confidentiality comes from the RRSIG record, which encrypts each answer with the zone signing key.
DNSSEC replaces the need for a DS record at the parent, so no key data is exposed on the wire.
DNSSEC gives integrity and authenticity, not confidentiality, so queries and answers stay readable on the wire unless an encrypted DNS transport is used.
questions.why: DNSSEC signs records so their origin and integrity can be checked but does not encrypt them, so the content of queries and answers remains readable on the wire.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what DNSSEC protects against, how the chain of trust runs from the root down to our zone, and one limit or operational risk we must watch when we turn it on.
lessons.modelAnswer: DNSSEC protects against forged or altered DNS answers. Every record set in our zone gets a signature, and the public key is published alongside it. A validating resolver checks that signature, then checks that the key is vouched for by a DS record in the parent zone, and that parent is vouched for by its own parent, up to the root. So a resolver can tell a genuine answer from a spoofed one. The limit is that DNSSEC does not encrypt anything, so anyone on the path can still read our queries. The operational risk is the DS record. If we rotate the key signing key and forget to update the DS at the registrar, or enable signing and never publish the DS, validating resolvers return SERVFAIL and our names stop resolving for those users even though the zone itself is correct. We should check the chain after every key change.
rubricPoints: DNSSEC adds signatures so resolvers can verify that answers are authentic and unchanged.
The chain of trust runs from the root through the parent DS record down to the zone's signing keys.
DNSSEC provides integrity and authenticity but not confidentiality of queries.
A mismatched or missing DS record causes validation failure and an outage for validating resolvers.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly service facts and a verification chain that a learner can absorb from the teaching text, and no listed mission or planned engine targets DNS signing.

scenarios.title: Harbor Vale Medical Supplies: edge, overlapping addresses, and name lookups
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Vale Medical Supplies is a fictional company that sells clinic supplies. Its customer portal is a web application running in one AWS Region, and most of its traffic comes from hospitals in Europe and North America. The portal serves HTTPS pages and images that rarely change, plus an order-ingest service that receives orders over a raw TCP connection on a fixed port. Hospital IT teams allow-list specific IP addresses in their firewalls, so the order service must keep the same public IP addresses even if the backend changes. The company also just bought a clinic chain whose internal network uses the same 10.0.0.0/16 private address range as the main cloud VPC, and the clinic staff need to reach a billing service in the cloud. Renumbering the clinic network is not possible this quarter. Finally, clinic and data center servers use the company's on-premises DNS, and they must resolve names for the cloud-hosted billing service. Use the scenario above to answer the following. 1. Choose a distribution service for the customer portal (HTTPS, cacheable content) and for the order-ingest service (raw TCP, fixed IP addresses), and justify each choice against latency and the allow-list requirement. 2. Propose a way to let clinic staff reach the cloud billing service without renumbering either network, and explain what would go wrong if the two networks were simply joined by routing. 3. Describe how on-premises DNS should resolve the private name of the billing service, and state the TTL trade-off you would consider for any failover record.
subParts: Distribution choice for portal and order ingest
Hybrid DNS resolution and TTL trade-off
modelAnswer: For the customer portal, use Amazon CloudFront, a content delivery network: a service that stores copies of content in edge locations (data centers close to users) so most requests are answered nearby, cutting latency for HTTPS pages and images. For the order-ingest service, use AWS Global Accelerator, which gives you a pair of static anycast IP addresses (one address announced from many locations, so traffic enters the nearest point of the provider network) and carries TCP and UDP traffic over the AWS global network to your endpoint. Because the hospitals allow-list fixed IPs and the traffic is raw TCP rather than cacheable HTTP, CloudFront is the wrong fit for the order service and Global Accelerator is the right one. The portal can also use Global Accelerator, but CloudFront's caching is the stronger benefit for mostly static content.

Put a private connection in front of the billing service instead of routing the two 10.0.0.0/16 networks directly. AWS PrivateLink creates an interface endpoint: a private network address inside the clinic-side VPC that connects to a service in the cloud VPC, and it is set up so that only the service is exposed, not the whole network. Clinic traffic reaches the endpoint's address, which avoids the overlap because the clinic never needs a route into the cloud's 10.0.0.0/16 range. If you simply joined the networks with routing, a clinic host and a cloud host could both own the same address, so a packet to 10.0.5.20 would have two possible destinations and would go to the wrong machine or be dropped. Network address translation (NAT, which rewrites addresses as traffic crosses a boundary) is the other option, but PrivateLink is simpler for a single service.

Use Amazon Route 53 Resolver endpoints. An inbound endpoint is a set of addresses in the cloud VPC that on-premises DNS servers can forward queries to, so on-premises clients can resolve names held in a Route 53 private hosted zone (a DNS zone that only answers inside the VPCs you attach it to). An outbound endpoint lets cloud resources query on-premises DNS for corporate names. Create a conditional forwarder on the on-premises DNS server for the billing zone name that sends the query to the inbound endpoint addresses. For failover records, a time-to-live (TTL, the number of seconds resolvers may cache an answer) must be chosen with care: a short TTL lets clients switch quickly to a healthy target but increases query load and the number of lookups; a long TTL reduces load but keeps clients on a failed address until the cache expires.

scenarios.title: Harrow and Lane Freight: connecting the depot data centre to AWS
scenarios.scenario: Harrow and Lane Freight is a fictional regional trucking company that runs its warehouse management system in a small on-premises data centre at its main depot. The network team is moving part of the system to AWS and must keep both sides talking reliably. The design has three parts. First, AWS Direct Connect, a dedicated private link from the company's network into AWS that does not travel over the public internet, will be placed at a colocation facility, which is a shared building where many networks rent racks and meet. A cross-connect is a short fibre jumper that the facility runs between the company's equipment and the carrier's equipment. Second, a Transit Gateway, which is a managed regional router, will act as the hub of a hub-and-spoke design, joining several isolated private networks (VPCs) in AWS through one central point. Third, hybrid DNS, the name lookup service, must let depot staff resolve cloud-hosted names and let cloud servers resolve depot names. The engineer on call has four tasks. 1. The colocation facility will not order the cross-connect until a document arrives from the carrier. Name that document, say what it must contain, and explain why the facility needs it. 2. The depot router will exchange routes with AWS using BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol that networks use to announce which address ranges they can reach. Explain when static routing would be acceptable instead, and which path the Transit Gateway prefers when the same address range is learned over both the Direct Connect link and a backup VPN, where the VPN route has a longer AS path (the list of networks a route has passed through). 3. Depot staff cannot resolve wms.harrowlane.internal, and cloud servers cannot resolve the depot file server name fileserver.depot.harrowlane.local. Describe the Route 53 resolver endpoint needed in each direction and where a conditional forwarding rule fits. 4. Before sign-off, the team must confirm that a cloud subnet can reach the depot file server on the correct port. Explain why Reachability Analyzer is used here instead of a ping test, and what a blocked result would tell the engineer to check.
subParts: Name the carrier document and what it must contain
Choose static or BGP routing and the preferred path
Describe resolver endpoints and conditional forwarding
Validate the path with Reachability Analyzer
modelAnswer: The document is a Letter of Authorization, often paired with a Connecting Facility Assignment, usually written as LOA-CFA. It is a formal letter from the carrier that authorises a named engineer or company to request a cross-connect at a specific facility and building. It must name the colocation facility, the company placing the order, the carrier or provider, the port or cage location, and the time window or circuit reference. The facility needs it as proof that the request is authorised, so it can physically connect the carrier's equipment to the company's equipment without a risk of wiring the wrong port. Without it the order stalls, however ready the router is.

Static routing means you type the routes by hand and they never change on their own. It is acceptable for a very small, single-link setup where the address ranges never change and a human will notice a failure. BGP is a dynamic protocol: routers announce and withdraw routes automatically, so if the Direct Connect link fails the route disappears and traffic moves to the backup. For this design BGP is the right choice because it gives automatic failover. When the same address range arrives over Direct Connect and over the VPN, the Transit Gateway compares routes by first choosing the most specific prefix, then by the shortest AS path. The Direct Connect route with the shorter AS path wins, so the VPN with its longer path acts only as backup. The team can confirm this by checking the route table and the advertised AS paths.

Staff at the depot need to query the AWS-hosted name, so AWS must have an inbound resolver endpoint: a set of network interfaces in a VPC that accepts DNS queries coming from the depot network and answers them from the private hosted zone. Cloud servers need to query the depot name, so AWS needs an outbound resolver endpoint, which sends queries leaving AWS toward the depot's DNS servers. A conditional forwarding rule is attached to the outbound endpoint and says that any query for the domain depot.harrowlane.local should go to the depot's DNS server IP addresses instead of the public resolver. Common mistake: creating only one endpoint type and expecting both directions to work. Consequence: one side of the business keeps getting name errors while the network itself is healthy.

Reachability Analyzer checks the configured path between two resources without sending any real traffic. It looks at route tables, the Transit Gateway, network ACLs, and security groups, and reports whether the path exists and, if not, which component blocks it. A ping test only shows that packets did or did not arrive at a moment in time, and it can fail for reasons unrelated to the path, such as a host firewall blocking ICMP. Analyzer tests the exact protocol and port, so it can confirm the file service port is open. If the result is blocked, the engineer should look at the component named in the result, most often a security group rule or a missing route in a table, fix that one item, and rerun the analysis.

scenarios.title: Harbor Fresh Logistics: slow transfers and a host that times out
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Fresh Logistics is a fictional company that runs its warehouse management system from a data center it owns. Its cloud footprint is three VPCs (virtual private clouds, which are isolated private networks inside AWS): two in one Region and one in a second Region used for disaster recovery. The data center reaches AWS over an AWS Direct Connect link, which is a dedicated private connection, and the routers on both sides exchange address ranges using BGP (Border Gateway Protocol, the routing protocol that tells each network which address ranges it can reach). Three problems were reported this week. First, nightly inventory files of about 4 GB now take much longer to cross the Direct Connect link than last month. Second, a reporting server at 10.20.5.14 in one VPC answers small requests, but some large responses from it time out. Third, the operations team wants the data center and all three VPCs to reach each other without building a separate point-to-point link for every pair. Answer the following. 1. Explain which evidence you would collect first to find out why large responses from the server at 10.20.5.14 time out, and name the tool you would use to check whether a configured path exists between the reporting server and the warehouse system without sending live traffic. Say what each would tell you. 2. The team suspects a packet size mismatch. In two or three sentences, explain what MTU (maximum transmission unit, the largest packet a link carries without splitting it) is, why a mismatch makes large transfers stall while small ones succeed, and what you would check on the server and along the path. 3. Recommend how the data center and the three VPCs should be connected. Say whether you would use Transit Gateway (a regional hub router that each network attaches to once), VPC peering (a direct link between two VPCs that does not pass traffic onward), or both, and justify your choice against the no-full-mesh requirement. Include one routing step, such as route summarization (advertising one shorter address range in place of several longer ones), that keeps the routing tables small.
subParts: Evidence and tool for the timeout on large responses
Explaining the packet size mismatch and how to check it
Choosing the connection design and a routing step
modelAnswer: Collect VPC flow logs (records of the IP traffic metadata that each network interface accepted or rejected) for the server and look for REJECT entries on the flows that carry large responses. Also check the server's security group and network ACL rules and its instance metrics for dropped packets. Use Reachability Analyzer, a tool that reads the configured route tables, security groups, network ACLs and gateways and reports whether a path exists or where it is blocked, without sending any packets.
