Flow logs show what actually happened on the wire; the analyzer shows what the configuration would allow. If the analyzer finds a complete path, the fault is more likely on the host or in packet size, not in routing.

MTU is the largest packet size a link can carry without the packet being split into smaller pieces. Standard Ethernet inside a VPC is 1500 bytes, while jumbo frames allow up to 9001 bytes, and every hop on a path must agree on a size the others can handle. If one segment has a smaller MTU than the sender assumes and the ICMP messages that tell the sender to shrink its packets are blocked, large packets are silently dropped while small packets still fit and succeed. Check the interface MTU on the reporting server and on the gateway path, confirm that security groups and network ACLs allow the ICMP fragmentation-needed messages, and test with pings of increasing size with the don't-fragment flag set to find where they start to fail.

Use Transit Gateway as the hub. Attach the two Region-one VPCs and the data center through a Direct Connect gateway, so each network connects once to the hub instead of to each other network. VPC peering would need a separate link for every pair, and peering does not pass traffic through a third network, so three VPCs plus the data center would need many links and routing entries that grow with each addition. Connect the disaster-recovery VPC in the second Region by peering the two transit gateways across Regions. For routing, summarize the data center's address ranges into one prefix that is advertised over BGP, so the transit gateway route table holds one entry for the site instead of many, which keeps the routes well within the route limits.

scenarios.title: Patient booking portal: inbound and internal controls at Harbor Lane Clinics
scenarios.scenario:
Harbor Lane Clinics is a fictional company that runs a patient booking portal. Customers reach a public web tier, which calls an application tier, which reads a database holding appointment and health-related records. The network follows a three-tier design: a public web tier, a private application tier, and a private database tier, each in its own subnets inside one virtual private cloud (VPC, an isolated private network in AWS). A threat model is a written list of what could go wrong with a design, who or what could cause it, and which control stops it. AWS WAF (a web application firewall, which inspects the content of HTTP requests against rules such as blocking known attack strings or limiting request rates) sits in front of the portal. AWS Shield (a service that absorbs denial-of-service floods, where many requests try to exhaust capacity; Shield Standard is on by default) protects against floods. Between tiers, security groups (stateful virtual firewalls attached to each resource: if a connection is allowed in one direction, its replies are allowed automatically) and network ACLs (stateless rules applied at the subnet boundary, where replies must be allowed explicitly) control traffic. VPC flow logs (records of connection metadata such as source, destination, port, byte count, and an ACCEPT or REJECT action, but not the payload) show what actually happened. Dana, the lead engineer, has asked you to help with next week's security review. Please answer the following.
1. Name two threats that follow from this architecture, one on the inbound path from the internet and one on traffic between the application tier and the database tier. For each, state one mitigation from the controls described above.
2. Explain why WAF and Shield do different jobs. Say which one you would rely on for a volume-based flood and which one you would rely on for an SQL injection attempt, and give a reason for each.
3. A flow log entry shows ACCEPT on port 5432 (the default port for the PostgreSQL database) from the web tier subnet to the database subnet. The web tier should never reach the database directly. Describe how you would confirm this and what configuration gap most likely explains it.
subParts: Two threats, one inbound and one internal, each with a mitigation
WAF versus Shield: which fits a flood and which fits SQL injection
Investigating an unexpected ACCEPT flow log entry to the database
modelAnswer: Inbound threat: SQL injection or automated scraping of the booking form, where an attacker sends crafted input to the web application. Mitigation: attach AWS WAF with a managed rule set that blocks common attack patterns, and add a rate-based rule that limits requests from a single source. Internal threat: a compromised application-tier server connecting to the database and reading records it has no business reading. Mitigation: the database security group allows the database port only from the application tier's security group, not from a broad address range; the network ACL on the database subnet acts as a coarse backstop. A common mistake is opening the database port to the whole VPC address range, which means any compromised host in any tier can read patient records. The consequence is that one weak web server becomes a path to the entire patient dataset.

WAF inspects the content of web requests at the application layer, so it matches patterns in URLs, headers, and bodies. It is the right tool for SQL injection because the attack is hidden in request content. Shield is designed to absorb floods that overwhelm network or transport capacity, so it is the right tool for a volume-based denial-of-service attack; Shield Standard is automatic, and Shield Advanced adds more protection and support. I would rely on Shield, supported by the scaling of the front end, for a flood, and on WAF rules for SQL injection. A common mistake is assuming Shield will stop SQL injection, or that WAF alone will absorb a very large flood. The consequence is that the attack type goes unmitigated: a flood can exhaust capacity even with WAF rules in place, and crafted requests can reach the application even with Shield active.

To confirm, I would first check the flow log record's interface and direction fields to make sure the entry describes the connection I think it does, then review the security groups on the database instances and the web tier, and the network ACLs on both subnets. I would look for a database security group rule that references the web tier's security group or a CIDR range that includes the web subnet, and for a network ACL that allows port 5432 between these subnets. The most likely gap is a database security group rule that points at the wrong source, such as a broad address range or the web tier group, which was added for a past test. The fix is to allow the database port only from the application tier's security group, remove the web tier rule, and then confirm in the flow logs that new connections from the web subnet are REJECT or absent. I would also use CloudTrail (a log of API calls recording who changed what and when) to find when the rule was added and by whom, so the review can record the change.
